articles.text:
Following a string of incidents where AI models hacked websites and breached government systems during testing phases, the Federal Trade Commission is officially probing Anthropic and OpenAI over consumer harms, an insider told Axios.
On Wednesday, the FTC sent out civil investigative demands seeking a wide range of information from the AI firms on recent safety incidents.
The FTC did not respond to Ars’ request to review the subpoena demands. However, Axios’ source said the requests spanned more than 50 pages of questions and sought documents related to the incidents, internal security measures taken, and marketing materials that may suggest consumers were misled.

articles.title: “Memory-Centric Server Systems Are the Future”: SK hynix Presents Its Next-Generation AI Infrastructure Vision at OCP Global Summit 2026
articles.text:
As the volume of data handled by AI grows explosively, data bottlenecks have emerged as a new challenge. Can next-generation memory technology offer the solution? There is now an opportunity to hear SK hynix’s answer to this question.
SK hynix took part in OCP Global Summit 2026, held from the 12th to the 15th in San Jose, California, where it unveiled a wide range of next-generation memory solutions and presented the direction memory technology should take in the AI era.
OCP Global Summit is a technology conference for sharing and standardizing the design and specifications of data center hardware. This year, with the infrastructure technologies that will underpin the advancement of AI emerging as a central theme, the new server system proposed by SK hynix drew considerable attention. SK hynix demonstrated the next-generation solutions it is preparing for servers at the actual system level, proving their feasibility and once again affirming its technological leadership.
Proposing a Next-Generation Server System Based on ‘CXL Pooled Memory’… Confirming the Benefits Through Live Demos
▲ SK hynix’s exhibition booth
With a booth concept that balanced a sturdy gray frame with neon-blue lighting, SK hynix gave visual form to ‘reliability’ and ‘efficiency’—the core values of its next-generation memory solutions. The exhibition space was divided into front and rear sections. At the front, a ‘Memory Section’ showcasing the company’s current flagship products captured visitors’ attention, while the spacious ‘System Demo’ section at the rear allowed visitors to take a closer look at the SK hynix memory solutions that will make up the next-generation server ecosystem.
▲ Visitors touring the ‘System Demo’ section
The ‘System Demo’ section introduced three solutions in sequence, from left to right: CMM-DDR5, MARS, and CMM-Ax. CMM (CXL* Memory Module)-DDR5 is a memory solution that improves resource utilization efficiency by having multiple servers share a memory pool and use as much of it as they need, based on the CXL interface standard. At this exhibition, SK hynix unveiled its second-generation product (256GB), optimized for AI workloads and based on CXL 3.2. Compared with the previous generation, the product more than doubles bandwidth (80GB/s) and improves energy efficiency by about 30%. With CXL Pooled functionality also applied, it is drawing attention as a next-generation memory product that will effectively resolve bottlenecks in data-intensive, high-load environments.
* CXL (Compute eXpress Link): A next-generation solution that efficiently connects CPUs, GPUs, memory, and other components within a computing system to support large-capacity, ultra-high-speed computation. Based on the PCIe interface, it offers fast data transfer and provides a pooling function that uses memory efficiently.
▲ Visitors examining the CMM-DDR5 product
In September last year, SK hynix signed a business agreement with NAVER Cloud and has since been working jointly to resolve bottlenecks in cloud AI services using CXL-based memory solutions. At this demo, the company presented the results of validating—at the PoC* level—whether a KV cache*-sharing solution in an agentic AI* environment and an embedding-sharing solution in ‘OmniServe’, an omni-modal* service, actually work. Having analyzed real customer systems and workloads to confirm the applicability of its CXL-based solutions, SK hynix has laid the groundwork for a full-scale expansion of these solutions.
* Agentic AI: AI that sets its own goals and carries out multi-step tasks without user instructions.
* KV Cache (Key Value Cache): Temporary memory that stores previously computed results when a large language model-based AI agent generates text. It grows exponentially the longer a conversation becomes and the more tasks there are to process, so the ability to store and process it efficiently has a major impact on an AI agent’s performance.
* Omni-Modal: An approach that processes multiple forms of data—such as text, images, and voice—together within a single model.
* PoC (Proof of Concept): A stage that verifies whether a new technology or concept actually works.
▲ Visitors reviewing information about MARS
MARS (Memory Centric AI Rack System) is a next-generation system that maximizes efficiency by integrating partners’ solutions into a single rack*, with memory at its core. At this exhibition, SK hynix presented three demos together with several partners.
* Rack: A standard-sized frame used in data centers to stack servers, storage, network equipment, and other devices in layers. Because equipment is managed in rack units, the rack serves as the basic building block of data center infrastructure.
▲ A demonstration of AI agent serving technology using CXL pooled memory
In the AI agent serving demo, SK hynix—together with Arcee, Liqid, and Marvell—demonstrated a system that connects multiple servers and GPUs using pooled memory*. Through this, the company proved that transferring or reusing a KV cache based on CXL pooled memory significantly improves system performance compared with conventional methods that rely on network communication.
* Pooled Memory: Technology that groups multiple CXL memory units into a pool and raises overall memory utilization by allowing several hosts to effectively share its capacity.
▲ A demonstration of AI agent serving technology using CXL hybrid memory
In a demo conducted with AMD, Penguin, Xcena, and Arcee, SK hynix showed the effectiveness of a memory rack using CXL memory and CXL hybrid memory*. The results confirmed that the memory rack can efficiently store and rapidly reuse the large-scale KV caches that are continuously generated. In particular, the demo clearly showed two capabilities: quickly predicting which KV caches will be needed based on prior conversation and task history, and loading the required KV caches into DRAM in advance for fast processing. It also proved that, by storing the full KV cache on an SSD, the rack can deliver both fast read performance and high-capacity storage at the same time.
* CXL Hybrid Memory: A CXL-based hybrid memory solution that combines DRAM and SSD.
▲ A demonstration of technology that reduces service response latency using pooled memory
With Pickle, a personal AI agent service provider, SK hynix carried out a demo that reduces service response latency using pooled memory. The demonstration confirmed that streaming based on pooled memory can accelerate the data transfers between the multiple AI models essential to a personal AI agent, so that final results reach users more quickly.
▲ A demonstration of Efficient Long Context LLM Serving technology
CMM-Ax is a next-generation memory solution that combines computation functions with memory. By performing computations directly inside the memory, without moving data, it can reduce the power and cost burden on data centers. At this exhibition, through a demo of its next-generation AI inference system, ‘Efficient Long Context* LLM* Serving’, SK hynix showed that CMM-Ax can efficiently accelerate the long contexts that have been difficult to process on conventional GPU-based systems. The research behind these achievements was also officially recognized for its technical excellence, having been published to ‘MICRO 2026’, the most prestigious academic conference in the field of computer architecture.
* Long Context: The range of text that AI can process at once is defined as its context. The longer the context, the more information AI can reference at once to generate refined answers—but this also requires more memory capacity.
* LLM (Large Language Model): An AI model that learns from big data to generate and understand natural, human-like sentences. By greatly increasing the scale of its parameters, it acquires advanced language-processing capabilities such as complex context comprehension, reasoning, and translation.
Sharing Its Product Portfolio from HBM to HBF, … The Present and Future of Memory Technology in One Place
The Memory Section was arranged so that visitors could see the flagship products with which SK hynix is currently leading the memory market. In the product portfolio exhibition space at the far left, a lineup of products for AI infrastructure—spanning eSSDs and server DRAM—was on display.
▲ SK hynix’s main eSSD products
▲ SK hynix’s main server DRAM products
The eSSD lineup presented products with different uses tailored to diverse customer needs, organized by form factor: the high-performance ‘PS1010 U.2’; the high-performance ‘PS1110 E3.S’ and high-capacity ‘PS1101 E3.S’ currently under sequential development; and the ‘PEB210 E1.S’ and ‘PEB210 M.2 2280’, which support Direct Liquid Cooling (DLC) and are drawing attention as eSSDs for data centers.
For server DRAM, SK hynix introduced a DDR5 RDIMM lineup in a range of capacities—led by the ‘256GB 3DS* RDIMM*’, which delivers the industry’s largest capacity for AI workloads, and extending to 96GB and 64GB. Alongside the 128GB DDR5 MRDIMM*, it also exhibited the ‘192GB SOCAMM*2’, which improves power and space efficiency with a new form factor.
* 3DS (3D Stacked Memory): High-performance memory that connects two or more DRAM chips with TSVs (through-silicon vias).
* RDIMM (Registered Dual In-line Memory Module): A server module that combines multiple DRAM chips.
* MRDIMM (Multiplexed Rank Dual In-line Memory Module): A product in which two ranks—the basic operating unit of a module—operate simultaneously, dramatically improving speed.
* SOCAMM (Small Outline Compression Attached Memory Module): A low-power DRAM-based memory module specialized for AI servers.
▲ A touchscreen where visitors can check product information
SK hynix also set up a touchscreen model resembling an actual server, allowing visitors to check detailed product information.
▲ A visitor mounting SK hynix’s HBM4 product onto NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin model
The HBM* exhibition space in the center was designed so that visitors could take in both SK hynix’s HBM technology leadership and its solid partnership with NVIDIA at a glance. On the left side of the display, a model of NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin superchip highlighted the partnership between the two companies, while visitors could mount HBM4 and SOCAMM2 onto a server model themselves. On the right stood an HBM model magnified one million times, with an accompanying monitor playing a video on TSV* and Advanced MR-MUF*—the core technologies behind HBM. Between the two models, the actual HBM4E, HBM4, and HBM3 products were placed so that visitors could see firsthand how HBM products have evolved from generation to generation.
* HBM (High Bandwidth Memory): A high-value-added, high-performance product that connects multiple DRAM chips vertically to increase capacity and dramatically raise data processing speed. HBM has been developed in the following order: 1st generation (HBM) – 2nd generation (HBM2) – 3rd generation (HBM2E) – 4th generation (HBM3) – 5th generation (HBM3E) – 6th generation (HBM4) – 7th generation (HBM4E).
* TSV (Through Silicon Via): Technology that connects chips vertically through electrodes that pass straight through the silicon substrate.
* Advanced MR-MUF: A next-generation MR-MUF technology that applies warpage control—a chip-control technology that stacks chips 40% thinner than conventional chips without bending—and also improves heat dissipation.
▲ A model showing the structure of HBF
HBF (High Bandwidth Flash) is a next-generation NAND solution that, like HBM, applies TSV technology to combine the high capacity of conventional storage with high bandwidth. As the inference-centric agentic AI era unfolds, it is drawing attention as a key technology for efficiently handling the surging data usage of AI. On the left side of the display stood a model showing the structure of HBF, with a banner introducing its detailed specifications to its right. On an accompanying monitor and tablet, SK hynix introduced the key features of HBF, along with the respective strengths of HBM and HBF across different AI inference service environments, through videos and performance graphs based on internal simulations. It showed that HBM’s high-speed processing can be leveraged in environments where fast response times are critical, while HBF’s high-capacity characteristics can be leveraged in environments that require large-capacity memory to serve many users.
▲ A graphic conveying SK hynix’s vision, located on the outer wall of the booth
Meanwhile, a graphic conveying the company’s vision of providing optimized solutions across the entire memory hierarchy was displayed on the right wall of the booth. Beneath the journey from developing the world’s first HBM in 2013 to achieving its current technological leadership, the latest products and technology development status in each of the HBM, DRAM, and NAND fields were also introduced.
“We Will Break Through Technological Limits with a Memory-Centric, Next-Generation AI Rack System”
▲ Vice President Hosik Kim, head of the Memory Systems Research department, during his presentation
Alongside the exhibition, the presentation sessions also heightened expectations for memory-centric server systems. First, in the ‘Executive’ session held on the afternoon of the first day, Vice President Hosik Kim, head of the Memory Systems Research, took the stage as a speaker and gave a presentation titled ‘Introduction to Memory-centric AI Rack Systems (MARS)’.
Vice President Kim first noted that, as generative AI and hyperscale data centers grow rapidly, conventional CPU- and GPU-centric architectures face a bottleneck known as the ‘memory wall’ along with sharply rising power consumption. He then presented a ‘memory-centric AI rack system’ as the solution.
“This system implements rack-level memory pooling and dynamic zero-copy data sharing by connecting CPUs and GPUs with next-generation CXL technology,” he explained, “and it is structured to significantly increase the speed of data movement in high-load workloads.” He added, “By leveraging this, we can improve the KV cache reuse efficiency of collaborative agentic AI, accelerate the response speed of the multimodal omni model in personal agentic AI services, and solve the irregular memory access problems that arise in large-scale GNN* training.”
* GNN (Graph Neural Network): An AI model that learns from graph-structured data connected by nodes and edges. It is used in fields where the relationships between data are important, such as social networks, molecular structures, and recommendation systems.
▲ Vice President Youngpyo Joo, head of the System Architecture department, taking part in the panel discussion
In addition, Vice President Youngpyo Joo, head of the System Architecture, took part in a panel discussion held on the afternoon of the third day. Conducted under the theme of “Integrating SW frameworks and APIs across companies for PIM/PNM,” the panel discussed the importance of the SW framework that connects customers and products within an ecosystem where multiple companies are intertwined in both competition and cooperation, and it also addressed the need for standardization in this area.
▲ Team Leader Jongryool Kim of AI System Infra during his presentation
▲ Technical Leader Younghoon Min of AI System Infra during his presentation
▲ Technical Leader Juhee Lee of AI Platform SW during her presentation

articles.title: Whose Data, Whose Benchmark? A User-Centric Framework for Auditing Evaluation Resources
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19268v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Benchmarks shape how model capabilities are measured and interpreted, yet their scores can obscure whose conventions, contexts, and judgments define successful performance. We introduce a user-centric audit framework that distinguishes users who contribute benchmark content from those whose needs evaluation results are intended to represent. The framework operationalizes seven dimensions across benchmark content, metadata, documentation, and scoring procedures. Across 16 resources, we find that American-centered conventions account for 62.4-94.4% of matched signals in 11 text benchmarks, while geographic visibility in five image-text resources is concentrated and strongly associated with national GDP share (mean Pearson r = 0.780; Spearman p = 0.778). Documentation reveals a systematic source-target gap: all 16 resources operationalize source-user context, but none operationalize target-user context. Paired scoring experiments further show that meaning-preserving answer variants reduce DROP exact-match accuracy from 100.0% to 33.3%, while TruthfulQA exhibits metric-dependent reductions in reference similarity. Our framework and documentation checklist make user assumptions auditable, clarifying what benchmark scores represent and where evaluation claims are supported.

articles.title: PersEvalBench: Can LLM Evaluators Judge Contextually Appropriate Use of Persona Information?
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19314v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) evaluators are increasingly used to assess personalized assistants, yet whether they can reliably judge personalization has rarely been tested. We introduce PersEvalBench, a benchmark testing whether an evaluator can recognize appropriate and inappropriate uses of user history. It contains 403 multi-episode scenarios where user information should persist, transfer, or cease to apply. The benchmark covers nine controlled error subtypes across three families: under-personalization, over-personalization, and misapplied-state errors. Human audits confirm that generated errors match their intended types and that the prescribed uses of user information are reasonable.
Across five LLM evaluators, recognition of controlled personalization errors remains limited even with the full dialogue history. On the human-evaluated subset, under-personalization shows the largest gap: humans recognize 94.4% of these errors, compared with 63.9% for the strongest reported evaluator. Evaluators often recognize that a response is problematic but reverse the error direction, mistaking failure to follow an applicable preference (UNDER) for use of an inapplicable preference (OVER). Easier evidence access offers little help: highlighting the relevant history turns raises error recognition only slightly, suggesting that the remaining difficulty lies in judging what role that information should play in the response.

articles.text:
As OpenAI has jockeyed with Anthropic to win over developers with new models and tools this year, its advertising business at times has seemed like an afterthought. Not anymore.
Over the last few months, the company has unleashed a flurry of new products and tools to court advertisers, even as it has cut ad rates. That’s helped lure a lot more advertisers, new data show. The company has also gone on a hiring spree. Nearly half of the roughly 140 OpenAI employees working on ads joined between July and September, according to Crustdata, which tracks employees’ public profiles. Meta Platforms, where ad chief Dave Dugan spent 12 years, is the biggest source of talent.

articles.title: ForkGRPO: Efficient Exploration and Fine-Grained Credit Assignment for Diffusion Language Models
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19408v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. However, independently generating every rollout from the input prompt can leave alternative continuations from intermediate states underexplored, while trajectory-level advantages assign uniform credit to all tokens without distinguishing the contributions of individual reasoning segments. We propose ForkGRPO, an RL framework that couples efficient exploration with fine-grained segment-level credit assignment. It samples multiple continuations from high-entropy intermediate states along a reference trajectory, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes. The continuations provide complementary learning signals: within-state group-relative advantages guide which continuations to reinforce, while Monte Carlo state-value differences indicate which reasoning segments improve expected outcomes. Among the evaluated architecture-preserving RL methods, ForkGRPO achieves the best performance on three of four benchmarks, while improving over the directly comparable JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points and using up to 27.8% fewer generated tokens. ForkGRPO-Fast further achieves a $2.49\times$ training wall-clock speedup with negligible accuracy loss.

articles.title: How Do LLMs Understand Legal Philosophy? Diagnosing Legal-Philosophical Reasoning in LLMs
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19427v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Legal reasoning is a fundamental capability for large language models (LLMs) to complete legal AI tasks such as legal judgment prediction. In legal practice, this reasoning is shaped by legal philosophy: a judge's view of the nature and sources of law guides how legal materials are interpreted and applied, so judges working from the same statutes and precedents can reach different judgments. Existing research has largely overlooked whether LLMs can understand legal philosophy and apply it in legal reasoning, an ability we call \textit{legal-philosophical reasoning}. To fill this gap, we introduce LePhilBench, a benchmark for evaluating the legal-philosophical reasoning of LLMs that comprises two benchmarking tasks and a dataset. The two tasks evaluate how well LLMs understand legal philosophy and how well they apply it in legal reasoning, respectively. The dataset is manually and meticulously constructed. Its test set contains 220 U.S. Supreme Court opinions. A law professor designed fourteen annotation questions on legal philosophy, and three law-trained annotators with formal training in jurisprudence answered all fourteen questions for every opinion, yielding 9,240 legal-philosophical labels. LePhilBench takes the first step toward exploring legal-philosophical reasoning in LLMs.

articles.title: PA1-OPD: One-Step Prefix-Augmented On-Policy Distillation for Language Model Pretraining
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19601v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) improves language-model pretraining by matching teacher distributions at corpus prefixes, but provides no direct supervision at contexts induced by student predictions. We introduce PA1-OPD, which augments corpus-path distillation with teacher feedback after one student-sampled transition per selected prefix. This expands the supervised states while retaining next-token prediction and corpus-path KD. Data-anchored roots support parallel sampling, and differentiable tree attention shares prefix computation without changing inference. In two continued-pretraining settings, full coverage improves held-out cross-entropy over KD across C4, PG-19, and Pile at every evaluated checkpoint. In Stage2, selecting the 10% of roots with highest student surprisal adds 48.85% to KD's Macro cross-entropy gain over next-token training. Gains remain when branch supervision excludes successor states already on the corpus path, supporting the value of feedback beyond observed contexts. Additional depth or breadth improves aggregate results at unchanged per-term supervision weight, with benefits varying by corpus. These findings support local student-induced supervision as a complement to pretraining distillation.

articles.title: ASML Is Building a Hybrid Bonding Tool!
articles.text:
ASML has not announced anything yet, but its patent filings, a news report and its own roadmap all suggest so. We believe it will start with a die-to-wafer (D2W) hybrid bonding (HB) tool. This is harder to build than wafer-to-wafer but is where ASML could gain an edge. We see the move as a natural extension of ASML’s vertical integration, and one that should strengthen its customer ties.
In this article we unpack the tool’s design end to end, starting with patent filings. What makes it unique is that it runs on a track. That changes how the tool and the dies move: each die rides its own holder past the process stations, and the tools get closer at each station to process the dies. The track’s independent shuttles also lift station utilization, save on duplicate tooling, and enable heterogeneous integration.
We believe ASML could gain an edge in alignment accuracy and particle control for Hybrid Bonding. These are the two factors that set bonding yield. And ASML has expertise in solving the same problems in lithography.
Despite the advantages, ASML still needs to solve challenges around feed-forward metrology, the die-to-wafer contact, the modification of the non-bonding tools so they can process dies on the track, and keeping the whole loop clean.
We expect advanced logic, where D2W already runs in volume, to adopt ASML’s D2W HB tool first. This is bad news for Besi. Logic accounts for most of Besi’s HB business today concentrated at TSMC and Intel. ASML has been working with both for more than two decades and just announced a joint photomask initiative in September. We won’t be surprised to see a similar move in the back end process. Besi’s HBM prospects are also weakening. Korean challengers are catching up, in addition to an HBM adoption that we expect to slip to 2029 or beyond.
ASML is Building a Hybrid Bonder
We did a deep dive on hybrid bonding in 2024, and we still see it as the most transformative innovation in semiconductor manufacturing since EUV. Wafer-to-wafer (W2W) hybrid bonding (HB) is already in volume in image sensors and 3D NAND, and DRAM makers will be next. Die-to-wafer (D2W) HB is moving slower, because the industry still lacks mature tools that combine satisfying alignment accuracy and throughput (our check indicates upper bound in current applications is only one wafer per hour), which keeps cost per die high. Today D2W runs in volume only in logic: AMD has shipped hybrid-bonded V-Cache since 2022, and TSMC’s SoIC bonds at about 6um pitch today and targets 4.5um around 2029. The market expected HBM to become the big D2W volume driver from 2028. However, our view is different: we believe HBM will not adopt D2W HB before 2029, if at all.
Besi has led D2W and is the only supplier with tools in volume production. Everyone else is still trying to get a first tool qualified. But we believe the situation will soon change, because ASML is building a D2W hybrid bonding tool. Management hasn’t announced anything yet. But the company filed 27 bonding patent families between December 2022 and November 2024, most of them D2W, and the true count is likely higher because filings made after November 2024 are not yet public. The Elec also reported in March that ASML had started the architecture design of a hybrid bonder with Prodrive Technologies and VDL ETG.
In the anchor filing (WO2025201788A1), ASML drew how its bonding flow works. Interestingly, the system looks nothing like a traditional D2W bonder (see Advanced Packaging Part 5 for how those work). Instead of a bond head picking each die off a diced wafer and placing it, ASML moves single dies on independent holders around a track (Fig 1). Each die passes inspection, cleaning, plasma activation and metrology (topography, leveling and alignment) stations before it reaches the bonding station where the chuck lifts the bottom wafer up to meet the die. We unpack the design in the sections below.
Fig 1: ASML’s track-based D2W bonder, SA annotated and simplified
Source: ASML; SemiAnalysis Wafer Fabrication Equipment Model
ASML could be building a W2W hybrid bonding tool as well. According to a patent analysis by Inha University, ASML is likely building W2W HB equipment on its TWINSCAN platform, leaning on its wafer overlay accuracy. We focus on the D2W machine in this note, because it is the harder tool to build and the one where ASML could gain a real edge.
…as Part of its Vertical Integration Initiative
We believe this is a continuation of ASML’s effort to integrate vertically and tighten customer relationships. ASML bought Cymer for its light source in 2013, HMI for e-beam inspection in 2016 and Berliner Glas for optics modules in 2020. It shipped its first back-end product, the XT:260 i-line packaging scanner, in 3Q25. And most recently, ASML announced joint initiatives with TSMC, Intel Foundry and Samsung to move the industry from 6-inch to 12-inch photomasks for High NA EUV.
Building a bonder would be a natural next step. In fact, ASML’s own roadmap already puts bonding inside the front-end flow. Its 2024 Investor Day listed W2W and D2W hybrid bonding for NAND, DRAM and logic (Fig 2). And a July 2024 filing shows how the bonder and the scanner would work together by sharing die position data. Today a scanner printing on a bonded wafer must pre-align and coarse-align every die before it can expose. In ASML’s design the bonder already knows where it put each die and hands that map (a “coordinate system” in the filing) to the scanner, which checks a few marks and exposes. Customers get faster lithography on bonded wafers, and ASML gets to sell the bonder and the scanner as a pair.
Fig 2: ASML’s map of front-end 3D integration
Source: ASML Investor Day, 14-Nov-2024
We expect advanced logic to be the first adopter. Logic is where D2W HB already runs in volume, and where the alignment requirement keeps tightening. TSMC calls overlay “always the biggest challenge” for SoIC. As its HB pitch moves from 6um to 4.5um by 2029, the placement accuracy requirement will tighten further. ASML is strong in alignment, as we will elaborate below, so an edge here should help it win logic customers first. Advanced logic dies are also among the most expensive chips, so logic customers can afford a premium tool. We expect ASML to price its tools at a premium to peers.
In the next three sections, we discuss (1) the tool’s track system - the most unusual thing about it compared with what is on the market; (2) how ASML’s strengths in alignment, particle control and motion could make its HB tool superior; and (3) the challenges ASML or its supply chain partners still need to resolve to build a working tool. Let’s dive in.
What’s Unique About the Tool
One of the most interesting things about the tool is that it runs on a track. ASML names SuperTrak CONVEYANCE (Fig 3) as an example in its patent filing, so we assume it uses that track and we base our analysis on the track’s published design.
The fundamental difference from a traditional bonder is where the die lives. In a Besi-type tool, the die is prepared elsewhere, and a bond head picks it up only for the final placement. In ASML’s design, each die sits on its own holder from the moment it leaves the carrier and stays there until the bonding step. The process stations are built around the track: the die stops in front of a station, the station cleans, activates or measures it in place, and the die moves on.
Fig 3: SuperTrak CONVEYANCE track (HORIZON10 platform)
Source: Company website
Now let’s go through the process step by step. For illustration, we took the patent drawing and labelled every station in Fig 4. A gripper takes the die off its carrier and sets it on an empty substrate holder (206), which carries it along the track (202). The die stops in turn at the inspection, cleaning, plasma activation, topographic inspection, leveling, coarse alignment, position adjustment and fine alignment stations (210 to 226). At each stop the die stays on its holder, and the station does its work. Note the reversal here: in the patent it is the station’s sensor or head that moves in to reach the die, not the die that is carried into the tool as in today’s flow. After these steps the die arrives at the bonding station (228).
This bonding station deserves a closer look. The first thing to note is that the final placement is done by the holder (206) and the chuck (234), not the track: SuperTrak’s spec sheet puts the shuttles’ repeatability at about 10um, nowhere near the 50nm placement accuracy the bond needs. Next, zoom in on the right-hand part of Fig 4 for the bonding work. The chuck lifts the bottom wafer to within tens of microns of the die, the holder’s actuators adjust the die’s position, the die is pressed onto the wafer to form the bond, and the holder releases it. The empty holder then starts another loop.
Fig 4: Patent WO2025201788A1 Fig. 2 (left) and Fig. 6 side view (right), SA annotated
Source: ASML; SemiAnalysis Wafer Fabrication Equipment Model
This design has three major benefits:
First, independent shuttles lift the utilization of every station. The number of stations per step can be set from that step’s cycle time: a three-second cleaning step gets three stations, and a 1.2-second bond step gets one, so every station stays busy. The patent asks for exactly this, to “occupy all process stations simultaneously”.
Second, capacity is added by adding a station rather than a second tool, as long as the equipment chamber has room for it. That saves duplicate tooling and budget.
Last but not least, the design suits heterogeneous integration: a new die type is a new software recipe, so mixed chiplets could share one line.
That said, the track brings its own challenges around the non-bonding stations and the cleanliness of the whole loop. We come back to them later.
How ASML May Gain an Edge
Before that, let’s look at how ASML could bring its existing strengths to the HB tool.
First, a reminder of why alignment accuracy and cleanliness matter so much in hybrid bonding. As we elaborated before, a single 1um particle between two full-thickness wafers can unbond an area around 10mm across, resulting in a defective bond (Fig 5). So particle control is extremely important for HB. Alignment matters for two reasons: placement accuracy sets bond yield directly, and alignment time weighs far more on D2W throughput than on W2W because it compounds with the die count. These two hurdles are what make hybrid bonding almost a front-end process.
Fig 5: A small particle opens a void and an open contact in hybrid bonding
Source: SemiAnalysis
We believe ASML can tackle both with decades of experience solving the same two problems in lithography.
For alignment, we believe ASML can reuse its wafer-alignment sensor technology. Based on its patent filings, the bonding system puts a tiny diffraction grating on each die and reads the die’s position from the light the grating scatters. The principle is the same as ORION, the wafer-alignment sensor on every new TWINSCAN since 2017. ORION was built to read marks that CMP and etch have tilted or deformed (Fig 6), and a mark on a bonding die goes through the same CMP and plasma activation as the copper pads next to it, so it carries the same asymmetry. We believe the same sensor family can serve the D2W bonder.
Fig 6: A symmetric and a tilted alignment mark. Process steps shift the apparent center; ORION’s multi-color readout was built to see through that
Source: ASML, Aligning lithography to the nanometer, Dec-2021
Its sensing and motion capabilities also provide it with more room in total alignment error budget. Its NXT:2100i holds 0.9nm overlay on a single machine. And ASML can already measure the distortion of a W2W bonded wafer and correct the next lithography layer for it, bringing post-bond overlay from 40-60nm down to below 4nm (Fig 7). These are litho numbers, not bond results. But they mean ASML’s sensor and stage errors sit more than an order of magnitude below the 50nm a bonder needs. Higher stage precision leaves more room in a bonder’s error budget for the other factors: die shift on the holder, thermal drift and movement during contact.
Fig 7: ASML metrology plus scanner correction brings post-bond overlay to 2.5-3.9nm
Source: ASML Investor Day, 14-Nov-2024
Prodrive Technologies and VDL ETG are the likely component suppliers to help ASML’s bonder move fast on motion. Prodrive makes the linear motors and drives for ASML’s EUV maglev stages and has also built Hanwha Semitech’s SHB2 Nano bonder. VDL ETG builds ASML’s frames and modules (Fig 8).
Fig 8: Prodrive’s linear motor (left) and VDL ETG’s wafer handler module (right)
Source: Company websites
On cleanliness, the requirements for ASML’s EUV systems are more strict as a bonder’s. Few tool makers have fought particles at the nanometer scale for as long as ASML. EUV scanners move reticles and wafers in vacuum and keep reticle particle adders at a level “compatible with HVM requirements for sub-10nm node lithography”. We believe ASML has thought about the bonding surfaces too: its bonding apparatus filing adds a tool that cleans the substrate supports and a sensor that watches their flatness, particle load and distortion.
That said, contaminants in a bonder differ from those in a scanner. Most are dicing debris on die edges and particles landing on freshly activated, hydrophilic surfaces. We look for more detail on how ASML handles these bonder-specific contaminants in future filings.
After the paywall we discuss the challenges ASML needs to tackle to build a working tool, and how its tool will impact on Besi’s business prospects.

articles.title: Towards Efficient Simultaneous Inverse Text Normalization with Pretrained Text-to-Text Language Model and Read-Tag-Write Policy
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19492v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Streaming Inverse Text Normalization (ITN) is vital for converting spoken-form outputs from streaming Automatic Speech Recognition into formatted written text. Existing streaming ITN methods rely on hybrid systems combining neural tagging with expert-crafted finite-state transducer rules, limiting scalability across domains and languages. While end-to-end models offer superior scalability by learning directly from data, standard encoder-decoder architectures are inherently non-streaming due to global attention. In this paper, we propose an efficient streaming end-to-end ITN system, adapting a pretrained text-to-text model to leverage its robust linguistic knowledge. To enable streaming, we introduce architectural adaptations, a specialized training strategy, a Read-Tag-Write decoding policy, and inference optimizations. Experiments on Vietnamese datasets show accuracy comparable to non-streaming baselines, outperforming hybrid methods while satisfying real-time latency requirements.

articles.title: Evidence-Anchored Overdose Death Prediction from Death Investigation Reports
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19556v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Confirmation of overdose deaths in the United States is often delayed due to the complexities of certifying drug-involved deaths. Death investigation reports represent a rich but underutilized data source that could be used to predict whether a death is a suspected overdose (i.e., a death preliminarily identified as an overdose prior to the final cause and manner of death determination). We present an automated framework that classifies suspected overdoses from death investigation reports, while producing supporting explanations guided by expert knowledge. Through an expert-guided design process, we investigate 1) what type of explanations are best for model prediction performance, and 2) which architecture is better suited for this task: pipeline models that rationalize first and then predict, or self-rationalizing models that jointly predict and rationalize? Our experiments show that a pipeline model with explanations grounded in the input death investigation reports outperforms the other settings. Our best model also outperforms a rule-based system currently in deployment by 15%, while allowing expert interventions for final decisions.

articles.title: LLM-jp-4 Technical Report
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19331v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: This paper presents LLM-jp-4, a family of Japanese sovereign large language models (LLMs) developed with an emphasis on transparency, reproducibility, and practical usability. LLM-jp-4 comprises an 8B dense model and a 32B-A3B mixture-of-experts model, both trained from scratch on approximately 12 trillion tokens. To support independent verification and reproduction, we establish explicit criteria for selecting training data, external models, and software, and make the development process publicly available. Evaluation results demonstrate substantial improvements over previous LLM-jp models and competitive performance against open-weight models of similar scale. By documenting the development principles, training procedures, and empirical findings of LLM-jp-4, we aim to provide a reference for future sovereign AI development.

"We expanded our capacity consideration to see outside Arizona, whether we can get another chance to expand our capacity," said C.C. Wei during the company's earnings call with financial analysts and investors. "Texas is one [of our options]. We sent the teams to Texas to do all the evaluation.  We also talked to one of our customers, who is trying to build a fab, Terafab, let me be more specific."
Recently in transpired that Elon Musk's Terafab was in talks with TSMC over using the giant semiconductor production facility together. Elon Musk confirmed the negotiations, whereas TSMC did not comment.
"We are discussing with them to see whether we can be utilizing that actual capacity also," Wei added. "So, we are still in discussion. If we have any solid conclusion, we will share with you."
The information about negotiations between Elon Musk's Terafab and TSMC immediately triggered chatter that the parties are set to adopt TSMC's typical business model it uses for ESMC and JASM facilities under which it operates fabs co-owned with other investors. However, Musk then said that Terafab's facility would be operated by Terafab and TSMC could only sub-lease part of its cleanroom. Now, C.C. Wei said that if TSMC joins the project, it will insist on operating the fab.
"We are still in discussion," Wei replied when asked whether TSMC is not becoming a part of the Terafab project. "Let me say that. […] Either way, it will be possible, but the fab has to be run by TSMC."
The key question now is whether Musk and TSMC can agree on an arrangement that satisfies both parties. Musk wants Terafab to retain control of its manufacturing complex, whereas TSMC insists on operating any fab it uses. One potential compromise would be for Terafab to own the facility and lease a portion of it to TSMC, which would independently operate its production lines. Such an arrangement would allow Musk to retain ownership of the whole complex while giving TSMC control over select manufacturing lines. However, if Terafab itself uses Intel's 14A process technology at the facility, TSMC's presence there will be extremely complicated, if possible at all. In any case, so far the parties have not come to any agreement.

articles.title: DUALVIEW: Leveraging Broad and Output-Specific Evidence for LLM-based Multi-Output Text Regression
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19206v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: While work on LLM-based regression has largely focused on scalar prediction, multi-output text regression remains less explored. We present DualView, a parameter-efficient approach to leverage LLMs for multi-output text regression. \method{} first extracts broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM, then uses a dual-branch architecture to produce the full score vector. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs (up to 122B), DualView outperforms seven supervised regression baselines while requiring 82--1842 times fewer fitted parameters than the three strongest baselines. These improvements extend across individual output dimensions and persist even with limited training data. Notably, DualView using a smaller open-weight LLM can outperform unsupervised prediction with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Controlled ablations show that broad and output-specific evidence provide complementary predictive benefits, while lightweight shared predictors achieve strong performance with fewer trainable parameters.

articles.title: How to Evaluate When You Don't Know How to Evaluate? Choosing Reliable Setups for Base Language Model Benchmarking
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19185v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Evaluation of large language models (LLMs) remains largely pre-scientific: it involves many design decisions, with little guidance on how to make them. These choices can substantially affect measured performance and, consequently, decisions about subsequent pretraining. To identify effective evaluation setups, we investigate 8 aspects, such as task formulation or the number of in-context examples. We compare the setups using three widely-used signal criteria, repurposed as normative meta-measures: monotonicity, non-randomness, and ranking consistency of the evaluation scores across intermediate checkpoints. In an early pretraining scenario, we evaluate these setups on 26 monolingual 2B-parameter models trained on different types of data, using 80 tasks in four languages. We also examine the setups on three larger LLMs ($\geq$7B) in the same four languages and explore how the preferred setups change with model scale. Our results yield concrete recommendations: some choices, such as the use of multiple prompts, are consistently useful, whereas others, such as task formulation, depend on model scale. More generally, our framework serves as a recipe for the choice of evaluation setups in new scenarios.

articles.title: Sipeed reveals Chinese-made DGX Spark and Ryzen AI Halo rival, expected to cost $3,999
articles.text:
A Chinese rival to the DGX Spark and the Ryzen AI Halo, at least on paper, has emerged with Sipeed’s announcement of the MaixStation. The system, built on Axera’s new AX8860P, is in the same memory class with 128GB of LPDDR5X on a 256-bit bus at 273 GB/s. Sipeed told Tom’s Hardware Premium it expects the 128GB model to cost around $3,999, with launch discounts on Kickstarter, putting it level with the 128GB Ryzen AI Halo and well under the DGX Spark’s current MSRP of $6,950. Sign-ups are open now on Sipeed’s MaixStation page ahead of a Kickstarter campaign at the end of the year, with units shipping within three months after it closes. The NPU toolchain is due by the end of this month.
Coming today! Beat DGX Spark!MaixStation soon～ https://t.co/e7DvWweVntOctober 13, 2026
The AX8860P is a 16-core Arm Cortex-A55 part with an in-house NPU rated at 256 TOPS at native FP4 with no sparsity. The chip is produced in the 6nm process, Axera says. Sipeed claims the system has 25% faster prefill and 30% faster decode than the DGX Spark when running Qwen 27B (the company did not disclose which specific model, but later details that it expects a single MaixStation to run Qwen 3.8-27B) from a single node.
In its email, though, the company put its MaixStation about 10% ahead on both prefill and decode when compared to DGX Spark, with FP4 on each machine, with speculative decoding off, and said newer runs with a wider lead aren’t official yet. It teased the new product on its X account, showing a photo from the AX8860P’s announcement at an industrial fair in Shanghai on Tuesday.

For comparison, the DGX Spark also comes in 128GB at 273 GB/s with another SKU at 64GB, the two models priced at $6,950 and from $4,999. The former has been on sale since October 2025, at its current price since Oct. 2, and the latter is expected through partners on Oct. 23. For AMD, its Ryzen AI Halo has a 192GB Max+ PRO 495 model at 273 GB/s, released earlier this week at $7,299.99 for the Linux version, and the 128GB Max+ 395 model with 256 GB/s at $3,999.99. In all cases, 256-bit LPDDR5X is used, so the salient differences are memory capacity, compute, and software.
Memory is also a big share of what these systems cost: the best U.S. price for a 128GB DDR5 kit was $3,399 in August, and TrendForce expects conventional DRAM contract prices to rise another 10–15% this quarter. As for its unit prices, Sipeed says it used current DRAM prices rather than stock bought last year. It also suggested buyers could supply their own SSD, which could cut the price further, clarifying that the MaixStation takes a standard M.2 2280 drive rather than the Spark’s less common 2242.
Software-wise, the Spark ships with DGX OS, which is Nvidia’s build of Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, with CUDA and Nvidia’s AI software stack preinstalled. AMD validates ROCm, drivers, models, and frameworks together as a “Best-Known Configuration.” Neither the Spark nor the PRO 495 ships with Windows yet, though AMD says Windows versions are “coming soon,” and the Max+ 395 model already offers Windows 11 Pro. Sipeed, aside from its upcoming NPU toolchain, claims support for vLLM, SGLang, and PyTorch, with Axera adding ONNX, Hugging Face (HF) model formats, and an OpenAI-compatible API. MaixStation itself ships with Debian 13 and Linux 6.18, and Windows support for the PCIe card will depend on demand, Sipeed says.
Chinese solutions already exist on AMD silicon, such as GMKtec’s 192GB Evo-X5 Pro at $6,799 to $7,099. There’s also Minisforum’s MS-S1 Max-P495. What’s new with the MaixStation is the Chinese silicon underneath.
The Axera AX8860P, as recently launched, has, in addition to the above specs, PCIe 5.0 support, 64-channel video decode with 16-channel encode, and support for multiple form factors, including a single-slot, four-chip PCIe card capable of running up to 512GB of memory, with mini and pocket PC products planned. Like the eight-core AX8850 in Radxa’s and M5Stack’s M.2 accelerator cards, it pairs Arm Cortex-A55 cores with Axera’s NPU, now with twice the cores and up to 128GB of memory instead of 8GB. Two- and four-chip cascades reach a theoretical 512 and 1,024 TOPS, respectively, at a claimed scaling efficiency of about 80%. The CPU, against the Spark’s Cortex-X925 and Halo’s Zen 5, is small and in-order. It’s sufficient for the NPU but potentially more limited for other tasks.
The box itself measures about 11 × 11 × 3 cm and draws about 40W in typical use, powered over USB-C, according to Sipeed. Its ports include 10G SFP+, USB-C, an M.2 2280 slot for a PCIe 5.0 SSD, and an MCIO 8i connector for linking a second unit.
Sipeed says the MaixStation supports all configurations, that’s single, dual, and quad node, plus any “PCIe card mode for any card count you want.” The interconnect in use is a 256 Gbps C2C connection (up to 384 Gbps) “without [an] extra switch needed, and [up to] 8-node.”
The contrast is with the Spark’s QSFP ports, and Nvidia’s datasheet says linking four Sparks “requires [an] external switch.” The math, at 32 Gbps per lane, works out to 256 Gbps with the default eight lanes and 384 Gbps with the maximum of twelve. Remote-access test units and a few review units will follow during the Kickstarter campaign, the company told us.
Sipeed also commented on the openness of the platform, saying, “Yes, bsp sdk is open, you can use AI to port any distribution on it!” Sipeed has previously sold Axera boards, with products dating back to 2022 using the AX620A, AX650N, and AX630C.
The claims of the MaixStation being faster in some workloads are coupled with Sipeed saying “In fact you need [to] ask why DGX is so slow…” with potential financial implications, as Nvidia “just [wants to make] more money from users.” When an X user argued that Sipeed must be using extreme quantization at that bandwidth, the company suggested that the Spark’s specs may be overstated.
By our math, the decode claim is plausible with a 4-bit 27B model, which sits at about 13.5GB. Performance on comparable machines tops out near 20 tokens per second, which means around 270 GB/s. Prefill, which is compute-bound, is a harder sell, but Sipeed stated that “DGX Spark 1000TOPS is fake ‘sparse.’” That 1 PFLOP figure does rely on sparsity, but the DGX Spark’s dense rate of about 500 TFLOPS is still around double the AX8860P’s 256 TOPS.
Axera’s current stack has Pulsar2 as the NPU compiler and toolchain, with version 8.0 on HuggingFace last week, and the V7.0 docs already list the chip as the AX8860. There’s no operator support list for the chip yet, and the docs’ LLM chapter for older chips lists weights down to 4-bit integers but no FP4. Neither the ax-llm runtime nor AXCL, the host-side PCIe driver and runtime for Axera’s cards, lists the chip yet. Sipeed says the end-of-month release is AXDSL, a kernel-programming language, plus the Pulsar2 source code, and that SGLang and vLLM run on a custom backend built on it, so Hugging Face models run without a conversion step.
Enthusiasts are already eager to know the final specifications and pricing for the different models. On paper, as far as local LLM machines go, the MaixStation matches the Spark on memory size and claimed bandwidth, and the Max+ PRO 495 Halo on bandwidth alone. Testing performance claims will also have to wait for the toolchain and sample machines land, hopefully before the end of the year.

articles.title: INTACT: Inducing Latent Reasoning on a Frozen Backbone
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19568v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Latent reasoning replaces natural-language chains of thought with compact continuous "soft-token" representations, reducing the number of intermediate tokens that must be decoded autoregressively. We use a small external encoder to induce latent reasoning in a frozen backbone model. The encoder iteratively maps the backbone's hidden states to new latent blocks, constructing a latent reasoning prefix, after which the frozen model writes its remaining reasoning and its answer as text. Our method, INTACT, trains this encoder through distillation to reproduce the effect of written reasoning steps while keeping the model's behavior close to that of the frozen backbone, and then reinforces it on answer correctness. Across four frozen backbones from 1B to 8B, INTACT improves both GSM8K and average out-of-domain accuracy, including GSM8K gains from 75.8% to 79.3% on Llama-3.2-3B and from 77.6% to 79.7% on Qwen2.5-3B. It also reduces end-to-end latency per problem by 19% on Llama-3.2-3B and outperforms the evaluated latent-reasoning baselines at the 3B and 8B scales. Beyond the mathematics setting, the same recipe trained on a multi-domain corpus improves the frozen backbone on twelve evaluation benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, and commonsense, without task-specific adaptation.

articles.title: Do Syntax Heads Influence Model Behavior?
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19231v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Transformer language models develop attention heads that specialize in syntactic relations, for example, attending from verbs to their subjects. Do these heads play a causal role in the model's syntactic predictions? Evidence for such a role is mixed to negative: even when we force these heads to attend to a distractor noun other than the subject, the model's syntactic predictions are still more consistent with the subject than with the distractor. Interventions on specialized syntax heads had a significantly stronger effect on syntactic predictions than interventions on random heads, but only in one of the two measures we propose.

articles.title: Structure-Preserving Document-Level Data Augmentation via Discourse Parsing
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19497v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Data augmentation (DA) plays a vital role in improving model performance in low-resource or limited-supervision scenarios within Natural Language Processing (NLP). Existing DA methods, such as synonym replacement and back-translation, have demonstrated effectiveness on the word or sentence level; however, they frequently neglect discourse-level coherence and logical flow, which are essential for complex tasks dependent on inter-sentential relationships. In this paper, we propose a structure-preserving document-level data augmentation framework based on large language models (LLMs) and document-level discourse structure parsing. Our approach identifies rhetorical relations between sentence pairs and extracts key phrases, which are then replaced with semantically coherent but topically shifted content while preserving the original discourse structure. Experimental results on text summarization and question answering show that the proposed augmented data provides complementary supervision and improves combined-data training across the evaluated tasks. Comparisons with a standard RST parser and controlled ablations further support the proposed discourse representation.

articles.title: REWIND: Uncertainty-Guided Trajectory Repair for Test-Time Reasoning
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19561v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: An early mistake in the generated reasoning can constrain all subsequent reasoning. Repeated-generation methods, like MCMC-based approaches, attempt to improve output quality by sampling multiple generations, but their effectiveness can be limited by randomly selecting where to regenerate. On MATH500 with Qwen2.5-Math-7B, we find that incorrect responses have substantially higher mean token entropy than correct responses, with an average within-question relative increase of approximately 112%, suggesting that entropy can signal reasoning errors. Motivated by this finding, we introduce REWIND, a training-free controller that uses entropy dynamics to propose targeted suffix regenerations. Across three model families and five benchmarks, REWIND outperforms all baselines, with gains of 0.51-10.00 percentage points over the strongest baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of targeted, uncertainty-guided trajectory repair across models and tasks. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rewind-D310.

articles.title: Scaling LLM Inference via Parallelism: Throughput-Latency Trade-off
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19405v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) serving systems must balance latency and throughput while efficiently utilizing distributed GPU resources. This challenge arises because inference consists of two fundamentally different phases: prefill, which determines time-to-first-token (TTFT), and decode, which determines inter-token latency (ITL). The use of tensor parallelism (TP), pipeline parallelism (PP), and hybrid configurations exposes different trade-offs between these latency dimensions, making the optimal parallelism configuration highly dependent on workload characteristics, latency requirements, and context length. Moreover, despite the widespread adoption of distributed inference, there is still limited understanding of how parallelism configurations should be selected under varying workload conditions and service-level objectives (SLO). In this paper, we develop a systematic framework for characterizing LLM inference parallelism via throughput-latency trade-offs, SLO-aware serving, and long-context scalability. We introduce the notion of parallelism operating regions by constructing TTFT-ITL feasible sets and Pareto frontiers across different workload compositions, thereby revealing a systematic transition from TP-dominant to PP-dominant configurations as workloads become increasingly prefill-heavy. We further formulate SLO-aware parallelism selection using goodput, showing that stringent TTFT requirements favor PP-dominated configurations, whereas relaxed latency constraints progressively shift the optimality toward TP-dominated configurations with higher serving capacity. Finally, we demonstrate that increasing context length fundamentally changes the relative advantages of parallelism configurations, with PP-dominant configurations exhibiting more favorable scalability and SLO attainment in the long-context regime.

articles.title: What the Gemini agent means for startups
articles.text:
Small teams, short runway, and constant pressure to ship faster — it’s the reality we see every day among the founders we work with at Google for Startups. When you are building a company from the ground up, every hour spent on operational overhead or infrastructure plumbing is an hour taken away from your core product.
Last week at Gemini at Work 2026, we introduced the Gemini agent: a single, universal agent designed to work both as your personal assistant and as a dedicated member of your team. And this week, we made our new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, widely available — trained to maintain context across long, multi-step tasks.
Here is a look at how the Gemini agent works, five practical takeaways for founders, and how startups are already using it to punch above their weight.
What is the Gemini agent?
Instead of prompting separate chatbots for writing, coding, and data analysis, the Gemini agent is a single agent that takes high-level objectives and returns finished work. Three principles define it:
Unified: A single agent can now handle knowledge work, data analysis, creative asset generation, and writing and running code. For complex jobs, it dynamically spins up temporary, job-specific sub-agents and coordinates their work in parallel or in sequence.
Omnipresent access: It works across the surfaces you use every day — on the web, command line, desktop, and mobile, as well as natively inside Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Chat, and Calendar.
Persistent: It runs in the cloud with continuous memory across four dimensions (session, semantic, procedural, and episodic). It onboards itself like a new hire — learning your team, tools, and business context so you don't have to re-explain your startup with every prompt, and keeping multi-day tasks moving even after you close your laptop.
For founders wearing five hats at once, Gemini works like a digital chief of staff that's already briefed on your calendar, projects and documents. Ask it to research market trends, build a financial model in Sheets and turn both into a pitch deck, without repeating what the project or goals are at each step. It also works ahead of you. When an investor emails asking for your latest product update as a deck, Gemini spots the request and offers to handle it; one click and it comes back with completed work, ready for sharing or review.
Five takeaways for startups
1. Coworker agents and skills help you scale your output
Beyond personal assistance, you can create persistent coworker agents that work with your entire team. Each agent comes with its own Workspace account, email address, Drive storage, and directory presence. You can define a specific role — such as a launch coordinator, QA triager, or financial analyst — and your teammates can add agents to a Chat space or @mention it in a Google Doc comment to delegate work.
You can also equip agents with reusable skills — or let Gemini write skills for itself as it learns your processes. For example, with operational reporting skills connected to BigQuery and the Knowledge Catalog, anyone on your team can ask a plain-language question to build and save a live report. Once saved, those reports run on demand without incurring additional token costs. Gemini also offers pre-built specializations, starting with legal and financial services.
What it means for startups: Coworker agents can immediately increase the capacity of your teams, and skills can standardize repeatable processes like investor and operational reporting without burning tokens on every run.
2. Open and third-party model choice
Gemini is the agent, and the model underneath is your choice. As startup architectures mature, sending every task to a single frontier model quickly eats into gross margins. With the Gemini agent, you can dynamically route workloads across Gemini models, third-party models like Anthropic’s Claude, and lightweight open models like Gemma.
What it means for startups: You get flexibility without lock-in. You can optimize your cost per task — using compact models for high-volume, deterministic jobs and frontier models for complex reasoning — and swap models as your product evolves without rebuilding your workflows.
3. Connected to your services and tools
An agent is only as useful as the systems it can reach. In addition to Google Workspace, the Gemini agent connects directly to your engineering, data, and business stack, including partner solutions:
Development and collaboration: Git, Slack, Jira and more
Data and local files: BigQuery, Postgres, Snowflake, Databricks, and more alongside files on your desktop
Custom tools via MCP: Any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside your network so your engineers can build and share internal tools.
What it means for startups: Instead of spending engineering cycles maintaining custom connectors, your team can plug the agent straight into your existing codebase, databases, and MCP tools so it can act on live data wherever it lives.
4. Built-in security and governance
For B2B startups, the enterprise security audit is often where deals stall. Under the hood, every agent is assigned a cryptographic Agent Identity for clear audit trails, runs inside an isolated sandbox, and protected with built-in prompt injection defenses. External traffic is routed through Agent Gateway, allowing you to enforce governance policies. And managing coworker agents is as straightforward as managing users today, since they all have a Workspace account.
What it means for startups: When an enterprise buyer’s CISO asks how your AI workflows handle data privacy, prompt injection, and access control, you have an enterprise-grade architecture ready — helping you clear procurement hurdles.
5. Protect your runway with real-time cost controls
Autonomous agents that run sub-agents for hours or days can quickly run up a bill if a loop goes unchecked. You can now set hard, real-time spend caps directly in the Cloud Billing Console; if a cap is reached, the project's agent automatically pauses so a bug never turns into a billing surprise. Underneath, Gemini runs on Google’s specialized AI infrastructure, including our inference-optimized TPU 8i, which delivers 80% better performance-per-dollar than the prior generation.
What it means for startups: You and your developers can experiment with long-running, parallel agentic loops with a built-in financial safety net that protects your cash reserves and builds confidence with your backers.
Founders already building
Startups and AI-native innovators are already putting Gemini to work. Immersive storytelling platform Whenere used Dreamlands, an agentic 3D worldbuilding platform built on Gemini platform, to bring Pride and Prejudice to Fortnite — with Gemini generating textures for each new object in about 7 seconds for under 10 cents; one artist created nearly 250 custom assets in a single day and completed a historically accurate estate in under a week. They join application-building platform Lovable and fellow startups and innovators including  OpenEvidence, Recursion, and Replit and more.
Build with Google for Startups
The agentic era gives lean teams the leverage to punch far above their weight — whether you’re deploying coworker agents to cover internal operations or building agentic workflows directly into your product.
While these new Gemini agent capabilities are not publicly available yet, startups can contact our sales team to learn more and discuss how to get ready. In the meantime, you can explore the Google for Startups program to access credits, hands-on technical guidance, mentorship, global founder community programs and more.

articles.title: Moral Combat: Exploiting Moral Foundations Theory to Jailbreak LLMs
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19587v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Social psychology has long described how people can be persuaded to interpret a harmful act as moral. Recent research suggests that Large Language Models (LLMs) echo aspects of human psychology, from cognitive biases to social conformity. This raises a question with direct safety implications: can LLMs be moralized to bypass safety guardrails? We answer this question with a multi-agent framework grounded in Moral Foundations Theory (MFT). Given a harmful request that is initially refused, our agents diagnose which moral foundation (MF) the prompt is violating, identify a justifiable foundation under which the same request appears virtuous, rewrite the prompt accordingly, and reinforce it with generated precedents of comparable moral reframing. We evaluate our framework on harmful prompts from three well-known jailbreak datasets across five open-source and proprietary models. Our analysis reveals that models are highly susceptible to moralization, exhibiting high single-trial jailbreak rates with success increasing further under repeated attempts. We also find that safety benchmarks are imbalanced in the MFs they violate, concentrating on foundations toward which models already exhibit biases.

articles.title: KoAGE: Do Large Language Models Know, Learn, and Coin Korean Neologisms?
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19399v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Korean neologisms arise through diverse mechanisms, a demanding test of language models beyond lexical memorization. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce NeoTrace, an automated, rerunnable framework that collects and dates neologisms across genres. Its 4,271 entries support KoAGE, a cutoff-aware benchmark with three acquisition and two generation tasks---the latter, to our knowledge, the first to compare model coinages with attested neologisms under their original materials and community context. Across 21 models, lexical recall diverges from contextual inference: in a five-model temporal analysis, models define only 13-30% of cutoff-year words, yet can infer meaning from one usage. However, structural understanding remains limited: even correct definitions barely improve formation analysis of pre-cutoff neologisms. Given word-building materials, single models often follow human formation mechanisms, whereas multi-agent coinage favors abbreviation and depends on interaction framing. KoAGE thus separates what models know, learn from use, and coin.

articles.title: Selective Reasoning for Typed Decision Models: When to Start, Read, and Stop
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19644v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Typed decision models need an interface that can use additional reasoning while retaining candidate outputs. We train a shared candidate-answer reader on a frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone to unify direct decisions with on-demand, interruptible reasoning. The reader returns distributions from empty and partial reasoning prefixes. A benefit gate starts reasoning, a natural-state trigger requests explicit reads, and an entropy rule accepts acquired answers and cancels generation. Measurements distinguish answer-query work, generated output, and pipeline time. Across 768 questions from ProofWriter, LogiQA 2.0, and ARC-Challenge, accuracy rises from 70.96% for direct reading to 84.38%. Relative to 512-token terminal reading, accuracy improves by 7.29 percentage points with 2.25% more mean output work. Relative to 1,024-token terminal reading, pipeline time falls by 46.30% with an accuracy difference of -1.17 points. Exact-prefix controls isolate the saving from interruption, while read-scheduling controls distinguish reduced observation work from shorter response time.
