articles.title: Benn Jordan on Flock, privacy, and the new surveillance backlash
articles.text:
Today, I’m talking with Benn Jordan, musician, YouTuber, researcher, and investigative journalist. You might know Benn from those first two titles — he’s got a prolific discography of experimental music dating back decades.
But in the last couple of years, he’s become a high-profile face in the creator and media spaces for his work investigating Flock Safety, the maker of automatic license plate readers and the software that powers them.
Benn recently testified in front of Congress, at a hearing the Senate Judiciary Committee’s Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism held, dedicated to Flock and other ALPR systems. This hearing felt like the culmination of months and months of growing criticism and bipartisan backlash against Flock — all of which is taking a shape similar to the pushback against AI data centers.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
This has led to major fallout for Flock. Hundreds of cities, counties, and other local governments have begun canceling contracts, and Flock is now under investigation by Republican Sen. Josh Hawley. Last week, Reuters reported that Flock plans to cut about 18 percent of its workforce.
So of course I wanted to dig into all of that with Benn, not just because he played a role in that, but because he’s also become in some ways the face of a new front in the broader debate about surveillance and privacy.
A point you’ll hear Benn make is that he doesn’t actually hate Flock as a company — he thinks its posture toward critics has been a colossal PR failure that made it low-hanging fruit, while competitors like Axon and Motorola quietly build the same kind of networks. Instead, Benn now talks to Flock directly, including to its CEO Garrett Langley, and reports security vulnerabilities to the company when he finds them. (As a side note: we have also invited Flock’s CEO on the show; Garrett if you’re listening, we would love to have you.)
Benn says his outreach to the company is an olive branch he’s extended to Flock as part of his goal of working toward real, tangible solutions to surveillance overreach, rather than part of a crusade to tear one single company down.
That’s a real theme throughout our conversation: that Flock and other high profile names in surveillance are just part of the problem — our real focus should be on the interlocking relationship between private industry, government, and law enforcement that prioritizes secrecy over transparency.
We never voted for an insecure network of cameras on every street corner, and we’re certainly not being asked if we’re comfortable with access to this network being given to police officers with a penchant for abusing it. So Benn sees his work on YouTube and with other researchers, civil rights groups, and journalists as an accountability function that forces this conversation to the forefront. And so far, it’s working.
Okay: Benn Jordan on Flock, privacy, and the new surveillance backlash. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Benn Jordan, you’re a musician, YouTuber, and researcher. Lately you’ve been an investigative journalist. You are a witness in Senate hearings. Welcome to Decoder.
Thanks for having me.
I’m a huge fan of yours. It’s just a delight to have you here. A lot of people in the Verge audience know you as a musician, but lately you have been relentlessly focused on Flock cameras, which are automatic license-plate readers (ALPRs). You recently testified in front of a Senate hearing on those cameras and the surveillance they enable.
Give us a sense of your background. For people who don’t know you or haven’t been following you for years, where did Benn Jordan come from and how did you end up being the person who makes videos about Flock?
I’ve been a musician my entire life, pretty much. I’ve also always been kind of a hacker, or somebody who is that type of person who always takes stuff apart. If I get a product that wants me to pay for a service that’s already in the product, then that’s a puzzle I want to solve and I get excited about it. But a lot of times that blends into investigative journalism as well.
With the Flock stuff, it’s just that I live in Atlanta, which has more Flock cameras than anywhere else per square mile. About two years ago I started noticing them. I thought they were traffic cameras or something like that. Then I started looking into what they were actually doing and then started looking into things like security vulnerabilities. More than anything, everything that’s happening right now in the public, in the news, has to do with people just figuring out that these have existed the entire time.
A lot of my focus now is on the lack of transparency from the government, because the companies are always going to make money and try to make as much money as they can, especially if it’s from taxpayer money. But in this case, I feel like our government missed it. And that’s where we’re at.
There’s a question that’s been rattling around my head the entire time we’ve been having what I would call the modern privacy and surveillance debate.
When I say “modern,” what I mean is it feels like we woke up sometime in the last year and everything is recording us all the time and everything is watching us and the glasses have cameras in them and Mark Zuckerberg is saying phones don’t have a light, and that is meant to end a conversation.
That’s it. That’s the argument. Phones don’t have a light, no further questions. The Apple Watch is going to start doing automatic transcriptions, and everyone said, “Wait, hold on. No thank you. We actually don’t want this to happen.” But my personal experience of this is that my political coming of age was the Iraq War and the Patriot Act.
This is the stuff that people were talking about twenty-five years ago — don’t do warrantless wiretaps, don’t make the databases all connect to each other so you can take the metadata and de-anonymize people at will.
What is it about this time that has made everybody so angry? Because we could have been angry twenty-five years ago.
I’m always trying to get people more informed on the information that’s being collected about them every time they go to a website, every time they sign up for something, every time they check into a restaurant online, every time they use their phone. In this case, one of the reasons that people are really upset about is that you can’t opt out. That’s the first thing.
I can’t say, “I don’t want these Flock cameras or Axon cameras or whatever they are tracking my every move and giving it to law enforcement.” I have no option to do that. I was never given an option on whether to vote for them or vote for somebody who was in favor of them. It just kind of happened and you know people weren’t told about them. That would be the first thing — that you can still install a separate OS on an Android phone or you could turn off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth or just leave your phone at home. Whereas now you can’t actually go to the grocery store without somebody tracking your vehicle.
The second thing is that — and this is kind of related to opting in and opting out — I can pay for a new AI smartwatch or I can pay for an Amazon Echo device or something like that, or I cannot. Whereas this way I’m paying for this already. This is just my property taxes going up and I’m paying for surveillance.
In some ways it is the same as the NSA, but I feel like it’s much more local now.
You don’t get to go to the town board meeting and yell at the NSA. Although maybe you should. Honestly, that might be good for everyone. There is that part of it, and you’ve certainly been at a bunch of local town board meetings. I’ve watched a lot of videos of you talking to them and helping other people articulate their concerns.
That, to me, is one of the more fascinating aspects of all this. Flock went from a company that was selling cameras to everyone, and the idea that adding Flock cameras would increase the safety of your town went from all but assumed to, “Hold on, we all have a lot of questions,” and now this company is struggling a little bit. They’re losing contracts, they are retrenching, their communication strategy has changed.
What do you make of that? Is that just the power of local democracy in action, or is there something else?
It definitely is democracy in action. That’s the good news. The best news out of anything that’s happened is that with both Flock and data centers, it’s two things that have made people actually look up who their mayor is and who their city council members are and show up to meetings and then get involved in those local politics.
Because those local politics affect your life way more than national politics. They just don’t make the headlines. We’re not as involved. Your day-to-day following what Donald Trump is doing is likely not going to make that big of a difference other than what you argue about over Thanksgiving. Whereas local politics, that’s straight up, in the next year, going to have a big effect on your life.
People are getting involved in that, and then in cases like Asheville, North Carolina, where it’s actually changing the political landscape. People are so dissatisfied with the surveillance policies of their local politicians that it looks like that they may have a new mayor as a result of it, who also comes with a bunch of other interesting and progressive ideas that would probably help the city a lot more than the current mayor has.
That’s a big deal right there. The other part that discourages me a little bit, or the part that I find a little disappointing, is that Flock has become this buzzword, but a lot of people don’t look beyond that. I just heard in the race for governor in Georgia that the Democratic candidate yesterday talked about getting rid of Flock cameras and being anti-Flock, when this is somebody who as mayor of Atlanta welcomed Flock. You see a lot of that happening now, too, where they just say “Flock bad” and then they go sign an Axon contract or they put Verkada or Motorola cameras everywhere.
In my research, Flock has been the low-hanging fruit, just because they were the loudest and most defensive, whereas every other company was just taking a step back and cashing the checks.
One of the pieces of the puzzle here that is just fascinating is that Flock is a startup, essentially. They’re a new company, they have a new go-to-market strategy. They talk a big game about what AI can and can’t do and with what they as a platform should and should not enable. Your Axons and your Motorolas are government contractors. They are not companies that are meant to have a personality.
There’s something about Flock where Garrett Langley, the CEO, had a personality. He would go on TV and deride any critics as left-wing terrorists and that did not work. There’s something about surveillance in that case where that strategy didn’t work. There’s something about data centers where that strategy didn’t work.
We just ran a big piece about the people of Utah pushing back on Kevin O’Leary, who called them all Chinese agents, and they were like, “What are you talking about?” That cut across party lines. Again, you’ve been out there. I know you’ve talked to a lot of people pushing back on surveillance.
Is it just that Flock had a personality, and that enabled bipartisan pushback? Or is it surveillance more generally?
In terms of the media getting attention, Flock had a lot of personality and they were very defensive. I’ve met a lot of the people from Flock who are so villainized and they don’t seem at all the way that they’ve seemed in the clips that I’ve covered in my content. It’s very different. You would assume that there’s a publicist behind a lot of this.
Especially in something that serves law enforcement, where you would maybe have a publicist that’s used to dealing with Republicans and right-wing things, they just tell you to keep repeating the same thing over and over again and take a firm stance and dig your heels in. Most people who aren’t Donald Trump, when they do that, get wrecked. Flock got wrecked. They kept saying things and they kept denying security vulnerabilities and they used clever ways of reframing or redefining words and people picked up on it and now they are the villain.
Whereas companies like Axon are not as sexy for a journalist. They just aren’t, and that’s probably intentional on their part. Any company that’s taking your tax dollars or trying to court your government to give your tax dollars to them probably wants to be out of the spotlight.
We’ve covered Axon before. They do not want to be a company with characters. They are as anonymous as they can be.
One of the things that I want to see with you on the show, most importantly of all, is to describe what a Flock camera is and what the technology behind the hardware does that makes it new.
Because from watching all the videos that you make, I think, “It’s just an Android phone. They’re just putting a bunch of Android phones around town,” but it’s actually the database and the AI that makes it more dangerous than usual. Describe what the actual Flock hardware is and then how that connects to the system that makes it as controversial as it is.
So ALPRs have existed, I believe, since the 1970s. They started getting used in the United States in the late 80s and 90s. One of the classic ways that they would be used in the 2000s is they would be mounted on a police car. If a police car wanted to run someone’s plate, that way they didn’t have to type it in while they’re driving, and they could run a plate over to dispatch. I personally don’t have any problem with that. I think that makes sense. That’s a decent use. However, you would have issues where you would get plate misreads and then people would get taken out of their car at gunpoint as a result.
Flock is a lot different. Flock basically started a private nationwide network where any police department or city that’s using Flock’s network can opt into it and share their data with it. Police departments across the country can then run a license plate with 30 days of retention on everywhere someone’s been, anywhere in the country, as long as they’re sharing the data. So you would have someone in Texas being able to search somebody’s movement through New York or Atlanta or something like that.
They were doing this — they are doing this — without a warrant. Whereas any type of ALPR data sharing previous to Flock had to go through the National Crime Information Center, which does require a magistrate judge to look at the overall context of a situation and then issue a warrant to allow tracking.
That’s the innovation here. They built the private network, the private database, and convinced a bunch of law enforcement agencies to buy their system and they could opt in. There’s some kind of legal innovation here where by making it a private database, they could just excuse themselves from the warrant process.
But the actual hardware of the cameras is not all that impressive. There’s something about that that I really just want to hone in on. The idea of the Flock camera being the problem is secondary to the Flock network being the problem.
One way that I think about it, in the defense of Flock cameras and even outside of Flock itself, is that it’s all happening in public. This is all in public view. It’s generally the same as arguing that you’re allowed to take a picture anywhere in public. So why can’t they do this?
My argument against that would be if you have a police officer follow someone or go through public traffic cams, which are all over the country, and go through every single public traffic cam and wait for your car to come and then write down when that was there and do that for 30 days, that’s generally a serial killer situation.

articles.title: The Party Is Still Going Strong for Private Tech
articles.text:
The sentiment gap between public and private markets could not be wider right now. Wall Street investors have been increasingly worried about overborrowing by AI-related companies, as evidenced by skyrocketing yields on CoreWeave bonds, a selloff in semiconductor stocks and the yanking of the IPO of Firmus, the Australian data center operator.
Investors in private tech startups are still ebullient, blown away by how fast startups like Fireworks AI have grown.
This bifurcation was evident to me this week at Morgan Stanley’s annual private tech companies conference. The mutual fund and other investors fanning out across a lush seaside resort in Dana Point, Calif., were aware of the red washing over trading screens. But that didn’t prevent them from rushing to meet the dozens of startup founders there, particularly if they were in the hot defense or inference sectors.
“You can see there's a stark disconnect between the public markets and the private markets,” said Diana Doyle, Morgan Stanley’s head of technology equity and equity-linked capital markets on the sidelines of the conference.

articles.title: Titan-Llama: Retrofitting Pre-trained LLMs with External Neural Memory Modules
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19210v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Transformers are efficient to pre-train at scale because attention permits parallel computation across sequence positions, but long-context inference requires increasingly large KV caches. Efficient recurrent alternatives reduce the asymptotic complexity of inference, but their sequential dependence limits token-wise parallelism during training, making them harder to scale. Further, the current paradigm of extending long context tasks creates competing notions of retaining information precisely and keeping long-context inference efficient. To address this gap, we introduce Titan-Llama, a post-training method for retrofitting attention-based language models with a hierarchical memory architecture that updates parameters at test-time. Titan-Llama applies a blockwise attention mask and preserves full-fidelity attention over recent tokens while compressing historical context into recurrent, fixed-size neural memory modules (NMMs). Our formulation allows pre-trained attention layers to be replaced without training a new language model from scratch. On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Titan-Llama raises accuracy over segmented attention windows from 23.87\% to 40.51\% on QuALITY and from 14.50\% to 40.75\% on LongHealth. Inference benchmarks show more than 20\% faster prefill, 37\% faster decode at medium context lengths, and 24\% lower steady-state decode memory usage in the evaluated configurations. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating memory architecture mechanisms that utilize test-time training effectively modulates long-context behavior of pre-trained models, offering a practical route to adapting pre-trained transformers for efficient long-context inference. Our code is released on Github \href{https://github.com/sarahpannn/titans-pytorch/tree/main}{GitHub}

articles.title: Nick Wingfield Promoted to Co-Executive Editor of The Information
articles.text:
I am thrilled to announce three major editorial promotions for Nick, Abe and Meredith, along with some changes that recognize the incredible work of our newsroom and set the stage for more growth in what is shaping up to be the most exciting time in our history.
Nick Wingfield has been promoted to Executive Editor, responsible for ensuring the high bar of all our reporting. Since he joined The Information eight years ago after working at the New York Times and Wall Street Journal, Nick has pushed us to think bigger in our journalism, overseeing our features efforts and some of our most important beats. When we heard whispers that Jony Ive’s personal life was becoming a distraction from his work at Apple, he and Aaron Tilley mustered a slew of reporting that turned into one of our most memorable crash leders. That’s what he has done again and again. Working with talented reporters to drive maximum impact, across coasts, beats and more.
In his new role, Nick will run the day-to-day publication with me and Amir, with us all dividing up responsibilities for what we chase and ensuring the highest bar in what we publish while continuing to grow the team and build up new editorial areas. He will continue to manage his team of reporters.
Abe Brown has been promoted to Features Editor, with responsibility for all our features at The Information. As Weekend editor, Abe has proven himself as something rare in media these days: a careful and skilled editor with a zest for trying new things. While managing a section, he has also jumped in any day of the week to help edit our biggest stories with a tireless work ethic and great attitude. I am excited for more reporters to work with Abe and for him to push us in new directions.
I am thrilled to promote Meredith Mazzilli to Finance Editor. From the day she joined The Information, it has been clear that Meredith knows finance. While she has led all sorts of consequential coverage on ads, commerce, Musk and beyond, in recent months, she has helped our finance team carve out a huge lane around the financing of data centers and this turbulent moment. I’m excited to see how far she and the team can run against that massively important story. Meredith has also begun the work of bringing new talent to the team. I am thrilled to have her officially step into the role leading Finance, continuing to expand our reporting staff and find even more lanes where we can dominate.
I am also happy to share that Martin has decided he wants to shift his focus to the Briefing and future related Briefing franchises and will become Editor-at-Large. Over twelve years, Martin has had a hand in every aspect of this business. I am thrilled he will be working with us full-time to focus on writing and how to expand the Briefing franchise, while continuing to coach and advise the newsroom. And there will be more time to celebrate more than a decade of Martin as co-Executive Editor. He will continue to edit The Electric and, in the coming weeks, reporters who report to him will transition to other senior leaders to free him up to go full throttle in his new role.
We are making these changes now to celebrate the success of our incredible editorial leadership team, which remains unrivaled in the industry, and to prepare for the future.
The next few years are going to demand a lot of news organizations. Sweeping changes to how audiences consume news are just beginning and I honestly think most news organizations will have no idea what hit them. Meanwhile, the onslaught of “information,” much of it biased and fake, has only begun.
Our secret sauce—the high impact, ahead-of-the-curve, focused work no one else is doing—is exactly the right formula for this moment.

articles.title: Joint Subspace Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Decoding
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19026v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Sparse attention reduces the KV-cache traffic that dominates long-context LLM decoding, but practical methods largely operate at coarse granularity. Token-level selection offers finer control, yet presents two challenges: low-dimensional scoring may lose query--key structure needed for accurate ranking, while gathering scattered selected tokens can offset the resulting latency benefit. We introduce Joint Subspace Sparse Attention (JSSA) to address both challenges. For selection quality, JSSA learns a shared low-dimensional query--key subspace by minimizing token-score preservation error. We upper-bound the resulting non-convex objective with a tractable marginal objective that admits a closed-form spectral solution; direct refinement of the exact objective provides no measurable improvement in the tested settings. For execution efficiency, we develop a gather-free token-level indexed-attention kernel that supports distinct per-KV-head selections under the standard grouped-query attention (GQA) KV-cache layout. Across standard GQA, hybrid sliding-window/global attention, and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) models, JSSA consistently remains close to full-KV accuracy while avoiding the substantial generation-length inflation and architecture-dependent failures observed with competing methods. On an NVIDIA B200 GPU, JSSA achieves up to $6.43\times$ the decoding throughput of full-KV attention at 128K context. JSSA achieves reasoning accuracy comparable to model-native DSA without model training and reaches 96--99\% of its decoding throughput even at 700B scale large models.

articles.title: Measuring and Reducing Unusable Replies of LLM Agents
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19659v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: People delegate multi-step work to LLM agents and read only the reply that the agent hands back. Current evaluation scores task completion and the faithfulness of reports, and it leaves open whether the requester can understand and use the reply. We call this property reply usability and measure it with a reader model that takes the requester's position and tests whether the reply can be interpreted from what the requester has seen, is in the requester's language and answers the request. Its agreement with the majority of five annotators lies within the range of the individual annotators. Across eight models from seven families, 54% of 480 replies fail, and the best model still fails on 30%. Failed replies mostly point to material the requester has not seen or use labels that the agent coined during its work. Stating explicit requirements for the reply reduces the failure rate from 0.52 to 0.43 together with errors and omissions, and a secondary model that rewrites the reply reduces it to 0.36, which human annotators confirm in a blind comparison. Reply usability can thus be scored alongside task success and improved with one appended message or one call to a secondary model.

articles.title: ASML reports record $13 billion quarter, vows to expand capacity as demand for lithography equipment soars
articles.text:
ASML this week reported record quarterly revenue of $13.06 billion (€11.66 billion) and profitability of nearly $5.79 billion (€5 billion) as demand for advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment continues to accelerate and investments in AI infrastructure continue to increase. The company now expects demand for its lithography systems to exceed its production capacity in 2027 and 2028, despite plans to increase output substantially. Some clients are already interested in placing orders for equipment as far ahead as 2030, which makes ASML consider further capacity expansions beyond its previously announced intentions.
Record financial results
ASML reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $13.06 billion USD (€11.66 billion), up 55% year-over-year and 25% sequentially. The company's gross margin reached a record 57.5%, up from 51.6% a year earlier, while operating income rose to $5.79 billion (€5.17 billion). Net income reached $5.56 billion USD (€4.96 billion) , although this figure includes approximately $570 million (€510 million) from the re-evaluation of the company's investment in Mistral AI.
(Image credit: ASML)
During the quarter, ASML sold 121 lithography systems, including 113 new and eight refurbished machines, up from 91 systems in Q2 2026. The company generated $4.59 billion USD (€4.1 billion) from 17 EUV lithography systems and $4.82 billion USD (€4.3 billion) from 85 DUV (including 45 ArFi scanners) and 19 i-line litho tools. In addition, ASML recognized revenue from one High-NA EUV system in Q2. Of total equipment revenue, 54% came from logic chipmakers and 46% from memory manufacturers.
(Image credit: ASML)
Taiwan accounted for 32% of ASML's equipment sales in Q3 2026, followed closely by South Korea at 31%. China represented another 23%, while the United States accounted for 13% and the rest of Asia contributed just 1%. Combined, Taiwan and South Korea generated 63% of ASML's equipment revenue, which reflects substantial investments in advanced logic and memory manufacturing capacity that by far exceed those in the U.S. and Japan.
(Image credit: ASML)
ASML’s Installed Base Management business generated $3.68 billion (€3.29 billion), approximately $450 million (€400 million) above guidance, largely due to strong demand for productivity upgrades (more on this later), which contributed to the company’s record profitability.
For the fourth quarter, ASML expects revenue of $15.9 billion to $17.0 billion (€14.2 billion to €15.2 billion) and gross margin of approximately 57%. Full-year revenue should reach $49.3 billion to $50.4 billion (€44 billion to €45 billion), up approximately 36% YoY. The company projects EUV revenue should increase by more than 45% year-over-year, while memory-related equipment sales are expected to rise by approximately 75%, which indicates growing demand from DRAM producers.
Demand for litho tools spans to 2030
One of the biggest learnings from these results and accompanying statements is that semiconductor manufacturers are increasingly interested in securing lithography equipment years before they actually need it. According to ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet, customers expect demand for its products to exceed available supply through at least 2028, which encourages them to accelerate construction of new fabs as well as expand their existing capacity.
"Our leading-edge high-volume customers are sharing very good visibility as a result of the increasing number of long-term commitments they are securing with their customers," Fouquet said during the company's conference call with analysts and investors.  "This extended visibility has led them to conclude that demand for their products will outpace supply through at least 2028. As a result, customers are accelerating capacity build-out plans and preparing for further expansion beyond 2028 in order to better meet the anticipated level of demand."
(Image credit: ASML)
ASML is already receiving orders that are to be delivered in 2028, while some customers have expressed interest in equipment for 2029 and even 2030.
"As customers shift focus to their needs beyond 2027, our order momentum continues to build," Fouquet added. "We are increasingly receiving orders for 2028, and customers are also expressing interest in placing orders for 2029 and even 2030."
To address this demand, ASML plans to manufacture approximately 65 Low-NA EUV systems in 2026, up from 44 scanners shipped in 2025. Production of immersion DUV systems should remain approximately at last year's level, even though proveiously the company expected shipments of DUV tools to decline.
The company previously announced plans to increase production capacity for both Low-NA EUV and immersion DUV systems by 30% in 2027, followed by another potential 30% increase in 2028. Based on its 2026 EUV production target, this implies capacity for approximately 85 Low-NA EUV systems in 2027 and roughly 110 in 2028, assuming both increases materialize.
However, ASML now believes even this level of output will be insufficient and is investigating ways to expand its 2028 capacity beyond the previously planned 30% increase. However, the company has not disclosed revised production targets.
"Looking further ahead, we shared our intent last quarter to increase our capacity in 2027 by 30% for both Low NA EUV and DUV immersion systems, as well as to investigate adding a further 30% in 2028," explained Roger Dassen, Chief Financial Officer at ASML. "However, given the dynamics of this quarter, we now anticipate that our current planned levels of output in 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet the demand of our customers."
High-NA EUV adoption
Meanwhile, High-NA EUV adoption is progressing. Intel has already exposed more than one million wafers using High-NA systems and plans to start using High-NA EUV with its 14A process technology in 2028. Samsung plans to introduce High-NA EUV into high-volume manufacturing (HVM) in 2028 for DRAM and for logic later, while TSMC plans to use High-NA EUV scanners by 2030 – 2031. ASML says availability across its installed High-NA fleet is approaching 90%, which suggests that the tools are becoming mature enough for HVM deployment.
(Image credit: ASML)
Interestingly, Samsung's planned 2028 introduction may create additional demand for High-NA equipment from memory manufacturers, as they will need to compete against their larger rival. However, ASML has not disclosed specific shipment targets for these tools.
New tools, more capacity
ASML also intends to increase semiconductor production capacity by introducing more productive lithography systems. Its upcoming Twinscan NXE:3800F, scheduled for introduction in early 2027, will process up to 260 wafers per hour, compared with 230 wafers per hour for the existing NXE:3800E. While this represents 'only' approximately 13% higher throughput, this translates to 21,600 extra EUV exposures per month without corresponding increases in cleanroom space. Three such tools per fab enable 90 additional EUV exposures per hour, 2,160 per day, or 64,800 per month. The company also plans to introduce a new critical-layer immersion DUV system capable of processing 330 wafers per hour.
(Image credit: ASML)
Keep in mind that the actual fab capacity improvements depend on the number of lithography exposures required per wafer on a particular node, as well as the capabilities of other manufacturing equipment.ASMLASML
Another important element of ASML's strategy is its growing portfolio of productivity upgrade packages for existing EUV and DUV systems. Such upgrades enable chipmakers to increase wafer throughput without purchasing additional scanners, which can provide additional capacity considerably faster than procuring new tools or constructing new fabs.
Value-based pricing is a go
One of the controversial things that ASML discussed back in early Q2 was its value-based pricing, which many thought was a blanket price hike. This is not and CFO Roger Dassen this week confirmed that negotiations with major customers have been completed, although the financial benefits for ASML will not become visible immediately.
(Image credit: ASML)
The company expects the first effects of higher pricing to appear during 2027, with the full impact becoming apparent in 2028 and beyond, which essentially means that the company is not setting new prices on its backlog, but generally setting new prices on new tools.
"We completed those conversations," said Dassen. "So that has been done with the key customers. The effect of that is not really visible in 2026. It will start to become visible partly in the course of 2027. The full impact of that you will start to see in 2028 and beyond."
This strategy could further improve ASML's already substantial gross margins, particularly as customers have no alternatives for advanced lithography equipment.
China remains important
Despite export restrictions that prevent Chinese chipmakers from acquiring EUV scanners and advanced DUV systems, China remains a substantial market for ASML. The company expects China to account for approximately 20% of its total revenue in 2026, which implies annual sales of roughly €8.8 billion to €9 billion based on current guidance.
(Image credit: ASML)
Although China's share of ASML's business has declined from its levels in 2023 - 2025, the country's semiconductor manufacturers continue to invest in mature node capacity and equipment that remains available under existing export regulations. Meanwhile, it is impossible to predict what is going to happen if the U.S. lawmakers approve the MATCH Act.
Yet, ASML management emphasizes that its key growth opportunities lie with advanced logic and memory manufacturers, which are accelerating their investment in advanced lithography tools, including sophisticated DUV systems, Low-NA EUV machines, and High-NA EUV scanners.
The future of ASML
Thanks to gaining momentum in AI infrastructure investments, ASML reported record quarterly revenue of $13.06 billion (€11.7 billion) as demand for advanced lithography equipment continued to accelerate. The company expects demand to persist for years as its customers are interested in placing orders for tools to be delivered as far ahead as 2030. To meet growing demand, the company plans to expand production capacity beyond its previous targets for 2028. ASML also intends to introduce new EUV and DUV systems with higher productivity, offer productivity upgrades, and raise equipment prices to capitalize on unprecedented demand.

articles.title: Dynamo v1.6.0-nemotron-3.5-super-vl-dev.1
articles.text:
Release Notes
Dynamo v1.6.0-nemotron-3.5-super-vl-dev.1 is an experimental snapshot build with early NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL support on the Dynamo vLLM and TensorRT-LLM backends. It is not recommended for production and is not a QA-gated release. APIs, behavior, and defaults may change before stable support. Use it for evaluation, testing, and early feedback only.
Summary
Dynamo v1.6.0-nemotron-3.5-super-vl-dev.1 serves nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4, a multimodal MoE model with up to 1M-token context, on Dynamo vLLM and TensorRT-LLM. The vLLM runtime moves to a CUDA 13.4 vLLM nightly with Mamba2, top-p sampling, and FlashInfer fixes. The TensorRT-LLM runtime uses 1.3.0rc29 with quantized MTP head loading, draft KV-pool reuse, and a guided-decoding fix for multimodal input (#16549).
Kubernetes recipes cover aggregated and disaggregated vLLM targets on H100, H200, B200, B300, GB200, GB300, and VR200, plus aggregated and disaggregated TensorRT-LLM targets on B200. Every target uses NVFP4 weights, FP8 KV cache, MTP speculative decoding, session-affinity routing, and 1M context. The recipes include a shared model-cache PVC and download job, and an AIPerf SWE-bench Pro trace-replay benchmark under recipes/nemotron-3.5-super-vl-120b-a12b (#16544, cherry-picked in #16552).
Release Branch: release/1.6.0-nemotron-3.5-super-vl-dev.1, tip 5f601dba872b1a26b40090c319df8edbb8f946bd (2026-10-15)

About Nemotron 3.5 Super VL
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an NVIDIA 120B-A12B multimodal MoE preview model, published on Hugging Face as nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4. It reasons before answering, supports tool calling, and serves up to 1M tokens of context. This build serves it through Dynamo vLLM on Hopper, Blackwell, and Rubin, and through Dynamo TensorRT-LLM on B200, with MTP speculative decoding on both.
Full Changelog
vLLM Backend
CUDA 13.4 runtime: Moved the vLLM runtime to the cu134-nightly-bb87d227 base and refreshed the amd64 and arm64 compliance baselines against CUDA 13.4.1. vLLM-Omni is skipped on CUDA because the nightly needs Transformers 5.16.1 or later; CPU and XPU images keep Omni (#16549).
Model and sampling fixes: Backported vLLM #60797, which stores the convolution history in Mamba2 prefill checkpoints so cached prefixes resume with the correct state, and vLLM #58231, which preserves forced large logits in split top-p masking (#16549).
FlashInfer kernels: Backported FlashInfer #5267 (stochastic rounding on SM107) and an opt-in multi-wave KV split for long-context attention from FlashInfer #6331 and vLLM #61077, enabled with VLLM_FLASHINFER_MULTI_WAVE_KV_SPLIT (#16549).
Disaggregated serving with CPU offload: Dynamo now detects NIXL inside a vLLM MultiConnector, so a worker that combines NIXL transfer with CPU KV offload sets up the NIXL side channel correctly (#16549).
TensorRT-LLM Backend
TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29 with MTP fixes: Backported TensorRT-LLM #19558 and #19597, which load quantized MTP heads and their replacement modules, and #19303, which publishes the one-model draft KV pool so the draft no longer attends over unwritten pages on reused prefixes (#16549).
Multimodal with guided decoding: Guided decoding stays in CUDA graphs and drains its host functions before multimodal encoders run, avoiding a deadlock on image input. Dynamo also runs media preprocessing off the event loop so image decoding no longer blocks request handling (#16549).
Build and Compliance
Runtime attribution: License attribution now covers system Python roots, vendored Python distributions, and Rust and Go dependencies embedded in shipped binaries, with architecture-specific completeness checks for both runtimes. AI Simulate is pinned to the published 0.13.0-dev.2 release (#16549).
Recipes
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL recipes: Added recipes/nemotron-3.5-super-vl-120b-a12b, with a shared model-cache PVC and download job and SWE-bench Pro deployments (#16544, cherry-picked in #16552; recipe folder, recipe guide):
vLLM aggregated and disaggregated targets on H100, H200, B200, B300, GB200, GB300, and VR200, from 2 GPUs (H200) to 11 GPUs (VR200 7P4D). They use KV-aware routing with session affinity, MTP3 or MTP5, and CPU KV offload.
TensorRT-LLM aggregated (4 workers) and 2P2D disaggregated targets on B200 with MTP3, load-based placement, and session affinity for prefix reuse.
An AIPerf 0.13 job that replays 400 SWE-bench Pro agent trajectories (median input 222K tokens, 99% KV cache hit rate) to measure throughput and latency.
Getting Started
Deployment is Kubernetes-based (Dynamo Platform + DynamoGraphDeployment). Full steps — namespace and Hugging Face token secret, model-cache PVC, download job, DGD apply, and a /v1/chat/completions smoke test — are in the recipe guide. The benchmark workflow is in perf/README.md. Recipes expect a Hugging Face token secret named hf-token-secret.
Known Issues / Limitations
Experimental snapshot build — not QA-gated; not for production.
TensorRT-LLM recipes in this build cover B200 only.
TensorRT-LLM workers publish no KV events, so the router places new sessions by load and relies on session affinity for prefix-cache reuse.
The shared-model-cache PVC needs a ReadWriteMany storage class; set storageClassName in model-cache/model-cache.yaml before applying it.
GB200, GB300, and VR200 disaggregated recipes require the NVIDIA DRA driver with ComputeDomain support for multi-node NVLink.
The published VR200 results used a synthetic MTP acceptance length; the VR200 recipes default to natural acceptance.

articles.title: Are We Really Measuring Forgetting? Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19613v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. In this work, we identify three major pitfalls that may lead to misleading conclusions: the lack of heldout evaluation to distinguish genuine concept-wise forgetting from instance-wise overfitting, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training, and unfair method comparisons caused by applying the same training settings to different unlearning methods. To address these challenges, we introduce GEMMU (Generalizable Evaluation for Multimodal Machine Unlearning), a benchmark built on real-world knowledge and a principled evaluation protocol. Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods under GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps and challenges conclusions drawn from previous benchmarks. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous evaluation for advancing multimodal machine unlearning and provide guidelines for future benchmark design.

articles.title: SK hynix reportedly playing hardball with Trump admin over 3D NAND fab
articles.text:
Reports that Solidigm was considering building a 3D NAND fab in the U.S. came as a surprise last month, as no company has manufactured NAND flash memory in America for years. However, the potential investment now appears to be part of a calculated move by Solidigm's parent SK hynix, which is reportedly asking the U.S. government to authorize additional semiconductor manufacturing equipment shipments to its Dalian facility in China in exchange for a commitment to build a new NAND fab in the U.S., according to Reuters.
Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers
(Image credit: Microsoft)
The data center cooling state of play
The custom AI ASIC state of play
America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price
GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year
Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible
The Dalian fab is the world's only facility to produce 192-layer floating gate 3D NAND for Solidigm's data center-grade SSDs for AI, enterprise, and hyperscale data centers. Its manufacturing operations rely on equipment from major American suppliers, including Applied Materials, KLA, and Lam Research, whose exports to China require a license from the U.S. government. Although the U.S. authorities tend to authorize shipments of some tools to semiconductor facilities in the People's Republic that are operated by multinational companies like Samsung or SK hynix, they only want to keep the fabs running, as they are against expansions of capacity of fabs in China or introducing new manufacturing technologies to these facilities.
Solidigm has requested U.S. export licenses for additional tools, but the U.S. government has yet to authorize the shipments. Last December, the U.S. Commerce Department granted SK hynix a limited authorization for equipment deliveries to Dalian for 2026, but it has not issued a similar equipment export authorization for 2027, according to Reuters. In a bid to persuade the U.S. government to authorize shipments of necessary tools to its Dalian facility, SK hynix proposes to build a 3D NAND facility in America. This would fill an important gap in the Trump administration’s efforts to bring semiconductor manufacturing back to the U.S.
SK hynix's Solidigm subsidiary wants to install additional manufacturing equipment in the unused portions of its Dalian Mod B facility, which was completed in 2023. The company never fully equipped the building because of the memory market downturn at the time, so while some production tools are installed, substantial space remains unused and is available for additional tools. Given that Solidigm sells every single SSD it produces, unused capacity means lost revenue. Meanwhile, because the building was completed in 2023, installation of tools into that facility does not constitute a capacity expansion.
Additional NAND production in China could generate profits that Solidigm could use to finance its proposed American fab and support its operations until domestic manufacturing capacity becomes available. The company is also considering an initial public offering as early as 2027 to raise additional capital.
Solidigm has previously confirmed its commitment to further development of floating-gate 3D NAND technology. In an interview with Tom's Hardware at Computex 2026, Avi Shetty, who leads Solidigm's AI solutions and ecosystem business, said that the company intended to develop 5th and 6th Generation floating-gate NAND beyond its existing 192-layer technology. He also emphasized the importance of maximizing factory utilization and profitability. However, he did not disclose plans to expand manufacturing output at the company's Dalian facility, not to mention a new fab in the U.S.
Nonetheless, the new reports about SK hynix's intentions clearly indicate that the company not only intends to keep developing new generations of Solidigm's floating-gate NAND, but also to expand its production in China and the U.S.

articles.title: Similar Models, Broken Odds: Where Luce's Axiom Fails in Chatbot Arena
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19095v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Chatbot Arena ranks language models with the Bradley-Terry model, which gives each model one score and so assumes Luce's choice axiom. Choice theory predicts where this fails: near-copies are told apart more decisively than their scores imply. On 1.8 million Arena votes, votes between versions of one model are 1.37 times as decisive as Bradley-Terry predicts, between sizes of one generation 1.26 times and between models of one lab 1.12 times; a release a year later gives consistent multipliers, and the effect survives alternative tie treatments, prompt subsets and topics, and timing checks. How alike two models' answers are worded and formatted tracks the effect. A correction with four to six parameters predicts held-out votes better than Bradley-Terry and than models with hundreds of parameters, mostly by modelling ties; frozen and carried to new releases in a test fixed in advance, its gains are concentrated in ties, and better head-to-head odds are not established. The leaderboard order barely moves. With language-model judges and three-answer menus, a near-copy takes votes mostly from its twin when choices are pooled over prompts (log-odds shift +0.10, 95% interval 0.05 to 0.16); within a prompt the shift is smaller and clear for two of four judges.

articles.title: HACHIMI-II: From Role-Play to Learner Behavior Modeling for Faithful Student Simulation
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19654v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Simulated students let researchers test tutoring systems and teaching strategies before real learners are available, but only if the simulation reproduces where a particular learner succeeds and fails. The common approach asks a large language model to role-play a student, but a role does not model what this learner knows or will do next, so the model's own competence fills the gap. Simulated students perform at a level set by the model, differ little from one another, and seldom make the real learners' errors. We model the learner's behavior and recast student simulation as third-person prediction of the learner's next action. HACHIMI-II builds a student model from the learner's history, infers the learner's state for the current item or tutor turn, and compiles it into a behavior harness that constrains the next action. On three item-response datasets, the Wasserstein-1 distance between simulated and real student ability is 2.4--8.4$\times$ smaller than that of the strongest baseline. On two dialogue datasets, HACHIMI-II reproduces real student errors with the same knowledge type, locus, and mechanism 1.8--5.1$\times$ more often than the strongest baseline, and ablations trace the gains mainly to the explicit learner state. Predicting the learner makes capable models usable as simulated students.

articles.title: We tested the RTX Spark Superchip in Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra
articles.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang announced the RTX Spark platform with the grand ambition to “reinvent the PC” back at Computex 2026. By pairing the GB10 Superchip with a version of Windows on Arm tailored for the secure and contained execution of local AI agents, Nvidia and its partners at Microsoft, Dell, HP, MSI, Lenovo, and Asus are all hoping to pave the way to a future where the PC is an active, autonomous companion for work and creation.
The hardware foundation for that vision of the future is now in place. Last week, we flew out to San Francisco to get all the details on the RTX Spark platform, and we returned home with Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra in top-end trim to put it all to the test.
This system has the full RTX Spark Superchip with 20 CPU cores and 6144 CUDA cores alongside 128GB of LPDDR5X-9400 RAM, and I’ve been putting it through its paces over the past week to see just what it can do.
The embargoes for the RTX Spark launch are a bit peculiar. Today, we’ll be sharing our broad experience with the Spark platform, as well as competitive performance evaluations, but not any system-specific results such as battery life, build or display quality, or other details of that nature. We have other RTX Spark laptops in the Tom’s Hardware labs, and detailed reviews of those systems will be coming soon.
No, this approach doesn’t make a lot of sense when the experience of a mobile platform is intimately and inextricably tied to the specific implementation of that chip in a particular laptop design. And we know that battery life is the first and foremost concern of many interested in this platform. But again, all that information is coming soon.
For this first round of testing, we compared the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra with RTX Spark against two systems. The first is a 14" MacBook Pro with Apple's highest-end M5 Max SoC inside. That Mac has a 40-core GPU and an 18-core CPU, as well as 128 GB of LPDDR5X RAM. We don't have a mobile Ryzen AI Max+ 395 system in the labs right now, but we do have AMD's compact Ryzen AI Halo as a source of fresh data with the latest ROCm stack and llama.cpp builds.
Local AI performance
Judging local AI performance is a constantly moving target, and this review is no different. Our past testing has exercised the prompt processing and token generation phases of AI inference separately, with the understanding that a system that's fast at both those phases provides the best experience.
But in an agentic workflow, that benchmarking technique doesn't capture the total time required to complete a task across all the inference turns needed to reach a particular goal. To capture that entire end-to-end time, the folks at Artificial Analysis have developed a new benchmark, AgentPerf-local, that precisely replays inference traces across several agentic AI tasks. The value of this approach should make immediate sense: the faster an AI agent finishes a job, the more productive a system can be.
So instead of presenting raw time-to-first-token and tokens-per-second figures, as we have in the past, we’re sharing time-to-completion values as we would for more traditional CPU and content creation benchmarks.
Again, local AI benchmarking is a continuous work in progress, so let us know what you think of this approach, and we’ll take that feedback into account as we continue to develop our methods.
We ran AgentPerf-local with two compatible models: the dense Qwen 3.8-27B, which is popular as one of the most intelligent local models available for its size, and the Qwen 3.6 35B A3B mixture-of-experts model, which is less intelligent but easier for a wide range of systems to run quickly. We used the latest build of llama.cpp as our inference backend and built it from source on each test system to take advantage of CUDA, Metal, or ROCm acceleration, as appropriate.
Let’s look at Qwen 3.8 27B’s behavior first. We used Unsloth’s Q4_K_M quantization of the model. We ran it with DFlash2 speculative decoding on the RTX Spark and MacBook Pro, and with Qwen 3.8 27B’s built-in MTP on the Ryzen AI Halo for the best performance.
(Image credit: Future)
As we found in our benchmarking of Apple's Mac Studio with the M4 Max SoC, memory bandwidth is only one constraint for local AI performance. Despite its memory bandwidth advantage on paper, the M5 Max MacBook Pro still ends up taking about 25% longer to finish the AgentPerf benchmark with Qwen 3.8 27B than the Surface Laptop Ultra with RTX Spark.
Part of that may be down to software maturity, but it's also worth remembering that our Surface Laptop Ultra is a 15" system with a much larger 140W power adapter versus the 14" MacBook Pro's 96W charger.
The 16" M5 Max MacBook Pro also comes with a 140W adapter, and we'd be curious to see whether the extra power and higher thermal headroom afforded by that system’s larger chassis help close the gap here. But in any event, the RTX Spark platform is the fastest overall at this task today.
Meanwhile, AMD's nearly two-year-old Ryzen AI Max+ 395 just can't keep up with either of these newer systems in this demanding test. It needs about twice as long to finish our agentic tests with Qwen 3.8 27B as either the RTX Spark or the MacBook Pro do, at a whopping 40 minutes.
The fact that the Ryzen AI Halo is a mini desktop form factor rather than a notebook doesn’t much matter to these results, as any power and thermal headroom that design might afford can’t possibly overcome the performance gap here.
Next up, we have the lighter-weight Qwen 3.6 35B A3B.  We ran Unsloth’s Q4_K_M quantization of this model with MTP enabled.
(Image credit: Future)
The Surface Laptop Ultra ends up completing this test in just eight minutes, or about 25% faster than the 14” MacBook Pro’s 10 minutes. This test is also much friendlier to the Ryzen AI Halo, which finished the benchmark in a more reasonable 13 minutes. But that just emphasizes that you have to trade away model intelligence to get a reasonable level of performance out of Strix Halo.
AMD has recently gone on a publicity blitz to highlight the relatively low cost of entry for Strix Halo systems versus DGX Spark desktops and now RTX Spark laptops. But if time is money, and getting  more intelligent tokens out of your local AI system faster means more potentially profitable agentic work gets done, then a more expensive system upfront will be able to do more of that work and potentially generate more value over time.
Gaming performance: first impressions
Despite its RTX branding and the emphasis Nvidia places on its 6144-CUDA-core GPU (or 48 SMs), the RTX Spark platform faces some tough challenges for gaming. Most games available today are not going to be natively compiled for its Arm CPU, and even for those that might be, the maximum 300 GB/s of shared memory bandwidth the platform offers is well below that of even the RTX 5060 Mobile's dedicated 384 GB/s feeding 26 SMs.
The entire GB10 SoC is competing for a relatively small amount of memory bandwidth, and because graphics is generally a memory-bandwidth-bound workload, that's not a great start for feeding all of those SMs in games.
I started my gaming explorations with Gears of War: E-Day. In this exceptionally CPU-heavy game, it's clear that the baseline performance of the Grace CPU cores and the added overhead of the Prism x86 emulator are doing this title no favors.
GPU utilization only reaches the 85% mark on average at a near-1080p (1908x1272) render resolution with the High preset and 2X framegen, and we saw at least one major hang during a map transition that was less than confidence-inspiring for an immersive experience as we progress further into the game.
Gears of War: E-Day (1908x1272, High Preset, Mega Geometry On, MFG 2X)

Because of its CPU dependence, Gears is probably a worst-case scenario for this platform, but the fact remains that it's not a great experience, and turning down settings or lowering upscaling input resolutions just exacerbates the CPU-boundedness of this title. If any game could use a native Arm build, this is the one.
Control Resonant is significantly less dependent on the CPU, but that just means that the other potential gaming shortcomings of the RTX Spark Superchip seem to come into play.
After struggling a bit to achieve a solid frame rate and input latency at the Surface Laptop Ultra's native 3270x2180 output resolution even with DLSS upscaling, I found that running the game in windowed mode at 2560x1440 with DLSS Performance upscaling, the High preset, and MFG 3X to keep frame rates near the Surface Laptop Ultra's 120Hz refresh rate provided better results. (This system's tall 3:2 aspect ratio means that 16:9 fullscreen games don't cleanly scale up.)

But even then, input latency was above what I would consider acceptable on our standard GPU test rig, and enabling ray tracing at all dipped frame rates and spiked input latency even further, so I had to stick to raster-only rendering for the best results.
Overall, my early RTX Spark gaming verdict is that you can do it, and you can have a fine enough time, but it is not the primary focus of this platform. Gaming performance with the relatively limited memory bandwidth of the RTX Spark Superchip, combined with the system's CPU performance and the overhead of Prism emulation, mean that you'll be searching for a narrow range of settings where baseline frame rates, upscaling, image quality, and the smoothness boost of frame generation still yield acceptable input latency.
When I first approached gaming on this platform, I had expected that DLSS upscaling would be a required part of the experience, but in practice, you really need to lean on DLSS Frame Generation, as well, whether that's for added smoothness (as in Gears of War) or for both smoothness and the benefits of Nvidia Reflex due to developer choices behind the scenes (as in Control Resonant).
Even with Reflex, though, the Grace CPU generally seems to deliver input latencies significantly higher than I'm used to on our Ryzen 7 9800X3D test rig, and it's hard to get them much lower in these AAA titles by tweaking settings.
If you demand the lowest input latency and the highest performance with cutting-edge games, especially if you plan to enable RT, a separate gaming laptop with a dedicated RTX 50-series GPU will still provide a superior experience. And if you just don’t care about local AI at all, that advice applies even more strongly.
Bottom line
Nvidia's RTX Spark is an ambitious new PC platform for the traditional workloads of today and the potential agentic AI work of tomorrow. How often do we see an entirely new player try to elbow into the crowded and competitive PC space, especially one with a sweeping vision for how the PC will be used in the years to come? An incremental move this is not.
Our general performance tests and new agentic AI tests show that despite providing merely solid CPU performance and relatively low bandwidth for a unified memory architecture on paper, the Blackwell GPU on board GB10 has enough AI horsepower in practice to let the RTX Spark platform come out ahead of Apple's latest top-end M5 Max and AMD's Ryzen AI Max+ 395, aka Strix Halo, SoCs.
Whether you choose the highly intelligent dense Qwen 3.8 27B model and trade raw speed for intelligence, or make the opposite trade with the lighter and faster Qwen 3.6 35B A3B, the RTX Spark comes out on top. That bodes well for pairing popular agents like Hermes with intelligent local models on this platform.
But Nvidia's mission to reinvent the PC isn't a total grand slam in this first iteration.
First, this platform won't replace a dedicated gaming laptop. Even for those who only game on the side and have more forgiving standards for frame rates and input latency, the RTX Spark's gaming performance may not measure up to expectations.
When you put the overhead of Prism x86 emulation on top of the merely adequate performance of the Grace CPU, it’s clear that the Spark platform will have to work hard to keep up in the vast range of games that don’t have an Arm port.
The CPU-heavy Gears of War: E-Day is particularly unkind to the Prism-on-Grace stack, but even when a title like Control Resonant doesn't lean so heavily on the CPU, the limited and shared memory bandwidth of the GB10 SoC still poses an obstacle to cranking settings to the max despite the large amount of theoretical compute horsepower on tap.
We're also still waiting for Windows to fully catch up to Nvidia's ambitions for secure, manageable local agents. Our laptop expert Andrew Freedman and I couldn't test Microsoft's secure agentic AI promises within Windows 11, as the supporting features that Microsoft and Nvidia have promised to that end just aren't ready yet.
Still, for a first-generation mobile platform that joins complex silicon IP from multiple design teams onto one chip and relies on several OEM partners to bring it to life in highly integrated notebook form factors, the maturity of the RTX Spark platform is an impressive achievement. (Take it from someone who has seen a couple of rough product launches from the inside.)
Over the past week, I've been using the RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra as I would any other Windows laptop, and aside from a couple of tiny paper cuts, I have mostly just gotten my work done as I would with any other computer. And that’s a great — albeit a very, very expensive — place to be as the local agentic AI future coalesces.
Perhaps the biggest challenge for the RTX Spark platform is that the eye-watering price tags for the range of systems available at launch still buy a lot of cloud tokens from OpenAI and Anthropic. Emphasis on a lot. The Surface Laptop Ultra we tested lists for $5899 with only 1TB of storage, and lead times for that system are already out to late December.
If you're not as concerned about keeping sensitive data out of those labs’ clouds, or you don't expect to run afoul of acceptable usage policies, you'll get much smarter tokens much faster than you will from a local token factory like the RTX Spark, and you can get them on most any reasonably powered traditional PC you have available.
But if you're surfing the AI wave on local hardware for reasons of privacy, offline model availability, freedom to tinker, or just because you think it's cool, the RTX Spark platform blends the memory capacity, compute performance, and software resources you need to get there with the familiarity and broad compatibility of Windows on top. The fact that Nvidia, Microsoft, and their partners have delivered such a capable, compatible, and polished platform even in its first at-bat should put the rest of the PC industry on notice.
Nvidia’s efforts to reshape personal computing will face strong headwinds in the immediate future from the sky-high DRAM and NAND price hikes that the company’s own Vera Rubin rollout is partially responsible for. Perhaps when the dust settles in the next two to three years, and products built around the next-generation RTX Spark Superchips arrive, we can more confidently assess whether the company has accomplished its goal.
For now, the RTX Spark feels like a platform for those who fervently believe that open AI models will continue to get more intelligent within relatively small memory footprints, and that those potential future improvements are worth a hefty chunk of change to get ready for today. Maybe that's a smart bet in a world where compute is an increasingly precious resource. But unless you're a true believer with cash to burn, our first impressions suggest that you should wait until Microsoft and Nvidia fully lay the software foundation needed for this platform to deliver on its promises.

articles.title: Typed Decision Models on Tabular Data
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19536v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Typed decision models are language models that answer a question with a fixed set of possible answers by returning a probability for each answer instead of generating text. We study them on tabular data and compare four decision models with three large language models (LLMs) on row classification, fact verification and anomaly detection. Every request is sent in its original form and under 21 types of rewrite that keep its content, such as renaming the options or writing the table in another format. The decision models perform as well as the LLMs at a lower cost. Three of them are also far more robust to how the question is formulated. No model we test is robust to how the table is organized. For every model, at least a third of the row decisions change under some rewrite of the table or the question. The decisions to which a decision model gives low probability are the ones most likely to change. Decision models are a practical choice for tabular decisions, but their robustness remains an open problem.

articles.title: Can LLM Agents Efficiently Identify Appliance Faults? Insights From Diagnosing a Simulated Appliance
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19291v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: In so-called "Industry 4.0," integrated sensors, analytics tools, and other digital technologies supplement industrial workflows, potentiating enhanced visibility and automation. Prognostics and health management (PHM) and natural language processing (NLP) practitioners alike have explored the application of large language models (LLMs) to industrial asset management, but many prior works' focus on exam-like benchmarks has limited their assessment of LLMs' ability to automate practical operations. Herein, we introduce CoffeeBench, a fault diagnostics task for LLM agents, using a simulated appliance. The LLMs we evaluate struggle to consistently identify faults from the sensor information alone, but the best-performing ones can iteratively refine the fault-option space to eventually obtain a successful diagnosis. Our subsequent analyses, therefore, focus on: differentiating models by diagnostic efficiency (RQ1); examining the lagging performance of the three worst models (RQ2); and identifying viable heuristics for selective prediction (RQ3), including that initial diagnostic uncertainty and LLM-judged soundness of reasoning are high-signal predictors of diagnostic success. In addition to our benchmark results (Section 3.1), we provide practical insights for improving the performance of the open-weight models on CoffeeBench, such as by explicitly tracking episode state on their behalf to reduce timeouts (Section 3.2) or applying a deliberation loop to refine diagnostic hypotheses (Section 3.3).

articles.title: Singer or clanker? YouTube Music will tell you with new gen AI labeling.
articles.text:
Genuine human creativity takes time, but you know what doesn't? AI slop. There are countless AI models out there that can make something that passes for music, and you might come across those tracks on streaming services without realizing it. Google says it will begin labeling that content in YouTube Music, building on similar disclosures in the main YouTube app.
Google is not outright banning AI music or even speaking ill of it. "Generative AI is opening up new ways for artists to create, experiment, and share music," the company says in a blog post.
However, the company also acknowledges that people want to know if a song was created with generative AI tools. A new label for AI content on YouTube Music is now rolling out in the app and on the website, which looks a lot like a label Google began adding to AI-generated videos on YouTube earlier this year.

articles.title: More Than Seeing: Vision as Scalable Anchors in Native Multimodal Pre-Training
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19443v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Native multimodal pre-training trains a single model from scratch on text and multimodal data, enabling it to understand both language and visual inputs. However, how visual signals shape scaling behavior and support capabilities beyond visual understanding remains unclear. We investigate this question through controlled visual-content ablations across model sizes and training budgets. Specifically, we replace image embeddings with content-free padding token embeddings. Retaining visual content improves text prediction on image-text examples without materially changing the lowest text-only loss at a given compute budget, the optimal balance of model size and training data, or aggregate language scores. The relative multimodal loss benefit grows approximately as a power law of compute. To test benefits beyond understanding images, we evaluate spatial reasoning from text descriptions alone. Both conditions improve with model and data scaling. During training of the largest model, visual gains are most sustained in localization, navigation, and symbolic planning, which involve maintaining object configurations or composing spatial updates; gains in spatial relations, geometry, and physical commonsense are less consistent. These findings identify visual content as a scalable anchor for multimodal learning, with benefits that extend beyond visual inputs while preserving aggregate language performance.

articles.title: Samsung Presents ‘Design Is an Act of Love’ at Seoul Design Week 2026
articles.text:
Samsung Electronics today announced that it is presenting its “Design is an Act of Love” exhibition at Seoul Design Week 2026, taking place in Seoul, Korea.
The exhibition features 14 artworks inspired by Samsung products, displayed on the 2026 OLED TVs (model: S95H) fitted with frames customized for each work.
Building on the theme of the exhibition Samsung held with Korean artists at Design Miami Seoul 2026 in September, this iteration of “Design is an Act of Love” is being held with POLI.design in collaboration with emerging Italian artists. Through creative expression shaped by different cultures and experiences, the exhibition celebrates human diversity and individuality while sharing Samsung’s design vision rooted in understanding and caring for people.
“Through the eyes of different creative minds, familiar products become new expressions of personality, perspective, and ways of life,” said Mauro Porcini, President and Chief Design Officer of the Device eXperience (DX) Division at Samsung Electronics. “By bringing these interpretations together, we want to show how design can make technology a more personal part of everyday life. Ultimately, our ambition is to move beyond designing technology for people to designing technology that truly reflects them.”
14 Italian Artists Reinterpret Samsung Products Through Creativity and Imagination
The artworks draw inspiration from a range of Samsung products spanning mobile devices, home appliances, and TVs — including Music Studio 5, Bespoke AI Family Hub, and Galaxy Z Fold8.
The artists drew on their experience and imagination to reinterpret the forms and characteristics of Samsung products. They used AI as a tool to develop ideas and explore new forms of expression, with each work grounded in the artist’s own perspective and creativity.
Tommy Tokyo, a multidisciplinary artist whose practice spans virtual reality, animation, and digital media, created an artwork inspired by the Infinite AI air purifier. The work translates the product’s core concept of clean air into an expressive visual narrative. Caffè Design drew inspiration from The Serif TV’s iconic I-shaped silhouette, exploring how its distinctive design interacts with the surrounding space.
OLED TVs Showcase Expressive Design With Frames Customized for Each Artwork
The exhibition features 14 Samsung OLED TVs (model S95H), each fitted with a custom frame designed to complement its corresponding artwork’s colors and mood. Created specifically for the exhibition, the frames work together with the on-screen imagery to enhance the presentation of each work.
The Float Layer Design of the OLED TV (model: S95H) makes the screen appear to float above a metal plate. Together, the TV’s distinctive design and custom frames create a visual presentation that highlights the character of each artwork.
Visitors can experience Expressive Design — an approach that embraces human diversity and imagination — through the varied combinations of artworks and frames on the same TV model.
The exhibition will take place from Oct. 15-25 at Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP) in Seoul.

articles.title: J-tau: A Fully Localized Japanese Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19638v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: We present J-tau, the first publicly available Japanese benchmark for evaluating tool-using LLM agents in interactive customer-support scenarios. While tau-bench is widely used to evaluate LLM agents, it is English-centric and cannot evaluate agents in other languages. Existing multilingual extensions offer no public Japanese version and rely primarily on machine translation, leaving locale-specific entities such as addresses and currencies inconsistent with the target region. To enable reliable evaluation in Japanese, we carefully localize tau-bench through machine translation, entity adaptation, and human review. During this process, we also uncover and fix two flaws in the original tau-bench: invalid tasks and a score aggregation error that inflates certain models' results. Experiments show that J-tau yields fewer evaluation errors than a naively machine-translated counterpart and that our fixes resolve both flaws.

articles.title: Following the Flow the Law Requires: Training Voice Agents to Transfer to Unseen Regulated Procedures in Debt Collection
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.18881v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Voice agents built on large language models (LLMs) now handle customer calls, but in regulated applications completing the task is not enough: the agent must follow a conversational flow set by law. In debt collection, it must confirm it is speaking to the debtor before mentioning the debt, identify itself and the creditor, state the amount, and avoid prohibited language. Every creditor turns these rules into its own procedure and revises it. We ask whether a small, self-hosted policy can be trained once and then follow regulated procedures it has never seen. One machine-readable specification per deployment, FlowSpec, generates the policy instruction, gates the tools, supplies the supervision and defines the tests; the agent speaks only approved catalogue sentences. We fine-tune a 9-billion-parameter model on 2,506 conversations from 297 randomized procedures and evaluate a Thai outbound-call agent on four unseen deployment procedures (three debt collection, one non-debt), one from a wholly withheld lineage. Documented checks, fixed by the procedure, rise from 67--71 percents to 93--100 percents, while grounded checks, fixed by the conversation, already pass at 97--100 percents before training; scenario pass rate rises from 15/43 to 40/43. An audit of the shared specification finds 11 defects, 3 of which its own metric did not expose.

articles.title: From Copying to Composition: How Language Models Develop In-Context Learning
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19113v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows language models to adapt their behavior from instructions and demonstrations in a prompt, but accuracy alone does not reveal how contextual information controls their predictions. We study the acquisition and trainability of ICL with a controlled diagnostic that separates copying a nearby demonstration from integrating information across the prompt. Across 17 models, about a third prefer the copied answer, a few are undecided, and the rest prefer the rule-consistent answer, which goes with higher accuracy and with control by the requested value rather than the closest conflicting example. Checkpoint analyses show that models begin prioritizing task-relevant prompt tokens over conflicting examples long before their accuracy improves beyond chance level. In matched training experiments, synthetic documents that define endings and then query them shift models toward compositional responses on the controlled diagnostic, whereas fine-tuning on definition exercises built from rewritten real documents improves accuracy when prompts reassign label meanings. The results suggest that ICL is not acquired as a single, uniform capability. Instead, prompt control, answer preference, construction without candidates, and transfer can develop along distinct trajectories.
