articles.title: Two killed, one seriously hurt in explosion at Intel’s chip plant in Israel
articles.text:
Two workers have been confirmed dead and another seriously injured after an explosion at Intel’s Kiryat Gat plant in southern Israel on Wednesday, The Times of Israel reports. Police suspect a gas cylinder malfunction caused the explosion, and Israel’s Fire and Rescue Services said the fire involved nitrogen trifluoride (NF3), a toxic gas mainly used to clean the process chambers of chipmaking tools. So far, Intel hasn’t made any statements about the victims or about any potential production impacts at the site.
Go deeper with TH Premium: Chipmaking
(Image credit: tsmc)
Analyzing TSMC's fab expansion roadmap — multi-fab N2 ramp, CoWoS, SoIC, and uncorking bottlenecks
Leading-edge foundry roadmaps for TSMC, Intel, and Samsung
ASML's roadmap for chipmaking lithography tools examined
Chinese chipmaking tool roadmaps examined
The site houses Fab 28, which, per Intel, makes “processors, 5G, and AI products” on Intel 7, formerly 10nm Enhanced SuperFin. Intel 7 products include 13th and 14th Gen Core “Raptor Lake,” 5th Gen Xeon “Emerald Rapids,” and the I/O die of Xeon 6 “Granite Rapids,” although these are not explicitly linked to the site. Fab 38, adjacent to Intel’s existing Kiryat Gat fabs, was announced in December 2023 with a $3.25 billion Israeli grant but has been paused since mid-2024. Intel reportedly considered closing Fab 28 in July 2025, but no closure decision has been announced.
The Kiryat Gat police commander at the scene laid out the sequence: a blast occurred during a material transfer into the factory’s tanks after one truck had disconnected and another connected. At least eight Fire and Rescue Services teams, including hazmat, searched for trapped people, contained the fire, and monitored the hazardous substance.
“At this moment, I cannot point to any suspicion of criminal activity or negligence,” the commander added. Magen David Adom, Israel’s national emergency medical service, said two of the injured underwent resuscitation efforts and all three suffered severe burns. Ultimately, one of the injured was pronounced dead, a second later died of their wounds, and one remains hospitalized in serious condition inside the ICU, based on a statement from Soroka Medical Center in Beersheba.
The gas, although hazardous if inhaled, is not flammable. It’s not clear if the trucks were delivering NF3 or if it was directly involved in causing the explosion. Once the fire was put out, crews kept cooling the scene to prevent a secondary incident, and the commander said things appeared to be under control, with no sign so far of further leaks and no need to evacuate residents or factory workers. Kiryat Gat Mayor Kfir Suissa told residents to stay away while crews worked and added, “There is no danger to the public.”
At the time, there was no word on possible production delays, but these would be problematic as Intel 7 capacity was already tight. Last year the company’s CFO said that Intel 7 and Intel 10 constraints had limited its ability to meet demand, with shortages expected into 2026 with server wafers getting priority. Intel reports third-quarter results on Oct. 29 and will hold a call to discuss them, although the company has not mentioned whether it will address the explosion.

articles.title: Muse Spark Is Now an Open-Weights Model
articles.text:
Today, Meta is releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weights model to date. It’s available today on Hugging Face under the Muse Model License. Muse Spark Open runs optimized on the SGLang and vLLM inference engines, with optimization for NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel.
Building on our August release of Muse Spark, this open weights version has additional safety post-training to make it more robust against misuse as a standalone model without system guardrails. The result is a model that is a top open source choice for safety. Muse Spark Open is an 816B total/42B active parameter model with a context window of 1M tokens. Built for coding and agentic work, Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and shares the same base model as Muse Spark 1.3.
Meta loves open source, and as the creators of PyTorch, we’re committed to giving back to ensure the entire ecosystem fully supports Muse Spark Open. First, we’ve integrated Helion, our exciting new PyTorch-native high-level DSL for performant and portable ML kernels, to ship high-performance operations. Additionally, TorchTitan already supports Muse Spark out of the box for supervised fine-tuning and RL in the open, and we’re excited to see how far the PyTorch community can take it!
Muse Spark Open
Muse Spark Open is a coding-optimized open-weight model. Trained specifically for agentic coding workflows, it delivers higher first-attempt accuracy, reliable tool calling, and deep codebase understanding across the repos developers actually work in. You can read more in our previous model release blog here.
Enhanced Coding Capabilities
Strong at code generation, debugging, and codebase understanding. Trained on real developer workflows — multi-file refactors, debugging sessions, and long-running tasks — so the model keeps up with how you actually work. 1M context window means it handles your entire project including complex dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files without needing to break your task into pieces
Multimodal Understanding
Muse Spark Open has audio and audio-video perception — alongside image and document understanding. As a reasoning model, it processes image, audio, and text inputs — natively and reliably.
Agentic
Muse Spark Open is built from the ground up as an agentic model. It maps out steps, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long horizons — not just single-shot tool calls. It’s trained to browse the web (including multimodal browsing), and use an agentic harness to: spawn and coordinate subagents for decomposable work; and leverage computer use capabilities unified across desktop, mobile, and browser.  It’s trained on long-horizon, multi-site tasks, and generates separate commentary that lets the model state intent before acting—so you can always know what it’s doing and why.
Why Helion kernels?
Helion is a PyTorch native kernel authoring language designed for writing high-performance kernels across heterogeneous hardware platforms. Following early adoption from the open-source ecosystem, Helion became a part of the PyTorch Foundation in April 2026. Muse Spark Open ships with Helion implementations of operations such as RoPE, RMSNorm, quantization, etc., delivering 1.03 – 3.95x speedups compared to custom kernels written in hardware specific languages (e.g. NVIDIA CUDA and CuTe DSL) on NVIDIA GB300. These same kernels were directly portable for AMD, scoring similar performance improvements on AMD Mi350 with an overall 3% improvement in end-to-end throughput.
In addition, we also launched Helion megakernels for Muse Spark Open in SGLang. Written entirely in Helion, these kernels fuse multiple operations into a single persistent kernel to improve low latency inference, and can likewise be autotuned for different shapes and hardware.
Helion kernels can be further autotuned by users for broader hardware platforms and workloads – including different accelerator architectures (NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPU, etc.), quantization formats, tensor shapes, and parallelism strategies – without maintaining separate hand-tuned implementations for every configuration. Together, these capabilities make it easier to achieve portable performance while reducing the cost of developing and maintaining specialized kernels.
Post-training  with TorchTitan
TorchTitan is a PyTorch native platform designed for rapid experimentation and large-scale training of generative AI models. Starting today, TorchTitan adds a model definition for Meta’s Muse Spark Open , so developers can tune it to their needs.
TorchTitan features native support for multi-turn SFT and LoRA out-of-the-box, as well as reinforcement learning capabilities (TitanRL) that allow users to fine-tune Muse Spark Open.
Get Started
We’re sharing this work because we want everyone to have access to the best AI models. Muse Spark Open ships with custom, auto-tunable Helion GPU kernels in SGLang, delivering 1.03–3.95× kernel-level speedups on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs and a 3% end-to-end speedup on AMD MI350. You can also customize it for your use case by leveraging PyTorch’s TorchTitan to further tune the model.
Start Building Today: https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Spark-open-816B-A42B
Muse Spark is the full size model from our model family. We previously released Muse Glimmer, a small dense model. Start using it today, with ExecuTorch.
The post Muse Spark Is Now an Open-Weights Model appeared first on PyTorch.

articles.title: How Visko streams real-time world models on Google Cloud TPUs
articles.text:
Editor's note: Generative AI startups are moving rapidly beyond static clip generation to build interactive, real-time worlds. In this technical deep dive, we explore how AI startup Visko collaborated with Google Cloud TPU engineers to deploy Orbis — its continuously streaming Live World Model—on Cloud TPUs, going from initial kickoff to production handover in just 30 days.
What makes a live video world model so challenging to serve in production? The bottleneck isn't average throughput — it's beating a relentless real-time clock. Unlike offline video generators where a user submits a prompt and waits in a queue, a live world model streams continuously. Every new chunk of video and synchronized audio must finish rendering before the viewer finishes watching the previous one, or the world freezes.
Today, we're excited to share how Visko, an AI startup pioneering interactive world models, teamed up with Google Cloud to solve this exact challenge. Working side by side, Visko and Google Cloud engineers deployed Visko's end-to-end live inference pipeline — combining video generation, super-resolution upscaling, and synchronized audio—onto a single Cloud TPU slice. Together, the teams brought end-to-end generation down, rendering at 1.07x playback speed.
Here is an inside look at how we engineered the pipeline to hit that milestone in a single month, the architectural optimizations that moved the needle, and practical lessons for other startups building ultra-low-latency generative AI on Google Cloud.
Redefining interactive media with Live World Models
While most generative video platforms focus on rendering fixed, pre-baked clips, Visko is building what it calls Live Models: video world models that generate continuously and respond on the fly.
Visko's flagship model, Orbis, streams live video starting from a single text or image prompt. As the stream plays, viewers can enter new steering prompts in real time, dynamically evolving the scene without restarting or breaking continuity. For instance, in one test session, the livestream opens on a cat napping beside a crackling fireplace; when the viewer steers the scene to introduce a bowl of food, the bowl materializes seamlessly, and the cat stretches, stands up, and meows.
Since launching its public demo on September 1, 2026, Orbis has unlocked new possibilities across interactive entertainment, live commerce, AI companions, immersive education, and robotics simulation. To scale these interactive sessions reliably, Visko partnered with Google Cloud TPU engineers in August 2026 to port the Orbis live pipeline to Google's Tensor Processing Unit (TPU). Within 30 days, the full multimodal pipeline was running in real time on TPUs.
Visko’s ambition is to power a new generation of interactive worlds that people can step into and shape in real time. Streaming continuous video and audio under a strict clock is a fundamentally different system challenge than offline clip generation. Working side by side with Google Cloud's TPU engineers, we brought the full Orbis pipeline to TPUs in just 30 days — giving us the low-latency compute and memory bandwidth required to bring Live Models to creators and developers at scale.
"Visko is bringing an exciting new class of real-time, steerable workloads to the Cloud TPU ecosystem. By co-engineering their live multimodal pipeline on a singleTPU slice using JAX, torchax, and custom Pallas kernels, we proved how quickly a lean startup team can go from PyTorch prototype to render at 1.07x playback speed on Google Cloud's AI Hypercomputer."
– Dave Elliott, Head of Developer Advocacy for AI, Google Cloud
Live video is a hard-deadline problem
When you serve an offline clip generator, latency is forgiving — the user waits once while the backend processes frames. A live world model has no waiting room.
Every single chunk must be denoised, decoded from latents, upscaled to 1664x936 (at 18 fps), and paired with generated audio faster than realtime playback speed, for as long as the session runs.
Two structural constraints make live world models far more demanding than standard batch inference:
Batch size of one: Each live stream represents an individual viewer's interactive session. You cannot mask latency by grouping dozens of concurrent requests into a massive batch — the standard playbook for keeping AI accelerators saturated.
Strict sequential dependency: Every chunk depends directly on the one before it. Because the video model maintains a rolling memory of recent video latents so that chunk N+1 smoothly continues the action from chunk N, you cannot pre-render chunks out of order or parallelize across future timestamps.
For startup infrastructure engineers coming from LLM serving, it helps to think of live world modeling not as a tokens-per-second throughput benchmark, but as an unforgiving per-step latency SLO.
Architecting the multimodal pipeline on a single TPU slice
To keep infrastructure lean and cost-effective as Visko scales, the team designed the live pipeline to chain three distinct generative models on a single Cloud TPU slice running in BF16 precision.
When a viewer submits an initial prompt or a live steering update, all three generative models — the core video diffusion model, the super-resolution upscaler, and the audio generator — share the same chips, taking turns on the hardware for each chunk.
Figure 1: Visko's end-to-end Orbis live pipeline chains video diffusion, latent decoding, super-resolution upscaling, and pure-JAX audio generation sequentially on a single Cloud TPU slice, completing each chunk faster than the playback speed.
To combine rapid startup iteration with bare-metal accelerator speed, the software stack is built on three open-source pillars:
JAX: Google's high-performance Python array library for accelerators, compiled into optimized machine code by the XLA compiler.
torchax: An interoperability layer that runs PyTorch models directly on Cloud TPUs via JAX, enabling startup teams to bring existing PyTorch components over without an upfront, ground-up rewrite.
Pallas: The custom kernel programming language for TPUs in JAX.
Real-time performance breakdown: Hitting the clock
By profiling and optimizing each stage on a single slice in BF16, the engineering team achieved a total per-chunk latency of under the target while — maintaining roughly 7% headroom to absorb variance during live streaming:
Figure 2: Chart of per-chunk latency budget on one TPU slice.
Because video denoising accounts for nearly two-thirds of the total compute budget, that stage became the primary focus of our kernel and parallelism optimizations.
Inside the stack: Three optimizations that unlocked real-time streaming
1. Ulysses context parallelism across all TPU chips
A video chunk expands into a massive sequence of spatiotemporal tokens inside the video transformer. To distribute that workload across the TPU chips at batch size 1, the team implemented Ulysses context parallelism.
Instead of splitting model weights, Ulysses splits the token sequence across chips. Immediately before the attention layer, a high-speed all-to-all interconnect exchange regroups the tensors so that each chip holds the entire video sequence, but only for one-quarter of the attention heads. After each chip computes attention over the full sequence for its assigned heads, a second all-to-all exchange restores the sequence-split layout for the feed-forward layers.
Figure 3: Ulysses context parallelism across TPU chips at batch size 1. High-speed all-to-all Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) exchanges transition tensors between a sequence-split layout for feed-forward layers and a head-split layout for Pallas splash attention.
2. Custom Pallas splash attention from MaxDiffusion
To accelerate the attention computation itself, the team integrated a custom Pallas splash attention kernel from MaxDiffusion, Google Cloud's open-source reference library for diffusion models on Cloud TPU.
Splash attention brings FlashAttention-style tiling to TPU architecture: rather than materializing the full quadratic attention matrix in High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), it computes attention in compact tiles that remain inside ultra-fast on-chip VMEM. Startup teams can drop the exact kernel used in this port straight into their own pipelines via custom_splash_attention.py.
3. A 5.8x audio speedup by moving from torchax to pure JAX
We first brought all three Orbis models onto Cloud TPU with torchax, which runs PyTorch code on TPU through JAX and XLA without a rewrite. For the video and upscaling models, torchax paired with Pallas attention kernels met our latency target directly, and both stay in torchax in the final pipeline.
Only the audio model needed a rewrite. Moving the audio stage from torchax to native JAX made it 5.8x faster and brought the full pipeline under the playback deadline.
Field notes for AI builders: Cloud TPU lessons
Takeaways from tuning live multimodal inference on Cloud TPU:
Ulysses context parallelism for single stream video: At batch size 1, splitting the token sequence across chips with all-to-all interconnect exchanges was faster than both tensor parallelism and ring attention.
Native BF16 for continuous streams: FP8 quantization cuts memory bandwidth pressure, but small quantization errors build up across chunks in a continuous stream. Native BF16 kept visual quality intact within the latency budget.
Selective JAX ports: torchax kept the video and upscaling models in PyTorch, so the team only rewrote the audio bottleneck in native JAX.
XLA compilation caching: The first boot spends a few minutes compiling XLA graphs. Caching compiled artifacts brings worker restarts under a minute.
Building real-time generative models on Cloud TPU? Start here
If your startup is pushing the boundaries of live video, world models, or ultra-low-latency multimodal inference, you can build with the same toolkit that powered Visko's port:
Accelerate diffusion attention out of the box: Grab the open-source splash attention kernel used in this collaboration from MaxDiffusion, and explore the Pallas documentation to write custom TPU kernels.
Migrate PyTorch fast, then optimize selectively: Bring your existing PyTorch models onto TPU quickly with torchax, pinpoint bottlenecks with the Cloud TPU Profiler, and port latency-critical stages to native JAX.
Spin up TPUs on demand: Use TPU Flex-start VMs to provision TPU capacity for short development and benchmarking runs without a long-term reservation.
Scale with Google for Startups: Early-stage AI startups looking for cloud credits, technical mentorship, and access to Google Cloud's AI Hypercomputer stack can apply to the Google for Startups Cloud Program.
Special thanks to the Visko.ai team for the close technical partnership, and to the Google Cloud TPU engineers who lead the project including: Yixin Shi, James Huang, and Elisa Tsai.

articles.title: Tail Competition Explains Scaling in Best-of-N Sampling for Verifiable Problems
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19362v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Best-of-N sampling is a simple inference-time scaling strategy for large language models, yet its behavior under incomplete reward models remains poorly understood. We study Best-of-N as a competition between the extreme reward tails of correct and incorrect responses. This view shows that success depends not only on the probability of sampling a correct response, but also on whether correct responses dominate incorrect ones in the upper tail. Using extreme value theory, we characterize three asymptotic regimes: correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical explaining both monotonic gains and reward-hacking-induced degradation. We further derive finite-sample scaling laws for representative reward distributions, showing that, under Gaussian rewards, incorrect responses with sufficiently large variance can dominate selection even when their mean reward is lower. Unlike oracle selection, convergence with an incomplete selector can be polynomial rather than exponential. Finally, we propose a lightweight tail-tension criterion to estimate when additional sampling may become harmful. Experiments on synthetic data and real reward model scores are consistent with the theoretically predicted regimes, scaling laws, and diagnostic behavior, suggesting that tail competition provides a unified lens on Best-of-N sampling for verifiable problems.

articles.title: DecisionRobust: Benchmarking Robustness for JEV Style Decision Models Across Text and Vision
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19118v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Emerging decision models such as JEV provide typed interfaces that map task instructions and observations directly to choices, judgments, and scores. As these models are increasingly used for automated decision-making, understanding their reliability under adversarial manipulation becomes critical. We introduce DecisionRobust, a benchmark for systematically evaluating the robustness of decision models across textual and visual inputs. Our benchmark covers practical decision-making scenarios and a diverse suite of attacks, including semantics-preserving text perturbations, image perturbations, and prompt injection in both modalities. We curate evaluation sets through external validity checks and cross-model candidate selection. We evaluate 30 model configurations on text tasks and 17 on vision tasks, including 24 and 12 held-out models, respectively, that are excluded from candidate selection. Our experiments reveal several key findings. First, attacks expose vulnerabilities beyond the models used for construction and selection, although optimized image perturbations transfer weakly to many targets even with multiple surrogates. Second, relative model robustness varies across tasks and attack types, and resistance to input perturbations does not necessarily imply resistance to prompt injection. Third, label-consistency checks substantially reduce measured attack success across text and image settings, highlighting the importance of validating apparent failures. The benchmark is available at https://yifan-lan.github.io/DecisionRobust/.

articles.title: AgriJev: Efficient Agricultural Candidate Scoring with Multi-Scale Adapted Models
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19478v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Agricultural systems make decisions over heterogeneous entity types, textual judgments, and knowledge-question options. Generating a textual answer adds decoding and extraction steps to decisions that ultimately require a candidate choice. We introduce AgriJev, a family of adapted Qwen3.5 models at 0.8B, 2B, 4B, and 9B. A shared interface conditions on agricultural text, a judgment question, and candidate definitions, returning scores and relative probabilities in one forward call. We prepare source-aware training records and frozen evaluations from existing agricultural resources, retaining original groups and annotation provenance. Comparisons include original Qwen3.5 models and matched agricultural SFT models, both evaluated through native answer generation. Across 17 external test views, AgriJev-9B reaches 75.44% mean accuracy, exceeding the original and SFT generators by 5.89 and 3.79 percentage points. It outperforms the original generator on 13 views and narrows the mean gap to hosted Jev 1.13.0. On a fixed A100 workload, its median scoring latency is approximately half that of same-scale answer generation. Task-dependent gains and failures characterize a practical choice among agricultural model weights and inference contracts.

articles.title: Modernizing perimeter security: Scalable perimeters with VPC Service Controls
articles.text:
Agents represent a fundamental shift in cloud operations. They can act on behalf of users or autonomously, make non-deterministic decisions, and request data across projects at unprecedented speed and scale. Because agents are a distinct category of non-human identity (NHI), they require unique secure-by-default guardrails.
Traditional, manually-operated network perimeters are vulnerable to today’s machine-speed attacks. Overly permissive perimeters, built to avoid blocked connections, increase the risk of unauthorized data theft, but overly strict perimeters stall development under a flood of access denials.
Today, we're excited to announce key enhancements to VPC Service Controls (VPC-SC) that make perimeters easier to create, maintain, and scale. You can now add folders to perimeter membership, so that projects contained in them inherit policy. You can also manage granular exceptions and resolve denials with guided, scoped remediation.
The result is data protected by default, so you can scale autonomous agents across your enterprise without letting data leave your perimeter. This update is generally available, and at no additional cost.
Perimeters aligned to your architecture
VPC-SC provides a context-aware network security perimeter around your Google Cloud deployment, designed to secure your organization against data theft, even in the event of compromised credentials, identity and access management (IAM) misconfigurations, and insider threats. By extending network-layer protection across service-to-service interactions in Google Cloud's infrastructure, VPC-SC goes beyond traditional firewalls and creates an additional layer of defense that prevents access outside your corporate network — and is now easier for your organization to manage.
Cloud administrators configuring VPC-SC can now include folders in perimeter membership, automatically extending the folder’s access policy to every project and nested subfolder it contains. New workloads can inherit protection by default, with no further modification.
Figure 1: Simplified perimeter authoring in VPC-SC.
Perimeter membership updates when a project is moved, simplifying lifecycle maintenance. Security coverage follows the resource hierarchy that your organization already governs, and compliance verification requires only confirming that the resource is located in the correct part of the hierarchy.
Dry-run mode also supports folder membership, helping administrators evaluate the effect of a hierarchy-wide perimeter against live traffic before enforcement.
Folder and organization support in ingress and egress rules
Well-defined ingress and egress rules establish granular, context-aware perimeters without sacrificing operational flexibility across complex multi-project environments. Security administrators can now specify Google Cloud folders and organizations directly within those rules. A single hierarchy reference stands in for the set of projects beneath it, which keeps rules concise, keeps attribute counts well within quota limits, and extends access automatically to projects created later in the hierarchy.
Figure 2 : Simplified authoring of ingress/egress rules.
Using Private Service Connect endpoints in ingress and egress rules
Enterprises increasingly use private paths to reach desired endpoints in their deployment instead of exposing the traffic to the internet. Private Service Connect endpoints for Google APIs are now supported as an attribute in ingress and egress rules. Administrators can author a rule that authorizes access specifically over a designated private endpoint, producing a policy that corresponds directly to the connectivity architecture it is intended to govern.
Figure 3: Supporting Private Service Connect endpoints with ingress and egress rules.
For organizations that have standardized on Private Service Connect, including endpoints propagated across the estate through Network Connectivity Center, this provides both a more precise and a more concise means of expressing source for the request.
Service patterns in VPC accessible services
Service patterns in VPC accessible services provide granular control over Google APIs accessed with private Virtual IP addresses (VIP), permitting interoperability beyond just VPC-SC integrated services. If the workload requires controlled access to validated API endpoints over a private path, administrators can now allow only the specific API URL patterns required.
Additionally, the capability supports appending org-restriction-headers with egress requests to facilitate access to only authorized domains and resources. Because you don’t need to manage egress-proxy, you can accommodate legitimate operational requirements while maintaining a tightly-bounded private path, instead of choosing between a broad allowance and no access at all.
Figure 4: Granular control over Google APIs with service patterns in VPC accessible services.
Guided violation remediation
VPC-SC perimeter policies evolve continuously alongside the workloads they protect, and administrators periodically need to authorize a legitimate access request not yet covered. New Guided Violation Remediation in VPC-SC Violation Analyzer cuts resolution time for blocked requests from days to minutes by generating a policy fix with remediation recommendations, which you can validate in Dry-Run mode first.
Rather than just diagnosing why the violation occurred for a given denial, Violation Analyzer evaluates the blocked request against the applicable perimeter configuration, and proposes a specific configuration change, narrowly scoped by least-privilege design principles, to authorize the traffic: an ingress rule, an egress rule, an access level, or an update to VPC accessible services. This relieves pressure on administrators to broadly open up a perimeter just to resolve a violation and get an application working quickly.
Read more about how BlackLine uses Violation Analyzer to streamline investigations.
Figure 5 : VPC-SC Violation Remediation for faster turn-around.
Get started today
VPC-SC makes it simple and automated to deploy and refine granular network perimeter protection, even for autonomous agents. To get started:
Establish your folder baseline: Identify the folders in your resource hierarchy that correspond to the boundaries you intend to enforce, and define perimeters around them so that new workloads inherit policy on creation.
Run risk-free in Dry-Run mode: Observe production traffic safely without blocking active developers.
Unblock traffic with Violation Analyzer and Violation Dashboard: Use automated least-privilege remediation recommendations to resolve any  denials that surface.
Enforce with confidence: Secure your full data estate by transitioning to enforcement once your dry-run logs show your intended access with clean, authorized traffic.
To learn more about how VPC-SC can help simplify your data security posture and confidently secure your autonomous agent fleets, check out the VPC-SC documentation.

articles.title: Elon Musk calls out memory makers over 'extortionate' chip pricing, says Micron is playing smart for long-term loyalty
articles.text:
Elon Musk has criticized memory makers for what he calls 'extortionate' pricing amid an unprecedented shortage of both conventional DRAM and high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Although Musk did not identify the companies he criticized, his remarks seem to be directed at Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, as he praised Micron for its more 'reasonable' approach at the same time. Interestingly, Micron also enjoys exceptionally high profitability: its latest quarterly gross margin reached 81%.
Go deeper with TH Premium: Memory
(Image credit: SK Hynix)
AI data centers are swallowing the world's memory and storage supply
Samsung debuts three next-generation memory technologies for AI data centers
The future of DRAM: From DDR5 to future ICs
High-bandwidth memory roadmap
Inside the history of DRAM price-fixing lawsuits
"Micron has been reasonable regarding future memory prices, while others have been extortionate, which is something today's customers will not forget," Musk wrote in a post on X. "Micron is making the smart move for long-term customer loyalty."
Musk did not provide specific details of said extortionate pricing or disclose terms offered by different memory suppliers (which tend to be confidential). Consequently, it is impossible to determine whether Samsung and SK hynix charge substantially more than does Micron for comparable products. Nevertheless, Musk's remarks suggest considerable frustration with the pricing policies of South Korean memory manufacturers.
Over the past several quarters, memory has transformed from an easy-to-obtain commodity to a strategic asset, and makers of 3D NAND and DRAM have certainly benefitted massively from this shift. Historically, memory makers have responded to strong demand and rising prices with aggressive capacity expansions, which eventually led to oversupply and falling prices. This time around, however, manufacturers have raised memory prices severalfold without comparable increases in production capacity. As a result, supply still lags behind demand and will continue to do so for years to come, which puts further upward pressure on memory prices.
What makes Musk's praise of Micron particularly interesting is the company's financial performance, which clearly suggests that the company is taking advantage of the situation in the market. In its fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, Micron reported revenue of $54.23 billion and a GAAP gross margin of 81%, up from 40% a year earlier. The company's cloud memory unit earned $16.283 billion, and its non-GAAP gross margin totaled 83%; its core data center storage business sold goods worth $18.002 billion with a 90% gross margin; while sales of the automotive and embedded units totaled $6.824 billion with gross margins reaching 84%.
Perhaps the most surprising part of Micron's last quarter report was its mobile and client revenue of $13.114 billion and non-GAAP gross margin of 90%, which means that Micron earned higher profit selling memory and storage for client devices than it did for selling memory solutions for data centers. Such results clearly indicate that even supposedly reasonable memory prices can generate extraordinary profits in the current market.
Memory manufacturers are increasingly shifting toward long-term supply agreements (LTAs) that guarantee future supply and provide customers with predictable prices of DRAM, HBM, and NAND. So far, Micron has signed 26 strategic customer agreements that cover more than 35% of its expected revenue through 2030. These contracts include $32 billion in customer financial commitments, most of which consist of cash deposits. The company acknowledges that its new agreements reflect higher prevailing memory prices, and it by no means is trying to sell memory at a discount.
Samsung has reportedly secured long-term contracts covering 75% – 80% of its planned memory output in 2027, according to South Korea's ⁠Korea Economic Daily (via @Jukan05). SK hynix is reportedly pursuing similar arrangements as AI infrastructure investments continue to absorb available memory capacity.
Market insiders and analysts expect memory supply shortages to persist through at least 2028, and that gives manufacturers considerable leverage in contract negotiations. Memory suppliers have little incentive to reduce prices and are eager to enjoy their position, but Musk's warning suggests that today’s pricing policies could influence customer relationships once supply and demand eventually return to balance.

articles.title: Vision-Language Models Integrate Conflicting Evidence Like Biased Bayesian Observers
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19407v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Vision-language models must reconcile conflicting text and images. Prior work has characterized the resulting behavior in terms of modality biases--e.g., a "blind faith in text"--but why preferences vary across models, domains, and input conditions remains unclear. We develop a predictive account from a Bayesian perspective, positing that VLMs combine conditionally independent evidence from each modality with prior beliefs, subject to modality-specific biases. The resulting two-parameter cue combination model accurately predicts VLM preferences under unseen combinations of input degradation and transfers to new forms of unreliability without refitting. Separating evidence strength from integration bias explains how VLMs can follow text even while weighting visual evidence more heavily, reconciling reports of text and vision dominance under a single combination rule.

articles.title: A Unified Response Framework for Questions and Tutoring Dialogues
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19532v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Existing student models in educational applications largely focus on student responses to questions. However, as tutoring becomes more accessible at large scale, it is important to analyze dialogues between tutors and students, which may reveal fine-grained evidence on student knowledge. In this work, we propose a unified framework that models both student responses to questions and tutor-posed subtasks during dialogues on a shared item response theory (IRT) scale. We first identify mathematical subtasks in tutoring dialogues, rewrite them into self-contained questions, and identify the correctness of student responses to these subtasks. We then develop an IRT framework that estimates question/subtask difficulty from text, tracks students' evolving abilities across question-answering and dialogue interactions, and a novel method to leverages tutor moves between consecutive subtasks to regularize their difficulty values. We evaluate our framework on two real-world math education datasets containing both human- and AI-tutored dialogues. Results show that our framework outperforms strong baselines on both question difficulty prediction and response correctness prediction.

articles.title: HERO: Harnessing Evidence for Test-time Refinement and Prompt Optimization in Program Generation
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19184v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Harness optimization improves LLMs by refining reusable prompts and scaffolding, yet requires further adaptation for program generation tasks such as text-to-SQL and text-to-Python. Existing methods often rely on LLM reflectors to propose harness updates, which can fix observed failures but also disrupt previously correct behavior. Text-to-code tasks offer a natural way to mitigate this issue: we can execute generated outputs, allowing us to evaluate and verify the effects of proposed updates directly. Building on this signal, we introduce \textsc{HERO} (\textbf{H}arnessing \textbf{E}vidence for \textbf{R}efinement and \textbf{O}ptimization), which combines offline and test-time harness optimization. At the first stage, \method{} learns reusable prompt updates from execution-verified successes and failures and validates candidate revisions before adoption. At test time, we treat the generated code as an instance-specific harness and refine it using execution feedback. Across four SQL, Cypher, and Python benchmarks, \method{} achieves the best offline performance, improving pass@1 by \(7.6\) points over the initial prompt, while test-time refinement adds another \(2.0\) points and improves execution efficiency.

articles.title: Beyond Corrected Actions: Training LLM Agents on Textual Critiques
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19367v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for multi-turn agentic tasks that require interactions with users and environments over extended sequences of actions. A common approach to improving LLM agents is to use more capable expert models to provide training supervision, either by behavior cloning the expert's trajectories or by using the expert to correct the actions in trajectories generated by the weaker student model. However, expert LLMs can provide richer supervision than actions alone: they can directly generate textual critique that explain why specific actions are incorrect. We study whether training on such feedback benefits LLM agents and propose Critique-Augmented Agentic Fine-Tuning (CAFT), a framework that elicits textual expert feedback on student-generated trajectories. For each incorrect action, the expert yields both a corrected action and a textual critique explaining the student's mistake--which we then use as the training target for fine-tuning. Across four student models from the Nemotron 3 and Gemma 4 families on the agentic domains $\tau^2$-Bench Airline+Retail and WebShop, adding critiques to action-level supervision improves performance by 8% on average over action-only distillation. Additionally, CAFT checkpoints can also provide a better warm start for reinforcement learning than expert-trajectory distillation. Our results demonstrate that textual critiques can strengthen supervision for multi-turn LLM agents.

articles.title: Fantastic Metrics and How to Find Them: Meta-Evaluating Metrics for Multi-lingual Style-Personalized Generation
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19166v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Meta-evaluation of text generation metrics and LLM-judges is primarily conducted using metric-human correlations. However, prior work has shown that correlation is not an appropriate estimate of a metric's evaluation capability and can be unstable across evaluation settings, such as different datasets or languages. Therefore, we propose a regression-based meta-evaluation of metrics that learns on calibrated metric outputs to predict human ratings. We ground this measurement relative to a trivial constant-mean baseline and human agreements to provide a comparable measure of metric capability across evaluation settings. To test our meta-evaluation framework, we developed a large-scale multi-lingual style-personalized text generation (SPTG) benchmark, collecting multiple annotations across 10 topologically diverse languages and four evaluation dimensions, each with varying degrees of subjectivity. We meta-evaluated 32 metrics from three style evaluation paradigms (string-based, embedding-based, and LLM-judges) and their ensembles over these 40 evaluation settings. Our analysis revealed that even simple string- and embedding-based measurements can match strong LLM-judges when calibrated to human ratings. We also identified characteristics of human annotations that determine metric performance, as well as conditions under which a metric ensemble outperforms its individual constituents.

Abstract: This work concerns our submission for the Multilingual track of the 2026 BabyLM Challenge. We improve on our baseline using data that has been summarized and translated by an LLM, showing that higher-quality data can come from synthetic sources. We further improve with 2 simple changes: using a larger model, and using a character-level vocabulary. Both of these changes require LoRA-style fine-tuning for realizing their full potential. articles.title: TopicMerge: A Divide and Conquer Approach to Topic Modeling
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19323v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Recent advancements in topic modeling have split into two main paths: efficient embedding-based methods that offer scalability but are often outperformed on standard clustering metrics, and Large Language Model (LLM) approaches that achieve state-of-the-art clustering performance but at the cost of prohibitive computational expense and poor scalability. This paper introduces TopicMerge, a novel multi-stage pipeline that bridges these approaches to achieve both state-of-the-art clustering performance and computational efficiency. TopicMerge first employs an efficient clustering pipeline to deliberately over-segment a document corpus into a large set of fine-grained, semantically pure micro-clusters, which are then given initial semantic labels. It then introduces a novel, iterative merging algorithm where an LLM, guided by local neighborhood context, arbitrates on consolidating candidate pairs. These approved merges are then selectively executed and semantically relabeled by the LLM, hierarchically building broader, more coherent topics. Extensive experiments on the Bills and Wiki datasets show that TopicMerge achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance while reducing required LLM calls by over 92% compared to document-level methods, offering a practical and scalable solution.

articles.title: Weighted Ensemble Sampling for Rare-Event Estimation in Language Models
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19202v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Rare but severe failures of large language models can become practically significant at deployment scale. Estimating their probabilities with direct Monte Carlo sampling is highly inefficient, while proposal-based methods typically require auxiliary learning of an additional proposal distribution. We introduce \textbf{Weighted Ensemble (WE)}, a training-free framework for rare-event estimation in language models. WE samples exclusively from the original language model and improves upon direct Monte Carlo by periodically reallocating the sampling budget toward prefixes that appear more likely to reach the target rare event. To guide this reallocation without learning a separate proposal distribution, we exploit internal LLM representations as prefix-level signals and empirically validate their effectiveness. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on safety-related tasks spanning both small-scale and modern large-scale LLMs demonstrate that WE improves the efficiency and reliability of rare-event probability estimation.

articles.title: Pre-Trained Language Models as Zero-Shot Tools for Social Science Research
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19048v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Record linkage and demographic inference from names are routine demands in social science. Most approaches to these problems require labeled training data that are difficult or costly to acquire. I show that pre-trained language models perform both tasks accurately without requiring task-specific training. For record linkage, I introduce EnsembleLink, an algorithm that uses pre-trained embeddings alongside string-based scorers to retrieve a short list of candidates and then identify the likeliest matches. EnsembleLink matches or exceeds the performance of most prior approaches while generalizing across scripts and formats that those methods are unable to handle. For ethnicity inference from names, I show that large language models (LLMs) achieve up to 83.8% accuracy on U.S. voter files, compared to 78.0% for name-supplemented BISG. Open-weight models offer reproducible implementations that approach these models in accuracy. Moreover, LLMs are able to infer group membership for religious, caste-based, and other ethnic group categories outside of the United States, and reduce bias in downstream estimates of geographic racial gaps. Where pre-training encodes the world knowledge required by each task, task-specific labels add less information.

articles.title: The Download: reviving frozen pig kidneys and boosting nuclear power
articles.text:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists.
The kidneys, which are similar in size to human ones, were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working.
The results are a big milestone. But the team still needs to establish whether the approach could work for humans.
Dissect what the breakthrough means for organ transplantation.
—Jessica Hamzelou
How much more can nuclear power plants give?
In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant. Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about the nuclear industry trying to do just that.
Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants. On October 5, the Department of Energy awarded Vistra a $4.2 billion loan to upgrade three plants.
Pushing existing reactors to produce more could quickly provide more clean power for data centers. But just how much additional power can we count on?
Read the full story to find out.
—Casey Crownhart
This story is from The Checkup, our weekly climate and energy tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.
10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: BasiGo and its fleet of electric buses
BasiGo is one of MIT Technology Review’s10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.
BasiGo aims to replace the tens of thousands of diesel-powered buses on sub-Saharan African roads with electric ones that generate far fewer emissions. Its pay-as-you-drive business model helps make EVs more attainable for private bus operators, while the company provides leasing, maintenance, insurance and charging infrastructure.
The company has more than 150 electric buses on the road in Kenya and Rwanda, with a reservation list of 1,200 customers. Now it’s targeting another major source of pollution on the roads: trucks.
Here’s how BasiGo is working to electrify public transport in Africa.

articles.title: From Smart City to Race Circuit: Samsung’s The Wall in Control Rooms
articles.text:
On the front lines of crisis management, where timely decisions are critical, control rooms are evolving to meet the demands of today’s highly connected society. Moving beyond traditional monitoring, they have become centralized hubs that manage growing volumes of video and data while overseeing communications networks.
From industrial operations to sports and critical infrastructure, organizations around the world are turning to Samsung’s The Wall. Among them are the Iskandar Puteri Command and Control Centre (IPCCC), the integrated operations center for Iskandar Puteri City Council, Johor, Malaysia; and NASCAR, one of the world’s leading motorsports organizations.
▲ The Wall at the Iskandar Puteri Command and Control Centre’s control room
Engineered for Mission-Critical Control Rooms
While the information displayed on screen varies across industries, every control room requires robust security and unwavering reliability.
The Wall uses the industry-standard Advanced Encryption Standard 128-bit (AES-128) encryption algorithm and Samsung’s proprietary Knox Security platform to securely encrypt data transmitted from S-Box to Cabinet.
AES-128, a symmetric-key encryption algorithm adopted by the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), protects sensitive control room information while enabling fast data transmission and reception.
Designed for uninterrupted 24/7 operation, The Wall incorporates redundant power and signal systems. If an unexpected power failure or signal error occurs, the backup system activates immediately to ensure continuous monitoring and control.
The Wall’s modular chip-on-board (COB) architecture allows individual modules to be replaced quickly while the display remains on, minimizing downtime. With an LED lifespan1 of up to 150,000 hours — among the longest in the industry – it also helps reduce long-term total cost of ownership (TCO).
Optimized for control room environments, The Wall offers a modular, scalable design that can be customized to virtually any space. Advanced display technology ensures large volumes of information are presented with clarity and precision.
IPCCC: Cross-Agency Coordination for Faster Emergency Response
Urban crises often unfold as a chain of interconnected events. For example, if a water main bursts, traffic may need to be redirected immediately. If a major traffic accident occurs, firefighters conducting rescue operations and police managing the scene must coordinate in real time.
In Johor, Malaysia, IPCCC uses Samsung’s The Wall to support integrated city monitoring and coordination among relevant agencies. IPCCC selected The Wall for its image quality, color richness, and brightness, as well as Samsung’s reputation as a reliable long-term technology partner.
▲ The Wall supports IPCCC’s city operations monitoring with an immersive visual experience.
IPCCC brings together traffic, public safety, and environmental monitoring data onto a single, unified display. Anchoring the operations center is Malaysia’s longest The Wall installation, spanning 19.35 meters and capturing the city’s vast network of information on one screen.
Today, the massive display serves as the command hub for citywide operations — from security monitoring to coordinated incident response. By consolidating this information, The Wall supports stronger inter-agency coordination across departments.
▲ The Wall helps IPCCC city operations teams monitor traffic, public safety, and city services.
“Installing a curved large-scale display allows us to maximize the space while maintaining an efficient operational layout for our workstation and war room,” said Farah Izzati Binti Muhamad Fuad, Director of the Smart City Unit at IPCCC. “The ultra-wide screen enables us to monitor multiple smart safety systems, improving coordination and allowing our team to respond more quickly to incidents.”
NASCAR: Race Control for Split-Second Decisions
Beyond public services, control systems also play a critical role in sports — where capturing every moment of the action is essential. In motorsports, where speeds exceed 290 kilometers per hour and up to 40 cars race in close formation, officials must assess incidents and make decisions in fractions of a second.
▲ The Wall provides NASCAR’s Remote Race Control center with a large, clear view of live race data, video feeds, and on-track conditions.
NASCAR, the most popular motorsport in the U.S., built its Remote Race Control center around The Wall to support race control staff at the track with additional monitoring, analysis, and replay capabilities. Measuring 9.75 meters wide and 2.74 meters high, the massive display provides up to 24 officials a shared, high-resolution view, giving them the visual clarity to review and manage split-second race incidents together.
Equipped with a Micro AI Processor, The Wall analyzes complex live footage in real time to reduce noise. This enables dynamic camera feeds from around the track to be displayed in ultra-high definition with minimal noise and motion blur, helping officials make fast, accurate decisions.
At the launch in 2025, Steve Stum, NASCAR Vice President of Operations and Technical Production, highlighted the visibility that Remote Race Control would provide through more than 200 camera angles and multiple data points from every car, along with its potential to enable faster, more accurate competition calls and improve the racing product. Now in its second season of operation, the remote race control room gives officials greater visibility across races and supports more efficient and accurate officiating.
By consolidating multiple video feeds and data streams on The Wall, the remote race control room enables officials to view more information simultaneously and share feeds for collaborative review.
Describing the experience, Scott Miller, competition strategist at NASCAR, said, “It’s like having 20 monitors in front of you, as opposed to probably two or three sitting at a single work station.”
▲ Samsung technology supports NASCAR’s Remote Race Control center at its production facility in Concord, North Carolina.
Control rooms across industries are evolving to meet increasingly complex demands — whether ensuring the stable operation of infrastructure, enabling integrated citywide monitoring, or supporting live sports where decisions made in fractions of a second can make all the difference. Regardless of the application, every control room depends on a display that helps operators process vast amounts of information and make fast, accurate decisions. As a safe and reliable visual hub for mission-critical operations, Samsung’s The Wall will continue to provide the clarity needed to support decision-making across major industries worldwide.
LED lifetime refers to the rated operating time (L50) until an LED’s brightness decreases to 50% of its initial output. ︎

articles.title: Unsupervised AI agent deletes TV show’s entire edit weeks before release; program can't air
articles.text:
The Swedish edition of the athletic competition show The Challenge just faced a real challenge when an AI agent deleted months of work editing the show just weeks before release. The program director blames the disaster on a failed backup system, leaving no way to recover the edit and forcing them to recut the entire season from the raw footage that thankfully was not deleted.
According to Aftonbladet’s sources, the AI agent was given access to the production server and deleted the finished season. There are no reports on what the AI agent’s role on the production server is, but it seems that file management may be one of them due to file-handling permissions. TV4, the commissioner of the show, conducted an investigation and stated the mishap was due to “the human factor” and not AI.
One of the most prominent teachings of backing up is that data is still not safe from the user despite having redundancies; RAID systems protecting data from drive failures are one thing, while accidental deletions are another — however, an AI agent deleting your files is something else entirely.
We can’t speculate on what the AI agent’s job was, but file mishandling is something that isn’t unique to Mastiff’s production team. There have been several cases of AI agents deleting stuff they shouldn’t, like this story of an AI coding platform’s entire database being deleted, this story of Google’s Antigravity agent wiping a user’s entire hard drive, or Claude deleting a developer’s entire production setup, and many other catastrophic AI agent deletion cases.
However, TV4’s program director stated before its investigation of the incident that it was not an AI agent that acted independently, despite also stating that it wasn’t clear what happened. One clear thing, however, is that their backup system failed, which is worse than deletion, as the production team’s hard work can’t be recovered easily. There are ways to potentially recover the data if there are snapshots or version histories; even forensic recovery is an option, but TV4 has kept its investigation details private, so it’s hard to say how much is realistically recoverable, if at all.

articles.title: Bringing the borderless Lakehouse into the agentic era with innovations for Gemini
articles.text:
As enterprises shift their AI usage from experimental chatbots to autonomous agents, teams are hitting a critical bottleneck: accessing and reasoning over data scattered across multiple clouds, SaaS platforms, and on-premises systems. To turn AI agents into true systems of action, organizations need a foundation that can handle petabyte-scale reasoning without the security risks of data movement. Last week at our Gemini at Work event, we announced how Gemini can help you transform business workflows. To help power your agents with your enterprise data, we will dive deeper into the new Gemini integration with borderless Lakehouse to help you build, secure, and scale agents that work across your data estate.
Access data that lives outside of Google Cloud through Gemini
The ultimate value of the borderless Lakehouse is realized through the agents you build to transform your organization, with Gemini as the front door. With the new Gemini integration, data that’s either preconfigured or stored in your borderless Lakehouse is now directly integrated into Gemini. Currently in preview, this means you can set up access to new data sources, such as Databricks Unity Catalog or Snowflake Horizon, through Lakehouse catalog federation directly from Gemini.
Now your business users can use natural language to query records that live across clouds while your AI agents can ground their reasoning and generate code from the same data — all without moving it. By directly contextualizing AI agents across your borderless Lakehouse, you can help accelerate your organization’s AI adoption while simplifying access to critical information.
Gemini agents invoked by business users can access data that lives in BigQuery and Databricks Unity Catalog to provide comprehensive reporting and get insights using natural language.
Borderless Lakehouse advancements
In addition to this new, native integration with Gemini, we’re sharing  that several features we introduced earlier this year to power your data foundation with the borderless Lakehouse are now generally available, including:
Support for Cross-Cloud Interconnect and cross-cloud caching for AWS and Azure
BigQuery support for Apache Iceberg V3 specifications
Read-write interoperability on Apache Iceberg tables for both BigQuery and Managed Service for Apache Spark
Bi-directional caching with AWS Glue, Databricks Unity Catalog, and Snowflake Horizon Catalog using Lakehouse runtime federation
Integration with Knowledge Catalog
Zero-copy data integration with Salesforce, SAP and Workday, and now, Confluent Tableflow
Synchronization of Databricks Delta Lake assets through the Lakehouse console using Dataflow
Let’s explore.
Performance and reasoning at petabyte scale
While agent context windows are typically limited to ingesting hundreds of kilobytes at a time, enterprise workflows sometimes join petabytes of data across clouds. An agent-native data platform that needs to combine data across sources, like product and customer data, to your CRM cloud and warehouse telemetry needs to be able to process data at scale. When you do this over MCP, you are limited to megabyte scale because of context windows and payload size. By integrating at every layer of the data and AI stack, the borderless Lakehouse provides enterprise-grade scalability, enabling agents to reason over petabytes of data with similar performance to it being stored locally.
At the networking layer, Cross-Cloud Interconnect and cross-cloud caching provide high-throughput, low-latency paths to AWS and Azure, eliminating variable egress fees. When an agent joins Iceberg tables in Amazon Azure Data Lake Storage with data in BigQuery, every uncached byte it scans crosses a cloud boundary, so the network sets the pace. Cross-Cloud Interconnect gives the Lakehouse a dedicated, private connection between Google Cloud and AWS or Azure, at 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps per connection. Lakehouse queries travel over that connection rather than the public internet, so latency stays low and predictable. Cross-cloud caching serves repeat reads from inside Google Cloud, so agents can query data in other clouds without migrating it.
The borderless Lakehouse includes several key optimizations to integrate Iceberg metadata within the query engine. BigQuery now supports Apache Iceberg V3 specifications, including binary deletion vectors and sort orders. These features allow the engine to handle row-level updates and deletes more efficiently by eliminating the need to rewrite entire data files. We also upgraded BigQuery’s execution engine with a new FlatBuffers-based Parquet reader and parallelized I/O to help reduce CPU overhead and serialization bottlenecks and narrow the performance gap between open formats and native storage.
This builds upon recent performance innovations to the query engine designed to support agent workloads, which often come in herds and need to process small queries quickly and cost effectively. With BigQuery fluid scaling and history based optimizations, you can run scalable and efficient agent workloads while maintaining openness with Apache Iceberg.
Meanwhile, read-write interoperability on Apache Iceberg tables for both BigQuery and Managed Service for Apache Spark makes it easy for all of your data teams to work off the same Iceberg tables in Google Cloud Storage. This vertically optimized stack helps make your agents faster and more cost-effective, leveraging the power of BigQuery and Lightning Engine to activate data without moving it. To expand the analytical depth of the lakehouse, graph support for Iceberg in BigQuery lets you analyze relationship networks, such as supply chains, directly on open table datasets.
Comprehensive context and data access for your agents
An AI agent is only as smart as the context it can access. To help prevent hallucinations and improve accuracy at the metadata layer, the borderless Lakehouse unifies your enterprise data using the Lakehouse runtime catalog. Based on the Apache Iceberg REST Catalog, it provides bi-directional catalog federation with AWS Glue, Databricks Unity Catalog, and Snowflake Horizon Catalog. The Lakehouse runtime catalog also includes a new standard Hive Metastore-compatible endpoint, allowing engines like Apache Spark, Trino, and Presto to discover metadata without architectural changes.
The borderless Lakehouse also integrates directly with Knowledge Catalog, which automatically indexes your distributed data assets, to provide the precise business metadata and semantic definitions agents need to reason over your entire enterprise corpus — including unstructured data in Cloud Storage. This gives agents just enough context to be accurate while controlling token costs, helping you develop an intelligent and sustainable agentic strategy.
The borderless Lakehouse provides zero-copy data integration with your SaaS applications like Salesforce, SAP and Workday and integrates with a larger partner ecosystem, capturing enterprise data in Knowledge Catalog and acting as a single context engine for your agents. Today, we’re expanding the partner ecosystem with new integrations for Confluent Tableflow, now generally available, which syncs to Lakehouse runtime catalog so the Iceberg tables it produces show up directly in BigQuery, with no copying and no extra ETL.
Finally, organizations with Databricks-centric repositories can now easily import, transform and synchronize their Delta Lake assets into Lakehouse through the Lakehouse console using Dataflow.
Modernize with ease
Customer use of Apache Iceberg has more than tripled since the beginning of 2025, and enterprises building with Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse are seeing significant impact from it:
Etsy unified three petabytes with borderless Lakehouse, joining data in place to accelerate pipeline queries by 60%.
Commerzbank transforms raw distributed data into governed, agent-ready access.
Hightouch integrates directly with borderless Lakehouse so teams can power their marketing directly on an open Iceberg lakehouse and activate that data across the Google Cloud ecosystem.
Roundel modernized its Target Product Ads technology stack from the ground up with borderless Lakehouse, completely rebuilding its data ingestion, processing, and measurement pipelines.
If you are ready to get started with the transition to borderless Lakehouse for your organization, it doesn’t need to be difficult. For organizations currently using legacy Dataproc Metastore, we now offer an automated, zero-downtime migration path to the serverless Lakehouse runtime catalog. This preserves your existing schemas and lineage while unlocking the AI-ready features of the borderless Lakehouse, so you can stop managing infrastructure and start activating agents.
Get started today with the Build a borderless Lakehouse codelab or visit our website to learn more.

articles.title: DAGFormer: Global Topology Prediction for Transformer Cross-Layer Connections
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19625v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: We propose DAGFormer, a Transformer language model whose cross-layer connections are planned by a jointly trained topology predictor. Beyond the residual connections in a standard Transformer, DAGFormer adds direct connections from earlier layers to later ones, and the predictor controls the strength of every connection based on input tokens. Unlike existing cross-layer routing architectures, which set each layer's connections separately, DAGFormer plans the routing of the whole model at once. On matched OLMo-2 pairs from 75M to 1B parameters, DAGFormer lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by 17% to 25% over the vanilla Transformer, and a 1B DAGFormer trained on 5B tokens outperforms the vanilla model trained on 10B. Against four routing baselines with the same data and budget, it reaches the lowest perplexity at 75M, 300M and 1B. The gain carries over to 13 commonsense, science, reading and math evaluation tasks (2.0 to 2.5 points higher mean accuracy at 300M and 1B) and to instruction finetuning (63% to 70% AlpacaEval win rate against the vanilla Transformer, leading every routing baseline), and under structured pruning DAGFormer degrades the least in five of six settings.

articles.title: GraphRAG-LTM: A Layered Threat Modeling Framework for Attacks on Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19549v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) uses document-derived knowledge graphs to assemble evidence for large language model (LLM) answers. Its security depends on both the seed chunks retrieved for a query and the graph evidence assembled from them, yet attacks on this evidence path remain underexplored. We introduce GraphRAG-LTM, a Layered Threat Modeling framework that tests three nested levels of attacker access. BB Query uses ranking feedback to make query edits under a semantic-similarity constraint and demote relevant seed chunks. WB Query uses retriever gradients for the same objective. Graph-aware WB keeps the white-box adversarial query and deletes bridge triplets from the query-specific evidence graph, disrupting multi-hop evidence propagation through localized graph edits. Across datasets, retrievers, and LLM backbones, rank feedback alone reduces answer quality, gradient access strengthens query attacks, and bridge-triplet deletion further impairs supporting-fact retrieval. Further analyses show how seed retrieval and graph evidence jointly contribute to these failures.

On RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell and RTX 5090 the same entry point gains a backend="cake" decode and prefill path for the NVFP4 cache and a decode path for the DeepSeek-V4.1 mixed FP8/FP4 cache (SM120 and GB10/SM121), plus fused RoPE, NVFP4 quantize and paged-insert cache writers. These backends are opt-in.

Speculative-decode verification runs faster on B200 and B300
BatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheWrapper(backend="auto") on B200 and B300 routes multi-token decode rows (two to four query tokens per request, as in speculative or multi-token-prediction verification) of fp16/bf16 head-dim-128 grouped-query-attention models to cuDNN, which lowers verification decode latency. The route needs nvidia-cudnn-frontend[cutedsl]>=1.31.0. Single-token decode and runs with explicit determinism controls stay on FA2; FLASHINFER_DECODE_AUTO_CUDNN=0 pins FA2.
#5508 feat(cudnn): backend="auto" takes cuDNN for the multi-token paged-decode rows its default FROST engine serves faster (cudnn-frontend 1.30+)
Expert-parallel MoE comes to H100 in BF16 and to SM120 in W4A8
H100 serves an expert-parallel MoE round entirely in BF16 through MoEEpLayer with Sm90_Bf16_Bf16_Bf16_PushCake_MegaMoeConfig: BF16 dispatch, fused SwiGLU, a deterministic combine over a pre-reduced BF16 wire, CUDA Graph capture and up to 32 ranks on one node. SM120 workstations get a W4A8 MegaMoE backend (Sm120_Mxfp4_Mxfp8_Bf16_Cutedsl_MegaMoeConfig) with CUDA Graph replay and uneven token counts across ranks. SplitConfig(comm=..., kernel=...) picks an NVLink one-sided, CAKE or NVLink two-sided communication backend, or the NCCL-EP or NIXL-EP transports, independently of the expert kernel.
#5958 feat(cake_mega_moe): SM90 native BF16 MegaMoE expert compute through MoEEpLayer (sm90_bf16_bf16_bf16_push_cake)
#6058 feat(cake_mega_moe): pre-reduced BF16 combine wire and fixed-cost levers for the SM90 MegaMoE backend
#4632 [SM120] Add W4A8 CuTeDSL MegaMoE backend
#5532 refactor(moe_ep): add a MoE-level communication interface for EP dispatch/combine
⚠️ Upgrade notices
Install nvidia-cudnn-frontend>=1.31.0. The cuDNN linear-attention backend and the automatic cuDNN decode route need the cutedsl extra: pip install -U 'nvidia-cudnn-frontend[cutedsl]>=1.31.0'.
After upgrading flashinfer-python, run flashinfer download-kernels to replace mismatched flashinfer-cubin and flashinfer-jit-cache wheels; --sm sm90a (repeatable) limits it to named architectures.
Rename callers of cutlass_fused_moe_prepare_workspace to cake_fused_moe_prepare_workspace, replace prepare_bgmv_moe(..., backend="blackwell") with backend="cake", and import the cuDNN Frost MoE configs from flashinfer.fused_moe (the flashinfer.experimental path is a one-release shim).
Sampling: batch-length seed and offset tensors apply one value per output row; callers passing distinct per-row values sample differently from before.
