articles.title: Evaluating Compressed Memory: Dependence, Utility, and Content Benefit
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19373v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Does a language model answer better because its compressed memory contains useful document information? Replacing memory vectors with zeros can lower a trained model's score without showing that it outperforms a model trained without memory. We combine zeroing with separately trained models that cannot access stored text or receive the same constant input for every document. Across nine systems, some models rely on memory yet perform worse than the trained alternative. For example, in experiments that predict states in generated stories, zeroing memory worsens a model's prediction loss, yet a model trained without memory achieves lower loss than the original model with intact memory. On TriviaQA, giving xRAG memory from another question's passage raises F1, which measures word overlap with accepted answers, from 19.38 without a document to 24.78. Its effect on how often outputs contain an accepted answer is statistically uncertain. The question's retrieved passage scores higher still (29.88 F1). Thus a gain over no document alone does not establish that the gain requires the question's passage. Evaluations must therefore specify the comparison model, absolute performance, and generation and scoring conditions.

articles.title: Bringing ExecuTorch to Arm Cortex-M CPUs
articles.text:
TL;DR
Deploying PyTorch models on microcontrollers has historically required converting to other framework formats, maintaining separate toolchains, and debugging cross-framework numerical mismatches. ExecuTorch eliminates this conversion step entirely.
The Cortex-M backend enables PyTorch models to run directly on Arm Cortex-M CPUs with Arm CMSIS-NN acceleration. It supports all capability tiers (Scalar, DSP, and MVE/Helium) from a single workflow.
We benchmark four of the five models from the MLPerf Tiny suite on the Alif Ensemble E8. Each model runs in 21.5 ms or less and uses under 90 KiB of RAM on a single Cortex-M55 core.
For heterogeneous SoCs, the Cortex-M backend also provides the CPU execution path alongside Ethos-U NPU delegation.
Minimal binary footprint. The ExecuTorch core runtime is under 20 KiB of flash, and operator selective build links only the operators your model needs, so total code size scales with the model rather than the framework.
Background
Microcontrollers power billions of always-on devices: wearables, industrial sensors, voice interfaces, and smart home appliances. These devices operate under extreme constraints: often less than 1 MB of SRAM, single-digit megabytes of flash, and power budgets measured in milliwatts. Despite these limitations, there’s growing demand to run meaningful ML workloads on these platforms and the hardware is evolving to meet it. Modern Cortex-M based microcontroller units (MCUs) now include DSP & vector ISAs, large tightly-coupled memories (TCMs), and power-efficient NPUs such as the Arm Ethos-U NPU that make ML inference more practical in resource constrained devices.
Until now, deploying ML on Cortex-M meant leaving the PyTorch ecosystem. Developers had to convert models to alternative formats, maintain separate toolchains for training and deployment, and debug numerical mismatches introduced during conversion. For teams that train in PyTorch, which accounts for over 90% of the research code published at top ML conferences, this translation step adds friction to every iteration cycle.
ExecuTorch was designed to eliminate this gap. Arm MCU support has been available through the Ethos-U NPU, and the Cortex-M backend extends it to Cortex-M CPUs, so a model can run on parts with or without an accelerator. The trained PyTorch model is exported, quantized and lowered for the device within the same stack that serves models on mobile, desktop and server.
The Cortex-M Backend
The ExecuTorch Cortex-M backend replaces standard PyTorch operators with CMSIS-NN-backed custom operators through ahead-of-time compiler passes. At inference time, these operators call directly into Arm’s CMSIS-NN library, an open source collection of optimized neural network kernels for Cortex-M processors.
Key properties:
CMSIS-NN accelerated. Quantized operations (linear, conv, add, mul, softmax, activations, etc.) are replaced with optimized implementations that call CMSIS-NN functions and additional optimized Cortex-M implementations directly.
Target-aware compilation. The CPU variant (M0 through M85) and ISA tier are specified at compile time, so the correct CMSIS-NN backend is selected, eliminating runtime dispatch overhead.
Purpose-built quantizer. Produces INT8 quantized graphs matching the data layout requirements of CMSIS-NN kernels, using PyTorch’s PT2E quantization framework.
Single compiler toolchain. The Cortex-M lowering path operates directly on the ExecuTorch edge dialect, keeping the compilation pipeline simple and debuggable.
Cortex-M Capability Tiers
The backend targets the full Cortex-M spectrum:
Tier
Cores
Key Feature
Use Case
Scalar
M0, M0+, M3, M23
Standard ARM instructions
Ultra-low-cost, minimal silicon
DSP
M4, M7, M33, M35P
SIMD multiply-accumulate
Mid-range MCUs, signal processing
MVE (aka Helium)
M55, M85
128-bit vector ops, beat-based execution
High-performance MCU ML inference
Arm Helium technology is where the biggest performance gains are. CMSIS-NN leverages Helium’s beat-based execution model to pipeline data movement and compute, providing significant throughput gains for the depthwise and pointwise convolutions common in edge ML architectures. That said, the same workflow targets all variants. The target configuration selects the appropriate backend automatically.
ExecuTorch is Embedded Friendly
Unlike mobile or cloud environments that must accommodate varied hardware at runtime, microcontroller deployments target a fixed hardware profile. Embedded developers possess precise knowledge of their deployment target, including the exact CPU core, available ISA extensions, SRAM allocation, and flash capacity.
ExecuTorch’s ahead-of-time stack is designed to exploit this. ExecuTorch makes target-specific decisions at compile time: graph-level optimizations, memory planning, weight packing, and kernel selection are all target-aware at compile time.
Concretely, for Cortex-M this means:
Graph-level compute elimination. Redundant dtype conversions, quantize/dequantize pairs, and memory format transposes are removed during lowering, so only necessary compute reaches the device.
Quantization parameter folding. Scale and zero-point arithmetic is precomputed into integer multiplier/shift form at export, so quantized kernel inference stays entirely in fixed-point.
AOT weight layout transposition. Convolution weights are transposed from PyTorch’s native layout (OIHW) to CMSIS-NN’s expected format (OHWI) at export time. The permute cost is paid once during compilation and never at inference.
Static memory planning across heterogeneous memories. All tensor and scratch buffers are allocated and laid out ahead of time, with support for spanning multiple memory regions (e.g., TCM and SRAM). Developers can also customize placement to put latency-critical buffers in fast local memory. No heap allocator, no fragmentation, and no runtime memory management required.
Target-specific operator replacement. The CortexMPassManager selects CMSIS-NN kernel variants matched to your core’s ISA tier (Scalar, DSP, or MVE) at compile time, not at runtime.
Developer Workflow
import torch
from torchao.quantization.pt2e.quantize_pt2e import convert_pt2e, prepare_pt2e
from executorch.backends.cortex_m.edge_compile_config import cortex_m_edge_compile_config
from executorch.backends.cortex_m.passes.cortex_m_pass_manager import CortexMPassManager
from executorch.backends.cortex_m.quantizer.quantizer import CortexMQuantizer
from executorch.backends.cortex_m.target_config import CortexM, CortexMTargetConfig
from executorch.exir import to_edge_transform_and_lower
# 1. Export
model = MyModel().eval()
example_inputs = (torch.randn(1, 1, 49, 10),)
exported = torch.export.export(model, example_inputs)
# 2. Quantize and calibrate
quantizer = CortexMQuantizer(use_explicit_layout=True)
prepared = prepare_pt2e(exported.module(), quantizer)
for sample in calibration_data:
prepared(sample)
quantized = convert_pt2e(prepared)
# 3. Re-export the quantized model
quantized_exported = torch.export.export(quantized, example_inputs)
# 4. Lower to Edge and apply the Cortex-M passes
pass_manager = CortexMPassManager(
target_config=CortexMTargetConfig(cpu=CortexM.M55),
use_explicit_layout=True,
)
edge = to_edge_transform_and_lower(
quantized_exported,
compile_config=cortex_m_edge_compile_config(),
transform_passes=pass_manager,
)
# 5. Serialize for integration into firmware
et_program = edge.to_executorch()
with open("model.pte", "wb") as f:
f.write(et_program.buffer)
The resulting .pte binary is linked into firmware alongside the ExecuTorch runtime and CMSIS-NN library, then flashed to the device. At runtime, inference executes the precompiled graph with minimal runtime overhead and no dynamic memory allocation for tensors.
Using the Cortex-M Backend Alongside Ethos-U
Many Cortex-M MCUs pair the CPU with an Arm Ethos-U NPU such as the U55, U65, or U85. ExecuTorch’s EthosUPartitioner delegates supported operations to the NPU via the Vela compiler, and operations left outside the partition run on the Cortex-M CPU within the same graph.
The Cortex-M passes run after Ethos-U partitioning and reuse the quantization parameters already in the graph. This allows a model quantized with EthosUQuantizer to use CMSIS-NN for CPU operations whose quantization, layout and shape constraints meet the Cortex-M backend requirements. Otherwise they fall back to ExecuTorch’s portable kernels, which are functional but not accelerated.
The practical benefit is that NPU operator coverage is not an all-or-nothing gate. A model with a handful of undelegated operations can ship today on mixed CPU/NPU execution, and move more of the graph onto the NPU as coverage grows.
MLPerf Tiny Benchmark Suite
We measured inference latency and memory usage across four of the five MLPerf Tiny Inference benchmark models on the Alif Ensemble E8. These benchmark models represent a set of common deep neural networks representative of TinyML workloads. The Alif E8 integrates multiple Cortex-M55 cores alongside Ethos-U55 and U85 NPUs; we measured on a single M55 high performance core running at 400 MHz, with the Ethos-U NPUs unused. ExecuTorch’s ahead-of-time memory planning means RAM usage is deterministic and bounded, with no fragmentation risk under sustained workloads. ExecuTorch’s operator selective build was used to only include those necessary for inference, creating a minimal flash footprint. All models were INT8 quantized using the CortexMQuantizer and the Alif ML Embedded Evaluation Kit was used as a test harness. These are our own measurements rather than an official MLPerf Tiny submission, so they are not directly comparable to published results on the MLCommons leaderboard.
All four models run in under 90 KiB of RAM, three of them in under 60 KiB, and the anomaly detection autoencoder in 5.2 KiB. Code footprint stays between 15 and 37 KiB because operator selective build links only the operators each model uses.

Demo: Real-time Person Detector
To show what the Cortex-M backend enables in practice, we deployed a µYOLO person detection model on a Renesas EK-RA8D1 board, powered by the Arm Cortex-M85. The deployment fits comfortably within MCU-class memory constraints:
Task: Real-time person detection
Model: µYOLO, pruned depthwise separable CNN backbone with linear predictor head
Model size: 452 KiB (INT8 .pte file)
Total flash: 640 KiB
Peak RAM: 254 KiB
Inference latency: 24 ms per frame inference @ 480 MHz
End-to-end throughput: 12.7 FPS
Input: 128×128 RGB camera frame
This example of resource-constrained, always-on vision on the edge supports applications such as robotics sensing, occupancy monitoring, safety systems, smart cameras, and presence-triggered devices.
Just as importantly, the example demonstrates the development workflow enabled by ExecuTorch. The model definition, training code, export flow, and embedded deployment live within the same PyTorch-based ecosystem. Intermediate representations remain executable, making it possible to compare model outputs throughout export and lowering rather than treating deployment as a black box. The resulting graphs can also be inspected with tools such as Model Explorer, while ETDump exposes per-operator execution costs for profiling on the target. Together, these tools make it possible to iterate on model architecture, accuracy, memory use, and latency while continuously checking that transformations have preserved model behaviour. Instead of exporting a model and only discovering numerical or performance regressions after deployment, developers can inspect and execute intermediate stages of the transformation pipeline.
The model definition, training and export flow are available in the ExecuTorch repository. To facilitate an easy bring-up of the demo without the need for a physical target, the in-tree application is targeted for the Corstone FVP. Board-specific bring-up for the on-device demo was based on code from the ra-fsp-examples repo, configured with the RA Smart Configurator, built using the Arm GNU Toolchain, and flashed using J-Link Flash. For measurements above, the weights of the most expensive operators were placed in DTCM, and the instruction cache was enabled. This resulted in an inference latency reduction from 191 ms to 24 ms, a nearly 8x improvement.

What’s Next
Expanded mixed-precision support. Extending A8W4 and A16W8 mixed-precision support across the full operator set.
Floating-point kernels. CMSIS-NN 8.0.0 introduced fp32 and fp16 MVE kernels. Exposing them via the Cortex-M backend enables non-fully quantized models to use the same lowering path without separate deployment flows.
Broader operator coverage. Adding support for attention operators, layer normalization, and other popular architecture patterns beyond traditional CNNs, along with CMSIS-DSP operators such as FFT so feature extraction can run as part of the graph.
More end-to-end examples. Voice activity detection, gesture recognition, predictive maintenance, and streaming wake word, the fifth MLPerf Tiny benchmark, which needs test infrastructure for multi-frame inference.
Additional hardware validation. Expanding the set of validated platforms and development kits.
We’re excited about what this unlocks for the embedded ML community. If you’re deploying ML at the edge, whether on a $1 sensor node or a Cortex-M55 running voice commands, ExecuTorch now provides a direct path from PyTorch training to on-device inference.

articles.title: Crossing the Gender Binary: Modelling Gendered Reference in Science Fiction and General Fiction
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19028v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Science fiction is widely credited with unsettling gender. This article asks whether that holds at the linguistic level, in how readily gendered reference gives way to its counterpart, a neutral term, or other social category, and whether it separates the genre from general fiction. It does so by masking man/men, woman/women, and person/people across same-period science fiction and general fiction corpora and classifying RoBERTa's five likeliest substitutes by gender. Retention and displacement are permutation-tested over five resampling rounds, and the underlying sentences are read closely. Both corpora cross the gender binary in both directions, but unequally: where woman is masked, the model predicts a masculine term about twice as often as it predicts a feminine term where man is masked. Each mismatch marks a statistical surprise, a word the corpus did not expect there. Against this shared pattern, science fiction shows greater gender permeability than the general fiction corpus, placing man in feminine contexts more often than general fiction while the reverse rate holds steady. Its degendering tendency is stronger too, drawing both gendered terms toward the neutral. Beyond the binary, a masked woman also draws substitutes naming a social category and no gender far more often than a masked man does. In measuring the gender permeability of man, woman, and person in linguistic distribution and testing whether genre changes it, the study gives science fiction studies linguistic evidence for thematic claims and computational literary studies a pipeline applicable to other category vocabularies, such as race and class.

While this enables pipeline parallelism, imbalanced module latencies introduce severe pipeline bubbles that limit throughput.
L17: A natural alternative is an aggregated architecture that co-deploys all modules across all devices, eliminating bubbles by keeping every device continuously active. However, this introduces request blocking: short requests are forced to progress in lockstep with longer ones in the same batch, and newly arriving requests must wait until the entire ongoing batch completes the full workflow.

Its core mechanism, flow decomposition, decomposes long agent requests into fine-grained execution units while preserving agent semantics, allowing short and newly arriving requests to proceed without being stalled by long-running ones.
L19: Complementing this, a flow-adaptive scheduler dynamically balances the throughput gains of decomposition against its scheduling overhead. articles.title: Retrieve What Helps, Only When It Helps: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Machine Translation
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19528v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Retrieving external knowledge can improve large language model (LLM) translation by providing supplementary information such as idiom interpretations and terminology. However, existing retrieval-augmented machine translation systems typically apply predefined retrieval strategies uniformly across all inputs. We argue that translation operates in a partial-evidence regime: LLM's parametric knowledge suffices for many inputs, while external evidence benefits a subset and usually supports rather than directly provides the desired translation. This creates two challenges: deciding when to retrieve and what evidence to acquire. We introduce Selective Retrieval-Augmented Translation (SRAT), an agentic reinforcement learning framework that learns when to translate directly or retrieve, what to retrieve, and how to integrate these decisions by optimizing final translation quality. To align evidence retrieval with downstream translation quality rather than simple semantic similarity, we further develop joint Plackett--Luce optimization and translation-quality contrastive training for retriever-training. Experiments on idiom, knowledge-intensive, and document-level translation with offline or online retrieval show that SRAT consistently outperforms never- and always-retrieve baselines, and quality-aligned retriever training provides further gains when similarity-based retrieval is insufficient. The results demonstrate the benefit of treating retrieval as a learnable translation action rather than fixed preprocessing.

articles.title: GPT-6-Astra solves 49 of 50 physics research problems at $2.40 apiece
articles.text:
On the TheoPhysEval benchmark, GPT-6-Astra solves 49 of 50 unpublished theoretical physics calculations as accurately as leading specialists. In some cases where the agent seemed to fail, the experts' own reference solutions turned out to contain errors. But the researchers say physics hasn't had a breakthrough like the ones in mathematics, because the agents lack "taste." They still think autonomous, top-level AI research could arrive soon. They already see consequences for how young physicists are trained and for equal opportunity in the field.
The article GPT-6-Astra solves 49 of 50 physics research problems at $2.40 apiece appeared first on The Decoder.

articles.title: The Sum of All Summaries: PROPALIGN for Graded Proposition Salience Evaluation
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19387v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Identification and ranking of salient propositions in documents is indirectly involved in many AI tasks, but few papers define proposition salience scores clearly, make diverse data available, or evaluate models directly on the task. This paper proposes PROPALIGN, a multiple-summary-based approach for propositional salience score estimation, and releases PROPALIGNBANK, an accompanying dataset for the method with 138K alignments of over 35K propositions. We compare several approaches to salient proposition extraction in English across a broad range of spoken and written genres, and demonstrate that naively asking models for judgments leads to inconsistencies. By contrast, graded, summary-based metrics are more stable. We further observe that while single models perform worse than humans, an ensemble of models incorporating linguistic features approaches manual annotation quality ceilings. In addition, analyses of the model outputs suggest insights into how models can extract salient information with and without the use of summaries.

articles.title: NEPSEE: A Double-Annotated Benchmark for Nepali Sentiment Analysis
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19190v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Many sentiment datasets use one annotator for each item, so the test labels show the conventions of that person. We build a Nepali benchmark from two annotators who labelled the same sentences blind. They labelled 5,614 sentences from tweets of Nepali public figures on a five-point scale. We keep only the 3,189 sentences where both give the same polarity. On the three-class benchmark, NepBERTa with a fixed tokenizer gets a macro-F1 of 0.877 and IndicBERTv2 0.867. Three commercial large language models (LLMs) get 0.882 to 0.896 zero-shot, and these differences are not significant. On the five-point scale, 766 sentences have two adjacent labels, for example Pos and SPos. We accept both labels and train on both. On this task, Claude Opus 5.5 beats the best encoders by 0.10 to 0.12 macro-F1. A tokenizer audit adds a second result. The default tokenizers of three Nepali BERT models delete the non-spacing Devanagari vowel signs and the virama. When we restore the marks, macro-F1 increases by 0.084 for NepBERTa but decreases by 0.095 for a model pretrained on stripped text.

articles.title: Nvidia RTX 5090 disappears from Micro Center amid rumors of a production halt
articles.text:
Buying a GeForce RTX 5090, widely regarded as one of the best graphics cards on the market, was already extremely difficult because of price hikes and near-zero availability. Now, it will be impossible to get one. Amid recent rumors that Nvidia is halting production of the GeForce RTX 5090, another sign of the card's disappearance from the U.S. market are emerging. Micro Center has reclassified the Blackwell flagship as "Not Carried," and many of its stores have sold out. Tom's Hardware has reached out to Micro Center for comment.
Go deeper with TH Premium: GPUs
(Image credit: Noctua)
Desktop GPU Roadmap
Nvidia's Enterprise GPU Roadmap
Testing DirectStorage with GPU decompression
The GeForce RTX 30-series upgrade matrix — does your Ampere GPU need an upgrade in 2026?
Rubin in-depth
The Stout Owl: The ultimate Noctua G2 PC
The “not carried” status on a product is different from simply being out of stock. When an item is out of stock, it just means the product is temporarily unavailable, but the retailer plans to restock once new inventory arrives from the manufacturer. In contrast, a "not carried" label implies the product is no longer part of the retailer's active catalog. Therefore, the retailer does not expect to restock the item.
Custom GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards from Nvidia partners such as Asus, MSI, and Gigabyte are still listed on Micro Center’s website for now. However, a closer look shows these models are out of stock at all of the retailer’s physical locations. This widespread unavailability lends credence to the rumors that Nvidia has reportedly stopped producing the GeForce RTX 5090.
The Asus GeForce RTX 5090 ROG Astral Edition 20 is the only GeForce RTX 5090 graphics card that remains in stock at most Micro Center stores nationwide. However, there is a catch. This particular model is only available as part of the exclusive Asus ROG 20th Anniversary Bundle priced at almost $11,000.
(Image credit: Micro Center)
Adding another twist to the unfolding story, one Redditor claimed to have seen Micro Center employees remove all GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards from the shelves on October 9, just a day before rumors of a production halt began circulating online. According to the account, when the Redditor asked the store manager why, the manager refused to explain.
The Redditor wanted to buy the Asus ProArt GeForce RTX 5090; however, a Micro Center employee reportedly said the graphics card "was pulled and being sent somewhere else," offering no further explanation. Nonetheless, the Redditor noticed two GeForce RTX 5090 cards still on the shelf and allegedly begged staff to let them buy one. The Asus GeForce RTX 5090 ROG Astral Edition 20 would require selling a kidney, and no doctor or surgical equipment was nearby. Therefore, the Redditor bought the Gigabyte GeForce RTX 5090 Aorus Stealth Ice, which Micro Center generously price-matched to the cheaper Asus ProArt GeForce RTX 5090.
The fairytale ending wrapped up with the Micro Center employee reportedly telling the customer, "congrats on getting the last 5090 we will probably sell..."Bought the last 5090 at my Microcenter from r/Microcenter
Nvidia has not officially commented on the GeForce RTX 5090's situation. Despite ongoing speculation, the chipmaker still lists the GeForce RTX 5090 on its website with a “starting at $1,999” price, an MSRP we have not seen in ages. The original rumor suggested that Nvidia had stopped producing the GeForce RTX 5090, but it has not been formally confirmed as a discontinuation.
It makes sense for Nvidia to reallocate the GB202 silicon that powers the GeForce RTX 5090 into its Pro lineup, where profit margins are considerably higher. Instead of focusing on the GeForce RTX 5090 for gaming, Nvidia can channel the GB202 into products like the RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell, RTX Pro 5500, and RTX Pro 5000, where the market will pay a steep premium for the same silicon.
Sadly, times are changing, and the GeForce RTX 5090 has shifted from flagship to a soon-unattainable halo product.

articles.title: From Qualitative Text to Integrated Evidence: The Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI) Procedure
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19164v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Mixed methods research offers established strategies for integrating qualitative and quantitative evidence, but less guidance for integrating two computational representations of the same qualitative corpus. This methodological study introduces Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI), a four-step procedure for explicit and traceable integration. We present PTI using 1,203 interview paragraphs from 29 mothers in Nepal. The two representations were ontology-guided Patient Voice (PV) coding with PVminer and data-driven themes generated through non-negative matrix factorization (NMF). A theme-complete crosswalk documented convergence, divergence, and preprocessing-sensitive differences. Depression status, based on Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) scores, served as a secondary external anchor for exploratory association checks. PTI provides a structured approach for integrating computational representations of qualitative text within mixed methods research.

articles.title: Cursor Staff Investigated Whether Confidential Data Reached SpaceX for AI Training
articles.text:
In the weeks before SpaceX’s AI unit in August introduced Grok Bot, its version of a personal AI agent, engineers at Cursor discovered a potential problem.
Cursor, the AI coding startup SpaceX was then in the process of acquiring, was developing Grok Bot, and as part of that process, employees across Cursor were using the tool extensively for testing and as a part of their everyday work. In late July, engineers raised concerns that Cursor might have sent data from that internal testing—potentially including confidential information about its customers, suppliers and business partners—to SpaceX’s AI unit. One of Cursor’s lawyers warned that if word got out that the company was using the data for training, that could cause a “huge trust problem,” according to internal communications viewed by The Information.

articles.title: Why AI-Written Software Needs a Flight Simulator
articles.text:
As companies create more applications using AI, corporate officers say demand is rising for a new type of software that stress-tests those apps, simulating how they handle network problems and other disasters that humans may not think to test for—including cyberattacks by rogue AIs.
Luis Chávez, CTO of coding assistant provider Replit, says his company uses an AI-assisted software known as a deterministic simulator, a kind of flight simulator for software. The deterministic part refers to how the simulator lets companies run the same disaster test again and again so they can try out different fixes for bugs that crop up during network failures or hacking attempts.
Traditional stress-testing methods rely on developers guessing every potential problem that may arise. Merely using today’s AI models to evaluate code often produces false alarms or fake warnings, corporate executives say.

articles.title: Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run: Scale workers ahead of demand
articles.text:
The open-source Temporal execution platform is rapidly becoming a foundational layer of modern software infrastructure — especially for orchestration in distributed systems and AI agent workloads. However, deploying and scaling workers in Temporal comes with unique challenges. Workers poll for tasks instead of serving requests, so request-driven serverless platforms can be an awkward fit. This often results in running worker fleets on Kubernetes or VMs, which you have to manage and pay for continuously. You build a metrics pipeline and tune autoscaling triggers, and scaling still trails bursts because of metrics lag. Every deployment means juggling upgrades and versions, and you pay for that compute whether or not there's work in the queue.
We built Cloud Run worker pools for exactly this kind of pull-based work: Your instances connect to a queue or stream, take the next item, and process it. Starting today, Temporal Cloud, which is the fully managed version of Temporal’s open-source platform, can scale them for you. Currently in preview, Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run let you deploy your workers as a worker pool, and Temporal sizes the pool to match the work on your task queues. When there's no work, it can scale the pool to zero. There's no cluster or autoscaler to run, and your worker code stays the same.
How Cloud Run worker pools fit with Temporal
A worker pool is Cloud Run's resource for continuous background work. It has no public endpoint, and each instance is allocated CPU for its whole lifetime, which matches how a Temporal worker runs. Temporal manages your Cloud Run worker pools as follows:
Your Temporal workers run as Cloud Run worker pool instances in your project and poll Temporal Cloud for tasks.
Temporal Cloud tracks your task queues and sets the worker pool's instance count through the Cloud Run Admin API, using the IAM permissions you grant. Temporal never opens a connection to your instances, so you don't need to open ports or add firewall rules for it.
You run each build version as its own Cloud Run worker pool. An older build's worker pool can sit at zero instances until a workflow that started on it needs it again.
Your Temporal workers run in your project, under your service account, and on your network. Temporal decides how many of them run.
What you can build with Temporal Serverless Workers
The combination of Cloud Run worker pools with Temporal Serverless Workers opens up a variety of interesting use cases:
Autoscaled agentic workers: AI agents run multi-step chains of LLM reasoning and tool calls. Temporal's durable execution and Cloud Run worker pools work together here. Temporal workers spin up instantly to handle bursts of LLM steps, embeddings or API calls, then scale to zero when the queue empties. Workers get keyless access to Google Cloud AI APIs. You can also attach a GPU for inference, and the workers attached to the GPUs will still scale to zero. Temporal runs each model and tool call as a durable activity; if a worker disappears mid-step, the activity retries on another worker and the workflow continues.
Long-running Workflows: Temporal Workflows can run indefinitely, allowing for building applications that track the state of real-world resources over long periods of time. This pattern is typically known as the “Entity Pattern,” because the Workflow represents the state of some entity. However, these long-running Workflows don’t usually have consistent compute requirements: Some individual steps are short, some are long, and other times, the Workflow is sleeping, waiting for external input, such as from a human or another system. Cloud Run worker pools provide flexible compute to support this pattern: Individual steps can run for as long as is required, and Temporal will automatically scale down the worker pool when there is no work to be done.
Bursty batch work: Worker pools bill only while instances run, so a worker pool that sits idle between batch runs costs nothing while it's at zero instances. For jobs like billing runs or media transcoding, Temporal scales the pool out as batches arrive and back in once the queue drains. Your maximum instance count caps how many instances you pay for. Tasks beyond that capacity wait in the queue rather than being dropped.
Why Cloud Run worker pools for Temporal workers
Before, running Temporal workers on Cloud Run services took some workarounds:
an HTTP listener, because services expect containers to listen on a port
instance-based billing, so workers kept their CPU between requests
minimum instances, so the service didn't scale to zero
By running Temporal workers on Cloud Run worker pools, you don’t need those workarounds anymore, and you have:
No endpoint to manage. There's no public URL or load balancer to lock down, and no health-check port to implement.
Steady CPU at a lower price. Instances don't idle or throttle. Cloud Run doesn't remove instances because they look idle, so Temporal alone decides when the pool shrinks. Worker pools list at almost 40% less per vCPU-hour and GB-hour than instance-billed Cloud Run services.
Scaling without revision churn. Changing the instance count doesn't create a new revision, so Temporal can resize the pool as often as the load changes.
How Temporal manages scaling and versioning of worker pools
Temporal decides when to add capacity using one main signal: the delay between a task landing in the task queue backlog and a worker picking it up. If that delay grows, the available workers are saturated. Scaling occurs as follows:
Server-side detection: The Temporal server tracks this backlog-to-worker latency for each task queue.
Push notification: When the latency crosses its trigger conditions, the server sends a push notification to the worker controller instance.
Provisioning: The worker controller then adds capacity to the worker pool. New instances take time to start and connect before they can poll for tasks, so capacity lags behind the signal.
Because Temporal keeps spare capacity, the pool grows ahead of demand instead of after tasks pile up. Scale-in is more conservative. Temporal waits for a stabilization period after the last time a task found no available worker (90 seconds by default), and it pauses between successive reductions. Cloud Run’s configurable graceful shutdown extends shutdown from 10 seconds to 10 minutes. That gives SIGTERM-aware workers time to finish or checkpoint. The instance count stays between a minimum and a maximum that you set. If the first task after an idle period can't wait for an instance to start, set the minimum above zero.
Deploying new workflow code without breaking running executions is hard. Temporal workflows are stateful and deterministic, so if you swap their code mid-run, you get non-determinism errors. Serverless Workers on Cloud Run solve this by requiring Temporal Worker Versioning. You don't patch code with conditional branches. Instead, you deploy each Worker Deployment Version as its own worker pool deployment, identified by a deploymentName and a buildId. Using distinct worker pools solves two problems:
Workflows that started on a particular Worker Deployment Version continue to run and complete on that version.
Each Worker Deployment Version is scaled and drained individually, matching compute spend and utilization to the requirements of your application. As existing workflows complete and drain on a previous Worker Deployment Version, the underlying Worker Pool is eventually scaled down to zero automatically.
You set a versioning behavior for each Workflow type, or set a Worker-level default:
PINNED: A workflow stays on the Worker version (Build ID) it started on and finishes there. Best for short-running workflows, order processing and multi-step APIs.
AUTO_UPGRADE: A workflow moves to the new "Current" or "Target" Worker Deployment Version as you roll it out. Best for long-running workflows, such as subscription billing or tasks that run for weeks.
Learn more about configuring worker versioning here.

articles.title: Samsung Hosts Silicon Valley Future Wireless Summit 2026
articles.text:
Samsung Electronics today announced that it is bringing together global telecommunications industry partners at the Samsung Research America campus in Mountain View, California for the Silicon Valley Future Wireless Summit 2026 on Oct. 15 (local time), following Partner Day held at the same venue the prior day.
Telecommunications experts from major global operators, manufacturers, government agencies, and academia are participating in the events, with more than 100 attendees gathering to exchange insights and explore the future of next-generation networks.
▲ A view of Partner Day in Mountain View, California, on Oct 14
Samsung is discussing the evolution of software-driven networks for the AI and 6G eras, as well as ecosystem-wide collaboration that creates new value across the telecommunications industry. The company is also showcasing its leadership in 6G communication technology, sharing achievements in AI-native technologies applied to its communication systems, and providing other updates.
Collaboration To Create New Network Value in the AI Era
Partner Day fostered engaging conversations grounded in the expertise and experience of leaders from across the industry. Participants examined software-driven network strategies and ecosystem-wide collaboration as the convergence of AI and networks accelerates the evolution of network infrastructure.
Samsung opened the event with a keynote highlighting the way AI is transforming the architectural foundation that has defined telecommunications networks for more than a century. The company emphasized that, moving beyond the limitations of existing technologies, the convergence of connectivity and AI will be a key driver of new ways of communication that humanity has long imagined. Drawing on the industry’s collective intelligence, Samsung then delved into the strategic direction of network evolution in the AI era.
▲ Woojune Kim, President and Head of Networks Business at Samsung Electronics, is giving his keynote speech at Partner Day, on Oct 14.
The panel sessions centered on experiences and key lessons learned from the commercialization of virtualized networks, exploring how the ecosystem can continue to evolve. Participants also discussed ways to move beyond connectivity by developing new services and translating them into tangible business opportunities.
“Networks in the AI era are evolving into intelligent infrastructure that can understand the diverse requirements of a growing range of new services, flexibly adapt through virtualization, and deliver optimal solutions for each need,” said Angelo Jeongho Park, Executive Vice President and Head of Global Strategic Sales, Networks Business at Samsung Electronics. “Together with our industry-leading partners, Samsung has successfully commercialized virtualized networks at scale. By adding advanced AI technologies to that foundation, we will transform communications infrastructure into a new engine for growth and lead the way toward the industry’s next leap forward.”
AI-Driven Innovation in Wireless Communications
The Silicon Valley Future Wireless Summit is opening with keynote presentations from telecommunications industry experts, followed by three panel sessions — “AI-Native 6G Networks,” “Taking 6G to Space With NTN,” and “Connecting the Physical and Digital Worlds” — along with technology demonstrations. Each session includes a lecture on the topic, as well as panel discussions that facilitate dynamic exchanges between participants.
The “AI-Native 6G Networks” session positions AI as the core technology driving innovation in network performance and operational efficiency, with discussion centered on the technical challenges and global collaboration needed to evolve 6G into a truly intelligent network infrastructure.
The “Taking 6G to Space With NTN” session reviews the current status and outlook of low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellations, discusses the technical barriers of space-based communication and satellite connectivity as a potential solution, and addresses satellite communication standards and roadmaps currently under discussion within the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP).
Concluding the day is the “Connecting the Physical and Digital Worlds” session, where participants are discussing new ways to deliver next-generation user experiences by sensing physical spaces and seamlessly linking them to digital services, such as Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC) and physical AI.
The technology demonstration session showcases cutting-edge 6G core technologies jointly developed and validated by Samsung and partner companies, including AI RAN implementations, eXtreme Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (X-MIMO) systems, Distributed MIMO (D-MIMO) technologies, and ISAC. Samsung is demonstrating field validation results for the performance of AI-enabled RAN across all layers, transmission performance in the 6G candidate frequency band (7 GHz band), the user experience at cell boundaries, and sensing performance that utilizes base station infrastructure.
▲ An overview of the 6G core technology exhibition booth operated by Samsung Research at the event venue in Mountain View, Silicon Valley, on Oct. 14-15
“Together, 6G and AI-native technologies represent the next step in telecommunications, bringing people closer together than ever before,” said Jinguk Jeong, Executive Vice President and Head of the Advanced Communications Research Center at Samsung Research. “The Silicon Valley Future Wireless Summit 2026 demonstrates our commitment to closely collaborating with industry partners to advance telecommunications.”
Strengthening the Global 6G Ecosystem
Silicon Valley Future Wireless Summit 2026 and Partner Day come amid Samsung’s efforts to expand its collaboration on 6G and AI-native communication technology with global partners, including telecommunications operators, research institutes, and business groups.
This year, Samsung has initiated collaboration with LG U+ and conducted field validation with Verizon at a major international soccer fan event in Dallas, Texas, for ISAC technology development. The company is also strengthening research partnerships with major telecommunications operators globally, including NTT DOCOMO, KDDI Research, KT, SK Telecom, and SoftBank. These collaborations are part of ongoing efforts to make 6G technology a reality.
Samsung will continue to deepen collaboration with global partners and advance research at the convergence of AI and communications. By connecting its research strengths with business expertise, the company aims to translate innovation into greater value for the industry and reinforce its leadership in AI-native, 6G networks.

articles.title: CAFE: Confining Feature Distillation to Language-Routed Adapters for Compact Multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19134v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Feature distillation is usually expected to add to logit distillation. We find that this expectation does not hold for two common feature losses in compact multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR), and analyze why through their gradients. The gradient of a projection-based loss is orthogonal to the task gradient, while that of Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), a similarity-based loss, is weakly aligned with it. CKA lowers the word error rate (WER) on non-English languages, but at the expense of data-rich English. Three loss-level remedies (one trained, two probed) all fall short, and the CKA gradient overlaps with the subspace English uses in the shared encoder by 97.5% to 99.5% (about 81% by chance). Guided by this diagnosis, we propose CAFE (Confined-Adapter Feature distillation), which confines the CKA gradient to adapters that English bypasses, addressing the trade-off in the parameters rather than in the loss. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, CAFE lowers the average WER from 8.55% to 8.02%, beats an adapter-only capacity control at 8.51%, and makes English more stable across checkpoints. At 254M parameters, it trails the 0.6B teacher by 2 WER points and is competitive with much larger models across 48 test sets in 24 languages. We use 564k hours of training data and state-of-the-art models to keep the findings relevant to practice.

articles.title: EU negotiates sanction swap with China to rescue critical ASML supplier
articles.text:
The EU is currently in talks with China to lift restrictions the country imposed on Sindlhauser Materials GmbH, a German company in ASML’s supply chain, as the sanctions risk putting the company out of business. In return, the EU would remove restrictions it placed on one unnamed Chinese firm accused of aiding Russia in the war with Ukraine, according to an Oct. 14 Bloomberg report citing people familiar with the matter.
The deal was discussed during EU Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maroš Šefčovič’s visit to Beijing. The EU is expected to make the first move, with any delisting on its end requiring unanimous support from member states. Both sides also agreed to share more information and give advance warning on future export restrictions.
In July 2026, China put Sindlhauser, a German precision-manufacturing and advanced-coatings firm, on its export-control list, along with 13 other European companies, in apparent retaliation for the EU’s 21st Russia sanctions package, which sanctioned several Chinese firms accused of supplying Moscow with components that can be used to make weapons. Beijing’s official reason was the firms’ alleged dealings with Taiwan.
China’s selection of Sindlhauser is not random, as the company sits in ASML’s supply chain. According to Bloomberg, officials believe Beijing has spent the last year and a half gathering information on Western supply chains, and used the data to identify the seemingly obscure German firm as a pressure point on the world’s most important chipmaking-equipment company.
Sindlhauser relies almost entirely on Chinese rare earths and critical minerals. Therefore, the restrictions, which ban Chinese exporters from selling dual-use items to the firm, cut off its main source of input. They also prohibit foreign companies and individuals from passing on China-origin dual-use items to the firm, thus preventing Sindlhauser from simply sourcing the same materials through a third-party distributor.
After the listing, which initially sparked panic over the company’s survival, the German government and Bavaria’s state government stepped in, helping the company explore workarounds such as alternative suppliers and recycling existing materials. However, due to its heavy dependence on China, Sindlhauser now faces the risk of going out of business in the coming months if the sanctions remain.
EU officials in Brussels had been raising the case with Beijing for weeks, culminating in the delisting swap discussed during Šefčovič’s visit. The incident highlights China’s influence on several aspects of the global technology supply chain, including semiconductor manufacturing, which is critical to the AI boom. The country placed export restrictions on several rare earth metals, limiting their availability across the supply chain. Meanwhile, the West has been investing heavily in domestic supply chains to reduce reliance on China.

articles.title: ELARSpeech: A 30K-Hour Dataset Across 675 Underrepresented Languages for Long-Tail Multilingual Speech Technologies
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19388v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Massively multilingual speech modeling has made remarkable progress in recent years, yet existing training resources and benchmarks still underrepresent much of the linguistic long tail. To address this gap, we introduce ELARSpeech, a large-scale multilingual speech resource comprising 30,202 hours of speech across 675 underrepresented languages, curated from the Endangered Languages Archive. Combining human-annotated and unlabeled recordings, the corpus spans diverse recording conditions, domains, and language families. Beyond corpus construction, our experiments show how ELARSpeech supports extending ASR and TTS capabilities to diverse underrepresented languages, with further benefits from pseudo-labeling unlabeled data. At the same time, our speech representation analysis reveals remaining limitations in transferring existing multilingual models to the linguistic long tail. Together, ELARSpeech provides both a resource and a testbed for extending multilingual speech technology further into the linguistic long tail. We publicly release the dataset, all trained ASR and TTS models, and the complete data construction pipeline to facilitate research on long-tail multilingual speech technologies.

articles.title: Parallel Sparse Outputs for Tensor Compilers
articles.text:
arXiv:2610.19308v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Sparse tensor compilers are commonly used high-performance tools that optimize tensor algebra programs over notoriously complex sparse data structures. Despite the ever-increasing size and scale of sparse datasets, there exists astonishingly little research on developing a parallel sparse tensor compiler. Existing approaches fail to parallelize or make assumptions about access patterns or output formats that limit generality.
This paper presents Birdseed, the first tensor compiler to support all loop orderings over any standard sparse format in parallel. More specifically, Birdseed supports parallel sparse scatters and directly writes into list, bytemap, hash, and dense levels of fibertree sparse formats. Our approach exhibits asymptotic memory and time improvements over all previous work. We additionally demonstrate empirical speedups on challenging kernels to parallelize, such as histogram construction and SpMSpV.

articles.title: Dial Up the Cloud: NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 Controls Arrive on GeForce NOW
articles.text:
Dial in the next gaming session this GFN Thursday. New NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 controls give GeForce NOW members more choice over how supported games look and perform in the cloud, even without the latest hardware.
Then, step into the Shroud as Keen Games’ Enshrouded leaves early access with its 1.0 release, or let the bolts fly in Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2. Both are streaming on GeForce NOW at launch.
With 10 new games joining the cloud this week, members can put the new controls to work in supported titles and keep playing across supported devices without downloads, installs or expensive hardware upgrades.
Fine-Tune the Cloud With DLSS 4.5 Controls
More control, more cloud power.
NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 controls are now available on GeForce NOW, giving members more choice over how supported games look and perform in the cloud, even without the latest hardware. DLSS Super Resolution sharpens image quality, while Dynamic Multi Frame Generation delivers lower latency and reduces stutter for smoother streaming, and Ray Reconstruction enhances ray-traced visuals. In addition, Ultimate members streaming on GeForce RTX 5080-powered cloud rigs benefit from the maximum available options, including Dynamic Multi Frame Generation up to 4X.
From James Bond’s globe-trotting missions in 007 First Light — now with path tracing support — to CONTROL Resonant’s reality-bending Manhattan and the shadowy scares of Resident Evil Requiem, the controls help fine-tune supported games for image quality, responsiveness or a preferred balance between the two.
These new settings are available in the GeForce NOW app under settings, for Windows, macOS, Chrome OS and Steam OS platforms. Members can read here for more details on using the feature with their membership tier, and more information on how to get the smoothest cloud game streaming for some games on GeForce NOW.
Rise, Flameborn
Enshrouded 1.0 brings the co-op survival action role-playing game out of early access and into its full release. Rise as a Flameborn, the last ember of hope of a dying race, and venture into a vast world of survival, action and role-playing, where a corrupting fog has consumed a once-beautiful kingdom.
The title brings improvements to existing systems, alongside expansions in combat with nine new spells, new mage and archer skills, reworked wands and upgradeable Eternal spells and arrows. New enemy variants keep encounters fresh, while a new biome raises the player level cap to 50 and equipment cap to 55.
GeForce NOW offers Enshrouded 1.0 ready to play in the cloud at launch across supported devices. Skip the 60GB local install to save precious storage space, then step into the Shroud without waiting for downloads or needing to make room for the update.
Let the Bolts Fly
Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 is now streaming on GeForce NOW. The brutal, fast-paced sequel to the retro first-person shooter brings more enemies, more weapons and new ways to purge.
Picking up directly after the original game, a branching single-player campaign sends the fight to grimdark new worlds.
Choose between the formidable Sternguard Veteran Malum Caedo and the swift Sister of Battle Nyra Veyrath, each with distinct abilities, weapons and play styles. From towering hive cities to jungle mangrove swamps, new enemy types await in every biome.
GeForce NOW keeps the campaign ready in the cloud. No local rig upgrades or game installs stand between members and the fight — the Emperor’s work waits for no loading bar.
In addition, members can look for the following joining the GeForce NOW library:
Deep Dish Dungeon (New release on Steam, Oct. 13)
Planet Zoo 2 (New release on Steam, Oct. 13)
Total War: SHOGUN 2 – Complete Edition (New release on Steam, Oct. 13)
Valor Mortis (New release on Steam, Oct. 13)
Among the Trolls (New release on Steam, Oct. 14)
over the hill (New release on Steam, Oct. 14)

Beyond These Stars (New release on Steam and Xbox, Oct. 15), available on Game Pass
Tenebris Somnia (New release on Steam, Oct. 16)
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered (Xbox), available on Microsoft Store
Also this week, the performance of DLSS 5’s 3D-Guided Neural Rendering model is improving by 2X, enabling even more gamers to enjoy DLSS 5’s transformative uplift in lighting and materials at high frame rates and settings. The new, more performant DLSS 5 model will debut in NBA 2K27 on Oct. 16 on GeForce NOW, GeForce RTX 50 Series GPUs and RTX Spark laptops.
Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after they’re released and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates to announced titles.
Gamers who want to test out the new 4.5 controls and high-performance GeForce NOW cloud gaming can start with a day pass to try premium cloud gaming before committing to a membership. Better yet, the cost of the day pass can be applied toward a first monthly membership — making it easy to try GeForce RTX-powered cloud gaming with the latest releases, then level up for more.

articles.title: Muse Spark Open is Meta's answer to Qwen, GLM, and Kimi in the open-weight race
articles.text:
Meta's Muse Spark Open is a new open-weight model with 816 billion parameters that processes text, images, video, and audio with up to one million tokens of context. It performs roughly on par with the most capable open-weight Chinese AI models on benchmarks and is optimized to run locally on Apple's M5 Ultra.

articles.title: Anthropic’s Rapid But Slowing Growth Could Weigh on IPO Valuation
articles.text:
Anthropic reported rapid-but-slowing revenue growth in a meeting with potential investors in its planned initial public offering, leaving some attendees expecting the company will need to keep its valuation target in check.
At a private investor meeting Wednesday in San Francisco, the company said revenue hit $16.8 billion in the third quarter, according to people briefed on the numbers. That was a jump of about 45% from the second quarter. The figure was more than 3.6 times the company’s revenue for all of 2025. But it also represents a slower growth rate than Anthropic’s second quarter, when fevered demand for its Claude Code product drove revenue up by more than 140% from the first three months of the year.

articles.title: Malicious Russian disinformation bot traffic barely flinches after Ukraine strikes Yandex data centers and auto-migration kicks in
articles.text:
Russian bot traffic showed signs of slowing down after Ukraine bombed some of Yandex’s biggest data centers. Unfortunately, while the attacks have slowed down overall bot traffic from Russia, Cloudflare reports that malicious bots appeared to have simply transferred to other hosting ASNs like Radist and Selectel. Overall traffic on Yandex Search and Yandex.Cloud continues to stay at 10% to 15% of normal traffic levels, meaning the network remains disrupted. Cloudflare noted that traffic from the former is composed mostly of verified search crawlers indexing websites, meaning traffic from this service is mostly legitimate. On the other hand, the latter experienced a drop in malicious activities such as vulnerability scanning and probing after the data center bombings, but Cloudflare says that “high-volume automation did not vanish — it simply migrated to other hosting providers.”
This was evident with one Cloudflare customer in the gambling sector: it saw malicious bot requests from Yandex.Cloud drop to zero but started seeing the same activity being routed through other networks. “Overall, Russian bot traffic targeting gambling accounts remained essentially flat over the week, moving from 167.7 million to 170.1 million requests (+1.4%),” the company wrote in its analysis. “The automation never stopped running; the operators simply migrated their workloads to alternate cloud providers once Yandex.Cloud became unavailable.”
The company also looked at social media traffic and found a similar result — traffic from Russian-origin IPs only dropped by 0.6% in the same period while Russian bot traffic hitting “post,” “reply,” and “like” on one platform only decreased by 5.7%. Because of this, Cloudflare debunked the theory that Ukrainian strikes have caused a drop in social media manipulation, although it also noted that the scope of its analysis is limited to traffic that passed through Cloudflare services.
Since cloud-based workloads can easily be transferred between data centers, taking a few out will not necessarily end the services running out of them. Instead, owners and operators could simply migrate to another data center, which is exactly what Amazon advised its clients who have been affected by Iranian strikes on AWS Bahrain and AWS Abu Dhabi.
Cloudflare pointed out that this is why it’s difficult to defend against automated threats like bot networks — even though an IP prefix gets blocked or the physical infrastructure behind them gets annihilated, their operators could simply move their operations to another provider in a matter of hours and quickly return to normal traffic levels.

articles.title: NVIDIA Expands Advanced Technology Access for Europe’s Scientific Community Through Open Learning Resources, Collaborations and Compute
articles.text:
Much of today’s scientific progress begins with computation.
But turning accelerated computing’s potential into scientific progress — modeling climate systems, designing molecules, simulating materials and more — depends on more than breakthrough technology. Especially for smaller labs, early-career scientists or science-based startups, the hardest part of research can be everything that comes before the science: assembling tools, finding compute and building the expertise to use both.
At the AI in Science Summit in Dublin today, the European Commission launched the AI in Science Enablers Initiative, a shared framework connected to RAISE — the Resource for AI Science in Europe — that brings private-sector support closer to Europe’s research community.
Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements
NVIDIA is joining the campaign, providing:
Access to accelerated tools, models and platforms
Compute, cloud resources, data and scientific resources
Skills, training and technical support
Collaborative projects and pilots along with support for researchers and talent
Support for startups and ecosystem development
“Europe’s ambition in AI in science can only become reality if we bring together the strengths of our research community, industry and other partners,” Ekaterina Zaharieva, European Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation. “Through the AI in Science Enablers campaign, we are turning this ambition into concrete commitments that give researchers access to the tools, expertise and resources they need to innovate.”
Open Models
NVIDIA’s pledge begins with open source technology.
NVIDIA has released more than 250 open models, 250 open datasets and over 1,400 open source software projects spanning large language models, healthcare, robotics, climate science, physical AI, autonomous vehicles and scientific research. The models and datasets are available on Hugging Face and GitHub.
Building on this open ecosystem, researchers can build agentic reasoning capabilities with NVIDIA Nemotron — a family of architectures, open weights, open source models, training data and recipes — and scientific software including NVIDIA BioNeMo Agent Toolkit, NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo libraries, NVIDIA Earth-2 models and NVIDIA ALCHEMI NIM microservices to accelerate research across biology, chemistry, molecular design, weather and climate, energy, engineering, physics and material sciences.
Skills and Training
Building advanced intelligence capability across Europe requires knowledge that travels as freely as compute.
The NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute has launched a new open source courseware hub with hands-on course materials covering accelerated computing and deep learning — freely downloadable and openly licensed, with no enrollment, fees or deadline.
Modular by design, the courses can be adapted for university curricula, supercomputing center bootcamps or developer community events, and serve as a direct bridge to NVIDIA’s broader training and certification programs.
Access to Compute
NVIDIA is collaborating with cloud infrastructure partners and European national AI factories — including in France, Spain and Sweden — to open new routes for startups and small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to access sovereign European compute and services.
The NVIDIA Inception program for startups provides access to compute resources and technical support, lowering the barrier to entry for startups seeking high-performance infrastructure and technological education.
AI2F in France is the first AI factory to have collaborated with the Inception program for four months, demonstrating strong results.
The BSC AI Factory ran a pilot initiative and is now rolling out its first full accelerator program, with growing interest from other European national AI factories in replicating the model in 2027. Beyond startup support, this program is designed to contribute to a broader strategic objective: building self-sustaining AI ventures in Spain and Europe.
Sweden AI Factory, one of Europe’s 19 EuroHPC-funded AI factories, announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to open its infrastructure and expertise to Inception startups and SMEs enterprises across sectors including life and material sciences, autonomous systems and gaming.
Finally, EuroHPC supercomputing centers such as CINECA and JSC provide academia and startups with free access to NVIDIA GPU infrastructure and services for open research. NVIDIA complements this access with office hours, bootcamps and hackathons that help researchers fine-tune models on their own datasets.
As an example, NVIDIA is co-organizing an European AI hackathon this month alongside Austrian Scientific Computing, the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre, the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart and The Cyprus Institute, for Pharos-CY.
AI Infrastructure Expansion
To top it all off, NVIDIA is powering Europe’s most ambitious expansion of AI infrastructure to date, with 35 supercomputers currently in development across the continent — the largest single-year buildout of supercomputing capacity Europe has ever seen.
Together, these systems will equip over 3 million researchers with next-generation infrastructure, accelerating discovery across domains from climate science and drug development to materials research and beyond.
Explore NVIDIA technologies for science and open source courseware, and find hands-on training through the NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute.

articles.title: ASML struggling to keep up with demand for chipmaking equipment as AI spending continues to boom
articles.text:
ASML has said that the unprecedented spending and investment brought about by the artificial intelligence (AI) boom is not slowing down at all, as customers are already lining up to place orders for its advanced chipmaking tools for 2029 and 2030, according to a Reuters report citing ASML's Q3 2026 earnings published today, October 14. ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet said that the company would struggle to meet the demand despite plans announced in July to raise capacity by 30% in 2027 and another 30% in 2028. The company also confirmed on Wednesday that it will raise prices starting in 2027, with the full effect showing in 2028.

The Dutch company's comments follow its Q3 2026 earnings report, which detailed a net profit of €4.96 billion on net sales of €11.7 billion. It projects Q4 sales of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion ($15.9 billion to $17 billion), boosting its full-year sales projections from at least €43 billion to €44-45 billion. ASML's shares rose 2% on Wednesday, up almost 70% so far this year, with its  €586 billion market valuation making it Europe's largest firm by market cap.
According to Reuters, there had been concerns that the AI investment boom was losing steam. However, positive projections from the largest manufacturer of the tools for making AI chips and advanced semiconductors signal that chipmakers will keep expanding, sustaining demand across the AI industry well into the foreseeable future. "There were concerns that the AI trade was running out of steam," Gordon Kerr, European macro strategist at KBRA, said. "Demand for chips remains strong, and infrastructure spending is likely to continue well into 2027."
ASML's customers include logic chip manufacturers such as Samsung, Intel, and TSMC, which manufactures chips for Nvidia, all of whom are heavily investing in increasing chip production. Memory chip makers SK Hynix and Micron ⁠have also announced expansion plans that involve ASML machines. Meanwhile, the company's CFO Roger Dassen said it is "still kicking the tires on the exact size of that (Terafab) opportunity," referring to Elon Musk's 100 million square feet semiconductor manufacturing facility that aims to output millions of logic and memory chips. Terafab will reportedly receive its first EUV chipmaking tool from ASML in mid-2027.
ASML's order book reflects a wave of spending across the AI industry. As of April this year, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta reportedly collectively planned to spend $725 billion on capex in 2026, up 77% from last year's record $410 billion. Since then, Alphabet has raised its 2026 capex guidance from $180–190 billion to $195–205 billion, Amazon from $200 billion to $220 billion, and Meta has raised the floor of its range from $125 billion to $130 billion, keeping its $145 billion ceiling. Some of the spending reflects rising chip prices, with Microsoft CFO Amy Hood attributing $25 billion of the company's record capex budget to higher prices for memory chips and other components. Still, analysts such as Gartner expect global AI spending to rise 49.5% in 2026 to $2.7 trillion and another 36.2% in 2027.
